Answer: It is a function on A with Range = {1, 2, 3, 5}; it is not onto

Q: Q8(ii). Let A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}, check whether the set {(1, 1), (2, 4), (3, 2), (4, 1), (5, 3)} is a function on A. In case it is a function, indicate its range. Which function is onto?

Ans: Given: A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} and f = {(1, 1), (2, 4), (3, 2), (4, 1), (5, 3)}
By definition, a relation on A is a function if Dom f = A and there is no repetition in the first element of its ordered pairs.
The first elements are 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5, all distinct, so: Dom f = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} = A
Both conditions are satisfied, so f is a function on A.
Its range is the set of second elements: Range f = {1, 4, 2, 3} = {1, 2, 3, 4}
Range f ≠ A, because 5 ∈ A is not the image of any element.
By definition, a function is onto if Range f = A, so f is not onto.
Answer: It is a function on A with Range = {1, 2, 3, 4}; it is not onto

Q: Q8(iii). Let A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}, check whether the set {(1, 2), (2, 1), (3, 1), (4, 4), (5, 5)} is a function on A. In case it is a function, indicate its range. Which function is onto?

Ans: Given: A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} and f = {(1, 2), (2, 1), (3, 1), (4, 4), (5, 5)}
By definition, a relation on A is a function if Dom f = A and there is no repetition in the first element of its ordered pairs.
The first elements are 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5, all distinct, so: Dom f = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} = A
Both conditions are satisfied, so f is a function on A.
Its range is the set of second elements: Range f = {2, 1, 4, 5} = {1, 2, 4, 5}
Range f ≠ A, because 3 ∈ A is not the image of any element.
By definition, a function is onto if Range f = A, so f is not onto.
Answer: It is a function on A with Range = {1, 2, 4, 5}; it is not onto
Note: The Answers given at the end of the book print the range of this set as {1, 2, 3, 5}, but 3 never occurs as a second element and 4 does, so {1, 2, 4, 5} is the correct range.

Q: Q8(iv). Let A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}, check whether the set {(1, 2), (2, 3), (1, 4), (3, 5)} is a function on A. In case it is a function, indicate its range. Which function is onto?

Ans: Given: A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} and f = {(1, 2), (2, 3), (1, 4), (3, 5)}
By definition, a relation on A is a function if Dom f = A and there is no repetition in the first element of its ordered pairs.
The first elements are 1, 2, 1 and 3: the element 1 is repeated, in (1, 2) and (1, 4).
Also: Dom f = {1, 2, 3} ≠ A, because 4 and 5 have no pairs.
Both conditions of being a function fail.
Answer: It is not a function. (Of the four sets in this question, the functions in (i), (ii) and (iii) are all not onto, so no function here is onto.)

Q: Q9(i). If X = {-6, -5, -4, -3}, Y = {1, 2, 3, 4} then write a one-one function from X to Y

Ans: Given: X = {-6, -5, -4, -3} and Y = {1, 2, 3, 4}
By definition, a one-one function pairs every element of X with exactly one element of Y, with no repetition in the first element and no repetition in the second element.
One such function is: f = {(-6, 1), (-5, 2), (-4, 3), (-3, 4)}
Check: Dom f = {-6, -5, -4, -3} = X, no first element is repeated, and the second elements 1, 2, 3, 4 are all distinct.
Note: Several answers are possible.
Answer: f = {(-6, 1), (-5, 2), (-4, 3), (-3, 4)} is a one-one function from X to Y

Q: Q9(ii). If X = {-6, -5, -4, -3}, Y = {1, 2, 3, 4} then write an onto function from X to Y

Ans: Given: X = {-6, -5, -4, -3} and Y = {1, 2, 3, 4}
By definition, an onto function from X to Y must have Range f = Y, that is, every element of Y must be the image of some element of X.
One such function is: f = {(-6, 2), (-5, 1), (-4, 4), (-3, 3)}
Check: Dom f = {-6, -5, -4, -3} = X, no first element is repeated, and Range f = {1, 2, 3, 4} = Y.
Note: Several answers are possible.
Answer: f = {(-6, 2), (-5, 1), (-4, 4), (-3, 3)} is an onto function from X to Y

Q: Q9(iii). If X = {-6, -5, -4, -3}, Y = {1, 2, 3, 4} then write a function which is one-one and onto from X to Y

Ans: Given: X = {-6, -5, -4, -3} and Y = {1, 2, 3, 4}
By definition, a function that is one-one and onto (bijective) has no repetition in the second element and Range f = Y.
One such function is: f = {(-6, 4), (-5, 3), (-4, 2), (-3, 1)}
Check: Dom f = {-6, -5, -4, -3} = X, no first element is repeated, the second elements 4, 3, 2, 1 are all distinct, and Range f = {1, 2, 3, 4} = Y.
Note: Several answers are possible.
Answer: f = {(-6, 4), (-5, 3), (-4, 2), (-3, 1)} is one-one and onto (bijective) from X to Y

Q: Q9(iv). If X = {-6, -5, -4, -3}, Y = {1, 2, 3, 4} then write a function from X to Y which is neither one-one nor onto

Ans: Given: X = {-6, -5, -4, -3} and Y = {1, 2, 3, 4}
The function must have a repeated second element (so it is not one-one) and its range must not be all of Y (so it is not onto), while Dom f = X with no first element repeated.
One such function is: f = {(-6, 1), (-5, 1), (-4, 2), (-3, 2)}
Check: Dom f = {-6, -5, -4, -3} = X and no first element is repeated, so f is a function.
The second elements 1 and 2 are repeated, so f is not one-one.
Range f = {1, 2} ≠ Y, so f is not onto.
Note: Several answers are possible.
Answer: f = {(-6, 1), (-5, 1), (-4, 2), (-3, 2)} is neither one-one nor onto

Q: Project. (-2, 5), (-1, 0), (0, 1), and (2, 5) is a function. If the x-values and y-values of this function are switched, the relation that results is not a function. Provide an example of a function that will still be a function if the x-values and y-values are switched

Ans: Given function: f = {(-2, 5), (-1, 0), (0, 1), (2, 5)}
Switching the x-values and y-values gives: {(5, -2), (0, -1), (1, 0), (5, 2)}
In the switched relation the first element 5 is repeated, in (5, -2) and (5, 2), so it is not a function.
This happened because in f the second element 5 was repeated; after switching, that repetition appears in the first elements.
So the switched relation is a function exactly when the original function has no repeated second element, that is, when the function is one-one.
Example: take the one-one function g = {(1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 4)}
Its second elements 2, 3 and 4 are all distinct.
Switching the x-values and y-values gives: {(2, 1), (3, 2), (4, 3)}
The first elements of the switched relation are 2, 3 and 4, all distinct, and its domain is the whole of its first set.
So the switched relation is also a function.
Answer: For example g = {(1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 4)}; switching gives {(2, 1), (3, 2), (4, 3)}, which is still a function

A function from A to A
An onto function from A to B
mcqs.why: Step 1: first elements 1, 2, 3 are distinct and Dom R = {1, 2, 3} = A, so R is a function from A to B. Step 2: Range R = {4, 5} = B, so R is onto (the repeated second element 4 shows it is not one-one). The book's keyed answer is confirmed correct.

mcqs.q: Q1(ii). If A has two elements and B has three elements, then number of binary relations in A × B is ______
mcqs.why: Step 1: A × B contains 2 × 3 = 6 ordered pairs. Step 2: a binary relation is any subset of A × B, and a set of 6 elements has 2⁶ subsets, so the number of binary relations is 2⁶. The book's keyed answer is confirmed correct.

mcqs.q: Q1(iii). Which one of the following is an example of disjoint sets?
mcqs.why: Disjoint sets have no common element. Check each pair: the first pair is the same set; the second pair shares 2, 4 and 6; the third pair shares 9; only {0, 4, 8, 12} and {6, 10, 14, 18} share nothing, so they are disjoint. The book's keyed answer is confirmed correct.

mcqs.q: Q1(iv). If the universal set U = {x | x is a positive odd integer less than 30}, R = {1, 5, 7}, and S = {1, 3, 7, 11, 13}, how many elements are in (R ∩ S)'?
mcqs.why: Step 1: U = {1, 3, 5, ..., 29} has 15 elements. Step 2: R ∩ S = {1, 5, 7} ∩ {1, 3, 7, 11, 13} = {1, 7}, which has 2 elements. Step 3: (R ∩ S)' has 15 - 2 = 13 elements. The book's keyed answer is confirmed correct.

mcqs.q: Q1(v). If f is a function from A to B, then f is onto function if
options: second element of all ordered pairs contained in f is not repeated
mcqs.why: By definition a function f from A to B is onto exactly when every element of B is an image, that is when Range f = B. Dom f = A is part of being a function at all, and unrepeated second elements describe being one-one. The book's keyed answer is confirmed correct.

The domain is the set of first elements of the pairs: from (0, 0) take 0, from (8, 2) take 8, from (10, 3) take 10, and from (14, 12) take 14. Hence Dom R = {0, 8, 10, 14}; the set {0, 2, 3, 12} is the range. The book's keyed answer is confirmed correct.

mcqs.q: If U = {natural numbers up to 100}, A = {positive even numbers up to 100} and B = {positive odd numbers up to 100}, then A' ∪ B' = ?
If U = {natural numbers up to 100}, A = {positive even numbers up to 100} and B = {positive odd numbers up to 100}, then A' ∩ B' = ?
mcqs.why: Step 1: A' = {1, 3, 5, ... 99} and B' = {2, 4, 6, ... 100}. Step 2: A' ∩ B' = {1, 3, 5, ... 99} ∩ {2, 4, 6, ... 100}; no number is both odd and even, so there is no common element and the result is ∅.
Step 1: B ∩ C = {2, 4, 6} ∩ {2, 5, 9} = {2}. Step 2: A ∩ (B ∩ C) = {1, 2, 3, 5, 7} ∩ {2} = {2}, which equals (A ∩ B) ∩ C = {2} ∩ {2, 5, 9} = {2}, verifying associativity of intersection.

Step 1: B ∩ C = {2, 4, 6} ∩ {2, 5, 9} = {2}. Step 2: A ∪ (B ∩ C) = {1, 2, 3, 5, 7} ∪ {2} = {1, 2, 3, 5, 7}, since 2 is already in A; this equals (A ∪ B) ∩ (A ∪ C), verifying distribution of union over intersection.

Step 1: B ∪ C = {2, 4, 6} ∪ {2, 5, 9} = {2, 4, 5, 6, 9}. Step 2: A ∩ (B ∪ C) = {1, 2, 3, 5, 7} ∩ {2, 4, 5, 6, 9} = {2, 5}, which equals (A ∩ B) ∪ (A ∩ C) = {2} ∪ {2, 5}, verifying distribution of intersection over union.
