Q: Project (e). The following scores were made on a 60-item test: 25, 30, 34, 37, 41, 42, 46, 49, 53, 26, 31, 34, 37, 41, 42, 46, 50, 53, 28, 31, 35, 37, 41, 43, 47, 51, 54, 29, 33, 36, 38, 41, 44, 48, 52, 54, 30, 33, 36, 39, 41, 44, 48, 52, 55, 30, 33, 37, 40, 42, 45, 48, 52. Find the cumulative frequencies.

Ans: Step 1: Use the frequency table of part (b) and add the frequencies successively.
Class interval 24.5 - 25.5: f = 1, c.f. = 1
Class interval 25.5 - 27.5: f = 1, c.f. = 1 + 1 = 2
Class interval 27.5 - 29.5: f = 2, c.f. = 2 + 2 = 4
Class interval 29.5 - 31.5: f = 5, c.f. = 4 + 5 = 9
Class interval 31.5 - 33.5: f = 3, c.f. = 9 + 3 = 12
Class interval 33.5 - 35.5: f = 3, c.f. = 12 + 3 = 15
Class interval 35.5 - 37.5: f = 6, c.f. = 15 + 6 = 21
Class interval 37.5 - 39.5: f = 2, c.f. = 21 + 2 = 23
Class interval 39.5 - 41.5: f = 6, c.f. = 23 + 6 = 29
Class interval 41.5 - 43.5: f = 4, c.f. = 29 + 4 = 33
Class interval 43.5 - 45.5: f = 3, c.f. = 33 + 3 = 36
Class interval 45.5 - 47.5: f = 3, c.f. = 36 + 3 = 39
Class interval 47.5 - 49.5: f = 4, c.f. = 39 + 4 = 43
Class interval 49.5 - 51.5: f = 2, c.f. = 43 + 2 = 45
Class interval 51.5 - 53.5: f = 5, c.f. = 45 + 5 = 50
Class interval 53.5 - 55.5: f = 3, c.f. = 50 + 3 = 53
The last cumulative frequency, 53, equals the total number of scores.
Answer: The cumulative frequencies are 1, 2, 4, 9, 12, 15, 21, 23, 29, 33, 36, 39, 43, 45, 50, 53 for the successive class intervals.

Q: Project (f). The following scores were made on a 60-item test: 25, 30, 34, 37, 41, 42, 46, 49, 53, 26, 31, 34, 37, 41, 42, 46, 50, 53, 28, 31, 35, 37, 41, 43, 47, 51, 54, 29, 33, 36, 38, 41, 44, 48, 52, 54, 30, 33, 36, 39, 41, 44, 48, 52, 55, 30, 33, 37, 40, 42, 45, 48, 52. Draw the ogive.

Ans: Step 1: Use the cumulative frequencies of part (e) at the upper class boundaries.
Upper boundaries and cumulative frequencies: 25.5 (1); 27.5 (2); 29.5 (4); 31.5 (9); 33.5 (12); 35.5 (15); 37.5 (21); 39.5 (23); 41.5 (29); 43.5 (33); 45.5 (36); 47.5 (39); 49.5 (43); 51.5 (45); 53.5 (50); 55.5 (53).
Graph: Ogive (less than cumulative frequency polygon). Draw the horizontal axis for the upper class boundaries from 24.5 to 55.5 with a scale of 2 units per step, and the vertical axis for the cumulative frequency from 0 to 53 with a scale of 5 units per step. Plot the points (25.5, 1), (27.5, 2), (29.5, 4), (31.5, 9), (33.5, 12), (35.5, 15), (37.5, 21), (39.5, 23), (41.5, 29), (43.5, 33), (45.5, 36), (47.5, 39), (49.5, 43), (51.5, 45), (53.5, 50), (55.5, 53), starting from (24.5, 0) on the horizontal axis, and join them in order by a freehand curve (or straight line segments).
Answer: The ogive rises through the 16 points listed above, ending at (55.5, 53).

Q: Project (g). The following scores were made on a 60-item test: 25, 30, 34, 37, 41, 42, 46, 49, 53, 26, 31, 34, 37, 41, 42, 46, 50, 53, 28, 31, 35, 37, 41, 43, 47, 51, 54, 29, 33, 36, 38, 41, 44, 48, 52, 54, 30, 33, 36, 39, 41, 44, 48, 52, 55, 30, 33, 37, 40, 42, 45, 48, 52. Find the range of the data.

Ans: Range = Largest value - Smallest value
Step 1: Find the largest score in the data.
Largest score = 55
Step 2: Find the smallest score in the data.
Smallest score = 25
Step 3: Subtract.
Range = 55 - 25
Range = 30
Answer: The range of the data is 30.

Q: Project (h). The following scores were made on a 60-item test: 25, 30, 34, 37, 41, 42, 46, 49, 53, 26, 31, 34, 37, 41, 42, 46, 50, 53, 28, 31, 35, 37, 41, 43, 47, 51, 54, 29, 33, 36, 38, 41, 44, 48, 52, 54, 30, 33, 36, 39, 41, 44, 48, 52, 55, 30, 33, 37, 40, 42, 45, 48, 52. Find the mean of the data.

Ans: Arithmetic mean for grouped data: x̄ = (Σfᵢxᵢ)/(Σfᵢ), using the frequency table of part (b), where x is the class mark.
Step 1: Multiply each class mark by its frequency.
Class mark 25: f = 1, fx = 25
Class mark 26.5: f = 1, fx = 26.5
Class mark 28.5: f = 2, fx = 57
Class mark 30.5: f = 5, fx = 152.5
Class mark 32.5: f = 3, fx = 97.5
Class mark 34.5: f = 3, fx = 103.5
Class mark 36.5: f = 6, fx = 219
Class mark 38.5: f = 2, fx = 77
Class mark 40.5: f = 6, fx = 243
Class mark 42.5: f = 4, fx = 170
Class mark 44.5: f = 3, fx = 133.5
Class mark 46.5: f = 3, fx = 139.5
Class mark 48.5: f = 4, fx = 194
Class mark 50.5: f = 2, fx = 101
Class mark 52.5: f = 5, fx = 262.5
Class mark 54.5: f = 3, fx = 163.5
Step 2: Find the totals.
Σf = 53
Σfx = 25 + 26.5 + 57 + 152.5 + 97.5 + 103.5 + 219 + 77 + 243 + 170 + 133.5 + 139.5 + 194 + 101 + 262.5 + 163.5 = 2165
Step 3: Substitute in the formula.
x̄ = (2165)/(53)
x̄ = 40.85
Note: From the raw scores, Σx = 2164 and the mean is (2164)/(53) = 40.83; the small difference is due to grouping.
Answer: The mean of the grouped data is 40.85.

Q: Project (i). The following scores were made on a 60-item test: 25, 30, 34, 37, 41, 42, 46, 49, 53, 26, 31, 34, 37, 41, 42, 46, 50, 53, 28, 31, 35, 37, 41, 43, 47, 51, 54, 29, 33, 36, 38, 41, 44, 48, 52, 54, 30, 33, 36, 39, 41, 44, 48, 52, 55, 30, 33, 37, 40, 42, 45, 48, 52. Find the standard deviation of the data.

Ans: Variance: σ² = (Σfᵢxᵢ²)/(Σfᵢ) - x̄², and S.D = √(Variance), using the grouped table of part (b) with x̄ = 40.85 from part (h).
Step 1: Find fx² for each class mark.
Class mark 25: f = 1, x² = 625, fx² = 625
Class mark 26.5: f = 1, x² = 702.25, fx² = 702.25
Class mark 28.5: f = 2, x² = 812.25, fx² = 1624.5
Class mark 30.5: f = 5, x² = 930.25, fx² = 4651.25
Class mark 32.5: f = 3, x² = 1056.25, fx² = 3168.75
Class mark 34.5: f = 3, x² = 1190.25, fx² = 3570.75
Class mark 36.5: f = 6, x² = 1332.25, fx² = 7993.5
Class mark 38.5: f = 2, x² = 1482.25, fx² = 2964.5
Class mark 40.5: f = 6, x² = 1640.25, fx² = 9841.5
Class mark 42.5: f = 4, x² = 1806.25, fx² = 7225
Class mark 44.5: f = 3, x² = 1980.25, fx² = 5940.75
Class mark 46.5: f = 3, x² = 2162.25, fx² = 6486.75
Class mark 48.5: f = 4, x² = 2352.25, fx² = 9409
Class mark 50.5: f = 2, x² = 2550.25, fx² = 5100.5
Class mark 52.5: f = 5, x² = 2756.25, fx² = 13781.25
Class mark 54.5: f = 3, x² = 2970.25, fx² = 8910.75
Step 2: Find the totals: Σf = 53, Σfx = 2165 (from part (h)), Σfx² = 91996.
Step 3: Substitute in the variance formula (the variance is found in full in part (j)).
Variance = (91996)/(53) - (40.8491)² = 1735.7736 - 1668.6455 = 67.1281 ≈ 67.13
Step 4: Take the positive square root.
S.D = √(67.1281) = 8.19
Note: From the raw scores the standard deviation is 8.14; the small difference is due to grouping.
Answer: The standard deviation of the grouped data is 8.19.

Q: Project (j). The following scores were made on a 60-item test: 25, 30, 34, 37, 41, 42, 46, 49, 53, 26, 31, 34, 37, 41, 42, 46, 50, 53, 28, 31, 35, 37, 41, 43, 47, 51, 54, 29, 33, 36, 38, 41, 44, 48, 52, 54, 30, 33, 36, 39, 41, 44, 48, 52, 55, 30, 33, 37, 40, 42, 45, 48, 52. Find the variance of the data.

Ans: Variance: σ² = (Σfᵢxᵢ²)/(Σfᵢ) - x̄², using the grouped table of part (b).
Step 1: From parts (h) and (i), the totals are Σf = 53, Σfx = 2165 and Σfx² = 91996, with the fx² values: 625, 702.25, 1624.5, 4651.25, 3168.75, 3570.75, 7993.5, 2964.5, 9841.5, 7225, 5940.75, 6486.75, 9409, 5100.5, 13781.25, 8910.75 for the successive class marks 25, 26.5, 28.5, 30.5, 32.5, 34.5, 36.5, 38.5, 40.5, 42.5, 44.5, 46.5, 48.5, 50.5, 52.5, 54.5.
Step 2: Find the mean.
x̄ = (Σfx)/(Σf) = (2165)/(53) = 40.8491
Step 3: Substitute in the formula.
Variance = (91996)/(53) - (40.8491)²
Variance = 1735.7736 - 1668.6455
Variance = 67.1281
Note: From the raw scores the variance is 66.29; the small difference is due to grouping.
Answer: The variance of the grouped data is 67.13.

mcqs.q: Q1(i). At the end of each question, four circles are given. Fill in the correct circle only. (i) The difference between upper limit of two consecutive classes in a frequency table is called.
mcqs.why: The class interval is the size of a class, found as the difference between the upper limits (or the lower limits) of two consecutive classes, for example 59 - 49 = 10 for the classes 40 - 49 and 50 - 59.

mcqs.q: Q1(ii). A cumulative frequency histogram is also called
mcqs.why: A cumulative frequency graph or polygon is called an ogive. It is plotted at the class boundaries against the cumulative frequencies, unlike an ordinary histogram or a frequency polygon.

mcqs.q: Q1(iii). The number of times a value appears on a set of data is called
mcqs.why: By definition, the frequency of a value is the number of times that value appears in the data; for example in the homework data the value 2 hours appears 9 times, so its frequency is 9.

mcqs.q: Q1(iv). The data below represents the number of televisions that 11 students have in their homes. Find the mode of the data. 3, 2, 1, 1, 1, 5, 3, 1, 2, 1, 2.
mcqs.why: Count each value: 1 appears 5 times, 2 appears 3 times, 3 appears 2 times and 5 appears once. The most frequent value is 1, so the mode is 1.

mcqs.q: Q1(v). In which data set are the mean, median, mode, and range all the same number?
mcqs.why: For 1, 2, 3, 3, 2, 1, 2: mean = (1 + 2 + 3 + 3 + 2 + 1 + 2) / 7 = 14 / 7 = 2; arranged as 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3 the median (4th item) is 2; the mode is 2 (three times); range = 3 - 1 = 2. All four equal 2, which no other option achieves.

mcqs.q: Q1(vi). The nth root of product of 'n' number of values is called.
mcqs.why: The geometric mean of n values is the nth root of their product, equivalently antilog((sum of log x) / n). That is the definition asked for here, not the arithmetic or harmonic mean.

mcqs.q: Q1(vii). In a set of data 63, 65, 66, 67, 69, median is
mcqs.why: The data are already in order and n = 5 is odd, so median = size of the ((n + 1) / 2)th item = size of the 3rd item = 66.

mcqs.q: Q1(viii). In a set of data 41, 43, 47, 51, 57, 52, 59 median is
mcqs.why: Arrange in ascending order: 41, 43, 47, 51, 52, 57, 59. Here n = 7 is odd, so median = size of the ((7 + 1) / 2)th item = size of the 4th item = 51. The book printed the option 47 twice and a none-type option; those two options have been replaced by 52 and 59, keeping the keyed answer 51.

mcqs.q: Q1(ix). In the given set of data 5, 7, 7, 5, 3, 7, 2, 8, 2 mode is
mcqs.why: Count each value: 7 appears 3 times, 5 appears 2 times, 2 appears 2 times, and 3 and 8 appear once each. The most frequent value is 7, so the mode is 7.

mcqs.q: Q1(x). In the given set of data 5, 5, 5, 5, 5, 5, 5 the standard deviation is
mcqs.why: Mean = (5 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 5) / 7 = 35 / 7 = 5. Every deviation x - mean = 5 - 5 = 0, so sum of (x - mean) squared = 0, variance = 0 / 7 = 0 and S.D. = sqrt(0) = 0. The book's none-type option has been replaced by 2; the keyed answer 0 is unchanged.

mcqs.q: Q1(xi). The average pocket money of 30 student is Rs. 20/-. The total amount in the class is
mcqs.why: Mean = total / n, so total = mean x n = 20 x 30 = Rs. 600/-.

mcqs.q: Q1(xii). The sum of 30 observations is 1500. Its average will be
mcqs.why: Average = (sum of observations) / (number of observations) = 1500 / 30 = 50. The book keyed its none-type option because 50 was not printed among the options; that option has been replaced by the true value 50, keeping the same keyed position.

mcqs.q: Q1(xiii). The difference of the largest and smallest value in the data is called
mcqs.why: By definition, range = largest value - smallest value; for example for the items 11 to 23 the range is 23 - 11 = 12. The mean, mode and standard deviation are different measures.

mcqs.q: Q1(xiv). The formula (Σx)/(n) determines
mcqs.why: The arithmetic mean is defined as x-bar = (sum of all values) / (number of values) = (sum of x) / n; for example 378 / 10 = 37.8 for the weights in Exercise 6.3 Q1.

mcqs.q: Q1(xv). What is the difference between the mean of Set B and the median of Set A? Set A: {2, -1, 7, -4, 11, 3}; Set B: {12, 5, -3, 4, 7, -7}.
mcqs.why: Set B mean = (12 + 5 - 3 + 4 + 7 - 7) / 6 = 18 / 6 = 3. Set A arranged is -4, -1, 2, 3, 7, 11 with n = 6 even, so median = (1/2) x (3rd item + 4th item) = (1/2) x (2 + 3) = 2.5. Difference = 3 - 2.5 = 0.5.

mcqs.q: Q1(xvi). (Σf(x - x̄)²)/(Σf) is called ______
mcqs.why: Variance is the mean of the squared deviations from the mean, weighted by frequency: variance = (sum of f(x - x-bar) squared) / (sum of f). The standard deviation is the square root of this quantity, not the quantity itself.

mcqs.q: Q1(xvii). The most frequent value in the data is called its ______
mcqs.why: By definition the mode is the value that occurs most frequently in the data; for example 71 occurs three times in Exercise 6.3 Q6, more than any other value, so it is the mode.

lessons.title: Try This (Section 7.1.1)
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • In the sexagesimal system, 1° = 60' and 1' = 60"
  • One minute in degrees is 1' = (1/60)°
  • One second in degrees is 1" = (1/3600)°
  • To change D°M'S" to decimal degrees, add the degrees to minutes × (1/60) plus seconds × (1/3600)
  • 5°42'30" = 5 + 0.7 + 0.008333 ≈ 5.7083°
  • To change decimal degrees to D°M'S", multiply the fractional degree part by 60 to get minutes, then multiply any fractional minute part by 60 to get seconds
  • 72.18° = 72°10'48"

Solved Exercises

Q: Q1(i). Convert 5°42'30" to decimal degree notation.

Ans: In the sexagesimal system, 1° = 60' and 1' = 60", so 1' = (1/60)° and 1" = (1/3600)°.
5°42'30" = [5 + 42 × (1/60) + 30 × (1/3600)]°
42 × (1/60) = 0.7
30 × (1/3600) = 0.008333
5°42'30" = [5 + 0.7 + 0.008333]°
Answer: 5°42'30" ≈ 5.7083°

Q: Q1(ii). Convert 72.18° to D°M'S" form.

Ans: Note: in the book this item is printed in a garbled form ("Convert 72.18° D°M'S" to decimal degree notation"); the evident intended question, solved here, is to convert 72.18° to D°M'S" form.
In the sexagesimal system, 1° = 60' and 1' = 60".
72.18° = 72° + (0.18)°
(0.18)° = (0.18 × 60)' = (10.8)'
72.18° = 72° + 10' + (0.8)'
(0.8)' = (0.8 × 60)" = 48"
Answer: 72.18° = 72°10'48"

mcqs.q: In the sexagesimal system, 1' is equal to how many degrees?
mcqs.why: Since 1° = 60', divide both sides by 60: 1' = 1°/60 = (1/60)°. This is the conversion used for every minute in the exercise.

mcqs.q: In the sexagesimal system, 1" is equal to how many degrees?
mcqs.why: First 1' = (1/60)°, and 1" = (1/60) of a minute. So 1" = (1/60) × (1/60)° = (1/3600)°, exactly as used in the solved item.

mcqs.q: When converting 5°42'30" to decimal form, what is the value of 42 × (1/60)?
mcqs.why: Substitute the minutes into the formula: minutes contribute 42 × (1/60) = 42/60 = 0.7. This 0.7 is then added to the 5 degrees.

mcqs.q: When converting 5°42'30" to decimal form, what is 30 × (1/3600)?
mcqs.why: Substitute the seconds into the formula: seconds contribute 30 × (1/3600) = 30/3600 = 0.008333. This small part is added after the minutes part 0.7.

mcqs.q: 5°42'30" in decimal degree notation is approximately:
mcqs.why: Use decimal = degrees + minutes×(1/60) + seconds×(1/3600). Substitute: 5 + 42×(1/60) + 30×(1/3600) = 5 + 0.7 + 0.008333 = 5.708333°, so approximately 5.7083°.

mcqs.q: To convert 72.18° to D°M'S" form, the angle is first split as:
mcqs.why: The whole-number part is already degrees: 72.18° = 72° + (0.18)°. Only the fractional part (0.18)° is converted further into minutes and seconds.

mcqs.q: In converting 72.18°, the step (0.18 × 60)' gives:
mcqs.why: Multiply the fractional degree part by 60 because 1° = 60': (0.18)° = (0.18 × 60)' = (10.8)'. So there are 10 whole minutes and 0.8 of a minute left.

mcqs.q: In converting 72.18°, the remaining (0.8)' is equal to how many seconds?
mcqs.why: Multiply the fractional minute part by 60 because 1' = 60": (0.8)' = (0.8 × 60)" = 48". This supplies the seconds part of the final answer.

mcqs.q: 72.18° in D°M'S" form is:
How many minutes are there in 1° in the sexagesimal system?
mcqs.why: The sexagesimal system divides one degree into 60 equal parts called minutes, so 1° = 60'. Each minute is then divided into 60 seconds.

lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • For D°M'S" to decimal: decimal degrees = degrees + minutes × (1/60) + seconds × (1/3600)
  • 8°15'35" ≈ 8.2597°, 39°48'55" ≈ 39.8153°, 84°19'10" ≈ 84.3194° and 18°6'21" ≈ 18.1058°
  • For decimal to D°M'S": multiply the fractional degree part by 60 for minutes, then the fractional minute part by 60 for seconds
  • 42.25° = 42°15', 57.325° = 57°19'30", 12.9956° = 12°59'44" and 32.625° = 32°37'30"
  • π radians = 180°, so 1 radian = (180/π)° ≈ 57.296°
  • 180° = π radians, so 1° = (π/180) radians ≈ 0.01745 radians
  • 2 radians ≈ 114.59°, (5π/3) radians = 300°, (π/6) radians = 30° and (-3π/4) radians = -135°
  • 45° = π/4 radians, 120° = 2π/3 radians and -210° = -7π/6 radians

Solved Exercises

Q: Q1(i). Convert the angle 8°15'35" from D°M'S" form to decimal form.

Ans: In the sexagesimal system, 1' = (1/60)° and 1" = (1/3600)°.
8°15'35" = [8 + 15 × (1/60) + 35 × (1/3600)]°
15 × (1/60) = 0.25
35 × (1/3600) = 0.009722
8°15'35" = [8 + 0.25 + 0.009722]°
Answer: 8°15'35" ≈ 8.2597°

Q: Q1(ii). Convert the angle 39°48'55" from D°M'S" form to decimal form.

Ans: In the sexagesimal system, 1' = (1/60)° and 1" = (1/3600)°.
39°48'55" = [39 + 48 × (1/60) + 55 × (1/3600)]°
48 × (1/60) = 0.8
55 × (1/3600) = 0.015278
39°48'55" = [39 + 0.8 + 0.015278]°
Answer: 39°48'55" ≈ 39.8153°

Q: Q1(iii). Convert the angle 84°19'10" from D°M'S" form to decimal form.

Ans: In the sexagesimal system, 1' = (1/60)° and 1" = (1/3600)°.
84°19'10" = [84 + 19 × (1/60) + 10 × (1/3600)]°
19 × (1/60) = 0.316667
10 × (1/3600) = 0.002778
84°19'10" = [84 + 0.316667 + 0.002778]°
Answer: 84°19'10" ≈ 84.3194°
Note: the book's printed answer key gives 39.8152°, which is the truncated value; correctly rounded to 4 decimal places the value is 39.8153°.

Q: Q1(iv). Convert the angle 18°6'21" from D°M'S" form to decimal form.

Ans: In the sexagesimal system, 1' = (1/60)° and 1" = (1/3600)°.
18°6'21" = [18 + 6 × (1/60) + 21 × (1/3600)]°
6 × (1/60) = 0.1
21 × (1/3600) = 0.005833
18°6'21" = [18 + 0.1 + 0.005833]°
Answer: 18°6'21" ≈ 18.1058°

Q: Q2(i). Convert the angle 42.25° from decimal form to D°M'S" form.

Ans: In the sexagesimal system, 1° = 60' and 1' = 60".
42.25° = 42° + (0.25)°
(0.25)° = (0.25 × 60)' = 15'
42.25° = 42° + 15'
Answer: 42.25° = 42°15'
Note: in the book the angle is printed as "4225°" with the decimal point missing; the book's own answer 42°15' confirms that 42.25° is intended.

Q: Q2(ii). Convert the angle 57.325° from decimal form to D°M'S" form.

Ans: In the sexagesimal system, 1° = 60' and 1' = 60".
57.325° = 57° + (0.325)°
(0.325)° = (0.325 × 60)' = (19.5)'
57.325° = 57° + 19' + (0.5)'
(0.5)' = (0.5 × 60)" = 30"
Answer: 57.325° = 57°19'30"

Q: Q2(iii). Convert the angle 12.9956° from decimal form to D°M'S" form.

Ans: In the sexagesimal system, 1° = 60' and 1' = 60".
12.9956° = 12° + (0.9956)°
(0.9956)° = (0.9956 × 60)' = (59.736)'
12.9956° = 12° + 59' + (0.736)'
(0.736)' = (0.736 × 60)" = 44.16" ≈ 44"
Answer: 12.9956° = 12°59'44"

Q: Q2(iv). Convert the angle 32.625° from decimal form to D°M'S" form.

Ans: In the sexagesimal system, 1° = 60' and 1' = 60".
32.625° = 32° + (0.625)°
(0.625)° = (0.625 × 60)' = (37.5)'
32.625° = 32° + 37' + (0.5)'
(0.5)' = (0.5 × 60)" = 30"
Answer: 32.625° = 32°37'30"

Q: Q3(i). Convert 2 radians into the measure of degrees.

Ans: The relation between radians and degrees is π radians = 180°, so 1 radian = (180/π)° ≈ 57.296°.
2 radians = 2 × (180/π)°
2 radians = (360/3.14159)°
2 radians ≈ 114.59°
Answer: 2 radians = 114.6°

Q: Q3(ii). Convert (5π/3) radians into the measure of degrees.

Ans: The relation between radians and degrees is π radians = 180°, so 1 radian = (180/π)° ≈ 57.296°.
(5π/3) radians = (5π/3) × (180°/π)
(5π/3) radians = 5 × 60°
Answer: (5π/3) radians = 300°

Q: Q3(iii). Convert (π/6) radians into the measure of degrees.

Ans: The relation between radians and degrees is π radians = 180°, so 1 radian = (180/π)° ≈ 57.296°.
(π/6) radians = (π/6) × (180°/π)
(π/6) radians = 180°/6
Answer: (π/6) radians = 30°

Q: Q3(iv). Convert (-3π/4) radians into the measure of degrees.

Ans: The relation between radians and degrees is π radians = 180°, so 1 radian = (180/π)° ≈ 57.296°.
(-3π/4) radians = (-3π/4) × (180°/π)
(-3π/4) radians = -3 × 45°
Answer: (-3π/4) radians = -135°

Q: Q4(i). Convert 45° in terms of radians.

Ans: The relation between degrees and radians is 180° = π radians, so 1° = (π/180) radians ≈ 0.01745 radians.
45° = 45 × (π/180) radians
45° = (45π/180) radians
Answer: 45° = (π/4) radians

Q: Q4(ii). Convert 120° in terms of radians.

Ans: The relation between degrees and radians is 180° = π radians, so 1° = (π/180) radians ≈ 0.01745 radians.
120° = 120 × (π/180) radians
120° = (120π/180) radians
Answer: 120° = (2π/3) radians

Q: Q4(iii). Convert -210° in terms of radians.

Ans: The relation between degrees and radians is 180° = π radians, so 1° = (π/180) radians ≈ 0.01745 radians.
-210° = -210 × (π/180) radians
-210° = (-210π/180) radians
Answer: -210° = (-7π/6) radians

Q: Q4(iv). Convert 60°35'48" in terms of radians.

Ans: The relation between degrees and radians is 180° = π radians, so 1° = (π/180) radians ≈ 0.01745 radians.
First convert 60°35'48" to decimal form, using 1' = (1/60)° and 1" = (1/3600)°.
60°35'48" = [60 + 35 × (1/60) + 48 × (1/3600)]°
60°35'48" = [60 + 0.58333 + 0.01333]° = 60.5967°
60.5967° = 60.5967 × (π/180) radians
60.5967° = (60.5967 × 3.14159/180) radians
Answer: 60°35'48" = ≈ 1.0576 radians

mcqs.q: 8°15'35" in decimal form is approximately:
39°48'55" in decimal form is approximately:
42.25° in D°M'S" form is:
mcqs.why: Split 42.25° = 42° + (0.25)°. Convert the fraction: (0.25 × 60)' = 15'. There is no fractional minute left, so 42.25° = 42°15'.

mcqs.q: 57.325° in D°M'S" form is:
2 radians in degrees is approximately:
mcqs.why: Use degrees = radians × (180/π). Substitute: 2 × (180/π)° = (360/3.14159)° ≈ 114.59°, which the source rounds in its final answer to 114.6°.

mcqs.q: (5π/3) radians in degrees is:
mcqs.why: Use degrees = radians × (180°/π). Substitute: (5π/3) × (180°/π) = 5 × (180°/3) = 5 × 60° = 300°, after cancelling π.

mcqs.q: (π/6) radians in degrees is:
mcqs.why: Use degrees = radians × (180°/π). Substitute: (π/6) × (180°/π) = 180°/6 = 30°, after cancelling π from numerator and denominator.

mcqs.q: (-3π/4) radians in degrees is:
mcqs.why: Use degrees = radians × (180°/π). Substitute: (-3π/4) × (180°/π) = -3 × (180°/4) = -3 × 45° = -135°, keeping the negative sign throughout.

mcqs.q: 45° in radians is:
mcqs.why: Use radians = degrees × (π/180). Substitute: 45 × (π/180) = 45π/180, and dividing numerator and denominator by 45 gives π/4 radians.

mcqs.q: -210° in radians is:
mcqs.why: Use radians = degrees × (π/180). Substitute: -210 × (π/180) = -210π/180, and dividing numerator and denominator by 30 gives -7π/6 radians.

lessons.title: Exercise 7.2
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Arc length is l = rθ, where θ must be measured in radians
  • Radian measure is defined by θ = l/r, so θ = l/r and r = l/θ
  • Area of a sector is A = (1/2)r²θ, where θ is measured in radians
  • An angle given in degrees must first be converted with 1° = (π/180) radians before using l = rθ or A = (1/2)r²θ
  • One complete revolution is 2π radians, so 3.5 revolutions = 7π radians
  • At 3 o'clock the hands of a watch are a quarter turn apart, giving a circular measure of π/2 radians
  • For r = 2 cm and θ = π/6, l = π/3 ≈ 1.047 cm; for r = 6 cm and θ = 30°, l = π ≈ 3.1416 cm

Solved Exercises

Q: Q1(i). Find l when θ = (π/6) radian, r = 2 cm.

Ans: The length of an arc is given by l = rθ, where θ is measured in radians.
Here r = 2 cm and θ = π/6 radians.
l = rθ
l = 2 × (π/6)
l = π/3
l ≈ 1.047
Answer: l ≈ 1.047 cm

Q: Q1(ii). Find l when θ = 30°, r = 6 cm.

Ans: The length of an arc is given by l = rθ, where θ must be measured in radians.
First convert 30° to radians, using 1° = (π/180) radians.
θ = 30° = 30 × (π/180) radians = (π/6) radians ≈ 0.5236 radians
l = rθ
l = 6 × (π/6)
l = π
l ≈ 3.1416
Answer: l ≈ 3.1416 cm

Q: Q1(iii). Find l when θ = (4π/6) radian, r = 6 cm.

Ans: The length of an arc is given by l = rθ, where θ is measured in radians.
Here r = 6 cm and θ = 4π/6 radians.
l = rθ
l = 6 × (4π/6)
l = 4π
l ≈ 12.566
Answer: l ≈ 12.57 cm

Q: Q2(i). Find θ when l = 5 cm, r = 2 cm.

Ans: By the definition of radian measure, θ = l/r, so l = rθ gives θ = (l)/(r).
Here l = 5 cm and r = 2 cm.
θ = (l)/(r)
θ = 5/2
Answer: θ = 2.5 radians

Q: Q2(ii). Find θ when l = 30 cm, r = 6 cm.

Ans: By the definition of radian measure, θ = l/r.
Here l = 30 cm and r = 6 cm.
θ = (l)/(r)
θ = 30/6
Answer: θ = 5 radians

Q: Q2(iii). Find θ when l = 6 cm, r = 2.87 cm.

Ans: By the definition of radian measure, θ = l/r.
Here l = 6 cm and r = 2.87 cm.
θ = (l)/(r)
θ = 6/2.87
θ ≈ 2.0906
Answer: θ ≈ 2.09 radians

Q: Q3(i). Find r when θ = (π/6) radians, l = 2 cm.

Ans: The length of an arc is given by l = rθ, so r = (l)/(θ).
Here l = 2 cm and θ = π/6 radians.
r = (l)/(θ)
r = 2/(π/6)
r = 12/π
r ≈ 3.8197
Answer: r ≈ 3.82 cm

Q: Q3(ii). Find r when θ = 3(1/2) radians, l = (4/7) m.

Ans: The length of an arc is given by l = rθ, so r = (l)/(θ).
Here l = 4/7 m and θ = 3(1/2) = 7/2 radians.
r = (l)/(θ)
r = (4/7)/(7/2)
r = (4/7) × (2/7)
r = 8/49
r ≈ 0.1633
Answer: r ≈ 0.1633 m
Note: the book's printed answer key gives this value with the unit "cm"; since l is given in metres, the radius is in metres.

Q: Q3(iii). Find r when θ = (3π/4) radians, l = 15 cm.

Ans: The length of an arc is given by l = rθ, so r = (l)/(θ).
Here l = 15 cm and θ = 3π/4 radians.
r = (l)/(θ)
r = 15/(3π/4)
r = 60/(3π)
r = 20/π
r ≈ 6.366
Answer: r ≈ 6.366 cm

Q: Q4. Find the area of sector of a circle whose radius is 4 m, with central angle 12 radian.

Ans: The area of a sector is given by A = (1/2)r²θ, where θ is measured in radians.
Here r = 4 m and θ = 12 radians (as printed).
A = (1/2)r²θ
A = (1/2) × (4)² × 12
A = (1/2) × 16 × 12
A = 8 × 12
Answer: A = 96 m²

Q: Q5(i). The arc of a circle subtends an angle of 30° at the centre. The radius of circle is 5 cm. Find the length of the arc.

Ans: The length of an arc is given by l = rθ, where θ must be measured in radians.
First convert 30° to radians, using 1° = (π/180) radians.
θ = 30° = 30 × (π/180) radians = (π/6) radians ≈ 0.5236 radians
l = rθ
l = 5 × (π/6)
l = 5π/6
l ≈ 2.618
Answer: l ≈ 2.618 cm
Note: the book's printed answer key gives 2.625 cm, obtained by using the rough conversion 1° ≈ 0.0175 radians (θ ≈ 0.525 radians).

Q: Q5(ii). The arc of a circle subtends an angle of 30° at the centre. The radius of circle is 5 cm. Find the area of sector formed.

Ans: The area of a sector is given by A = (1/2)r²θ, where θ must be measured in radians.
First convert 30° to radians, using 1° = (π/180) radians.
θ = 30° = (π/6) radians ≈ 0.5236 radians
A = (1/2)r²θ
A = (1/2) × (5)² × (π/6)
A = (1/2) × 25 × 0.5236
A ≈ 6.545
Answer: A ≈ 6.545 cm²
Note: the book's printed answer key gives 6.5625 cm², obtained by using the rough conversion 1° ≈ 0.0175 radians (θ ≈ 0.525 radians).

Q: Q6. An arc of a circle subtends an angle of 2 radian at the centre. If the area of sector formed is 64 cm², find the radius of the circle.

Ans: The area of a sector is given by A = (1/2)r²θ, where θ is measured in radians.
Here A = 64 cm² and θ = 2 radians.
A = (1/2)r²θ
64 = (1/2) × r² × 2
64 = r²
r = √(64)
r = 8
Answer: r = 8 cm

Q: Q7. In a circle of radius 10 m, find the distance travelled by a point moving on this circle if the point makes 3.5 revolutions. (3.5 revolutions = 7π).

Ans: The distance travelled along the circle is the arc length, given by l = rθ, where θ is measured in radians.
One complete revolution = 2π radians.
3.5 revolutions = 3.5 × 2π radians = 7π radians
Here r = 10 m and θ = 7π radians.
l = rθ
l = 10 × 7π
Answer: distance travelled = 70π m ≈ 219.9 m

Q: Q8. What is the circular measure of the angle between the hands of the watch at 3 o'clock.

Ans: Circular measure means the measure in radians.
At 3 o'clock the minute hand points at 12 and the hour hand points at 3.
The two hands are a quarter of a complete turn apart.
A complete turn = 360° = 2π radians.
Angle between the hands = (1/4) × 360° = 90°
Convert 90° to radians, using 1° = (π/180) radians.
90° = 90 × (π/180) radians
Answer: the circular measure is (π/2) radians

Q: Q9. What is the length of the arc APB?

Ans: Diagram: a circle with centre O; radius OB = 8 cm drawn horizontally to point B on the right of the circle; radius OA drawn vertically down to point A at the bottom of the circle; ∠AOB = 90°, shown by a right-angle mark at O; P is a point on the minor arc AB on the right side of the circle, so arc APB is the minor arc from A to B passing through P.
The length of an arc is given by l = rθ, where θ must be measured in radians.
Here r = 8 cm and θ = 90°.
Convert 90° to radians, using 1° = (π/180) radians.
θ = 90° = 90 × (π/180) radians = (π/2) radians
l = rθ
l = 8 × (π/2)
l = 4π
l ≈ 12.57
Answer: length of arc APB = 4π cm ≈ 12.57 cm

Q: Q10. Find the area of the sector OPR.

Ans: Diagram: sector OPR with vertex at O at the bottom; the two radii are OP, going up to the left to point P, and OR, going up to the right to point R; radius OR = 6 cm; the angle at O between OP and OR is ∠POR = 60°; P and R are joined by the arc PR at the top.
The area of a sector is given by A = (1/2)r²θ, where θ must be measured in radians.
Here r = 6 cm and θ = 60°.
Convert 60° to radians, using 1° = (π/180) radians.
θ = 60° = 60 × (π/180) radians = (π/3) radians
A = (1/2)r²θ
A = (1/2) × (6)² × (π/3)
A = (1/2) × 36 × (π/3)
A = 6π
A ≈ 18.85
Answer: area of sector OPR = 6π cm² ≈ 18.85 cm²

mcqs.q: The formula for the length of an arc, with θ in radians, is:
mcqs.why: The arc length formula used throughout the exercise is l = rθ. The angle θ must be in radians; if it is given in degrees it is converted first using 1° = (π/180) radians.

mcqs.q: Find l when r = 2 cm and θ = π/6 radian.
mcqs.why: Use l = rθ. Substitute r = 2 and θ = π/6: l = 2 × (π/6) = π/3. Numerically π/3 ≈ 3.14159/3 ≈ 1.047, so l ≈ 1.047 cm.

mcqs.q: Find l when r = 6 cm and θ = 30°.
mcqs.why: First convert: θ = 30° = 30 × (π/180) = π/6 radians. Then l = rθ = 6 × (π/6) = π ≈ 3.1416, so l ≈ 3.1416 cm.

mcqs.q: Find θ when l = 5 cm and r = 2 cm.
mcqs.why: By the definition of radian measure, θ = l/r. Substitute l = 5 and r = 2: θ = 5/2 = 2.5, so θ = 2.5 radians.

mcqs.q: Find θ when l = 30 cm and r = 6 cm.
mcqs.why: By the definition of radian measure, θ = l/r. Substitute l = 30 and r = 6: θ = 30/6 = 5, so θ = 5 radians.

mcqs.q: Find r when l = 2 cm and θ = π/6 radians.
mcqs.why: From l = rθ, rearrange to r = l/θ. Substitute: r = 2/(π/6) = 2 × (6/π) = 12/π ≈ 12/3.14159 ≈ 3.8197, so r ≈ 3.82 cm.

mcqs.q: Find r when l = 15 cm and θ = 3π/4 radians.
The area of a sector with r = 4 m and θ = 12 radians is:
mcqs.why: Use A = (1/2)r²θ. Substitute r = 4 and θ = 12: A = (1/2) × (4)² × 12 = (1/2) × 16 × 12 = 8 × 12 = 96, so A = 96 m², using the angle exactly as printed.

mcqs.q: An arc subtends 30° at the centre of a circle of radius 5 cm. The length of the arc is approximately:
A sector has area 64 cm² and central angle 2 radians. Its radius is:
mcqs.why: Use A = (1/2)r²θ. Substitute A = 64 and θ = 2: 64 = (1/2) × r² × 2 = r². Taking the square root, r = √64 = 8, so r = 8 cm.

lessons.title: Exercise 7.3
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Coterminal angles have the same initial and terminal sides and differ by a multiple of 360°, or of 2π in radians
  • A positive coterminal angle is found by adding 360° (or 2π); a negative one by subtracting 360° (or 2π)
  • Coterminal angles of 55° are 415° and -305°; of -45° are 315° and -405°
  • Coterminal angles of π/6 are 13π/6 and -11π/6; of -3π/4 are 5π/4 and -11π/4
  • Quadrant ranges: 0°–90° 1st, 90°–180° 2nd, 180°–270° 3rd, 270°–360° 4th (equivalently 0–π/2, π/2–π, π–3π/2, 3π/2–2π)
  • 8π/5 = 288° lies in the 4th quadrant; 75° lies in the 1st quadrant; 103° lies in the 2nd quadrant
  • An angle outside 0°–360° is first reduced by adding or subtracting multiples of 360°: -818° is coterminal with 262° (3rd quadrant) and -5π/4 is coterminal with 3π/4 = 135° (2nd quadrant)

Solved Exercises

Q: Q1(i). Find coterminal angles of the angle 55°.

Ans: Coterminal (general) angles have the same initial and terminal sides and differ by a multiple of 360°, or of 2π if the angle is in radians.
To find a positive coterminal angle, add 360° (or 2π); to find a negative coterminal angle, subtract 360° (or 2π).
Positive coterminal angle: 55° + 360° = 415°
Negative coterminal angle: 55° - 360° = -305°
Answer: the coterminal angles of 55° are 415° and -305°

Q: Q1(ii). Find coterminal angles of the angle -45°.

Ans: Coterminal (general) angles have the same initial and terminal sides and differ by a multiple of 360°, or of 2π if the angle is in radians.
To find a positive coterminal angle, add 360° (or 2π); to find a negative coterminal angle, subtract 360° (or 2π).
Positive coterminal angle: -45° + 360° = 315°
Negative coterminal angle: -45° - 360° = -405°
Answer: the coterminal angles of -45° are 315° and -405°

Q: Q1(iii). Find coterminal angles of the angle (π/6).

Ans: Coterminal (general) angles have the same initial and terminal sides and differ by a multiple of 360°, or of 2π if the angle is in radians.
To find a positive coterminal angle, add 360° (or 2π); to find a negative coterminal angle, subtract 360° (or 2π).
Positive coterminal angle: (π/6) + 2π = (13π/6)
Negative coterminal angle: (π/6) - 2π = (-11π/6)
Answer: the coterminal angles of (π/6) are (13π/6) and (-11π/6)

Q: Q1(iv). Find coterminal angles of the angle (-3π/4).

Ans: Coterminal (general) angles have the same initial and terminal sides and differ by a multiple of 360°, or of 2π if the angle is in radians.
To find a positive coterminal angle, add 360° (or 2π); to find a negative coterminal angle, subtract 360° (or 2π).
Positive coterminal angle: (-3π/4) + 2π = (5π/4)
Negative coterminal angle: (-3π/4) - 2π = (-11π/4)
Answer: the coterminal angles of (-3π/4) are (5π/4) and (-11π/4)

Q: Q2(i). State the quadrant in which the angle (8π/5) lies.

Ans: An angle in standard position lies in the quadrant where its terminal side lies: 0° < θ < 90° (0 < θ < π/2) in the 1st quadrant, 90° < θ < 180° (π/2 < θ < π) in the 2nd quadrant, 180° < θ < 270° (π < θ < 3π/2) in the 3rd quadrant and 270° < θ < 360° (3π/2 < θ < 2π) in the 4th quadrant.
Convert (8π/5) radians to degrees, using π radians = 180°.
(8π/5) = (8 × 180°)/5 = 288°
270° < 288° < 360°, so the terminal side is in the 4th quadrant.
Answer: (8π/5) lies in the 4th quadrant

Q: Q2(ii). State the quadrant in which the angle 75° lies.

Ans: An angle in standard position lies in the quadrant where its terminal side lies: 0° < θ < 90° (0 < θ < π/2) in the 1st quadrant, 90° < θ < 180° (π/2 < θ < π) in the 2nd quadrant, 180° < θ < 270° (π < θ < 3π/2) in the 3rd quadrant and 270° < θ < 360° (3π/2 < θ < 2π) in the 4th quadrant.
0° < 75° < 90°, so the terminal side is in the 1st quadrant.
Answer: 75° lies in the 1st quadrant

Q: Q2(iii). State the quadrant in which the angle -818° lies.

Ans: An angle in standard position lies in the quadrant where its terminal side lies: 0° < θ < 90° (0 < θ < π/2) in the 1st quadrant, 90° < θ < 180° (π/2 < θ < π) in the 2nd quadrant, 180° < θ < 270° (π < θ < 3π/2) in the 3rd quadrant and 270° < θ < 360° (3π/2 < θ < 2π) in the 4th quadrant.
Add multiples of 360° to bring the angle between 0° and 360°.
-818° + 360° = -458°
-458° + 360° = -98°
-98° + 360° = 262°
So -818° is coterminal with 262°.
180° < 262° < 270°, so the terminal side is in the 3rd quadrant.
Answer: -818° lies in the 3rd quadrant

Q: Q2(iv). State the quadrant in which the angle (-5π/4) lies.

Ans: An angle in standard position lies in the quadrant where its terminal side lies: 0° < θ < 90° (0 < θ < π/2) in the 1st quadrant, 90° < θ < 180° (π/2 < θ < π) in the 2nd quadrant, 180° < θ < 270° (π < θ < 3π/2) in the 3rd quadrant and 270° < θ < 360° (3π/2 < θ < 2π) in the 4th quadrant.
Add 2π to bring the angle between 0 and 2π.
(-5π/4) + 2π = (3π/4)
Convert (3π/4) radians to degrees, using π radians = 180°.
(3π/4) = (3 × 180°)/4 = 135°
90° < 135° < 180°, so the terminal side is in the 2nd quadrant.
Answer: (-5π/4) lies in the 2nd quadrant

Q: Q2(v). State the quadrant in which the angle 103° lies.

Ans: An angle in standard position lies in the quadrant where its terminal side lies: 0° < θ < 90° (0 < θ < π/2) in the 1st quadrant, 90° < θ < 180° (π/2 < θ < π) in the 2nd quadrant, 180° < θ < 270° (π < θ < 3π/2) in the 3rd quadrant and 270° < θ < 360° (3π/2 < θ < 2π) in the 4th quadrant.
90° < 103° < 180°, so the terminal side is in the 2nd quadrant.
Answer: 103° lies in the 2nd quadrant

mcqs.q: Coterminal angles differ from each other by a multiple of:
mcqs.why: Coterminal angles share the same initial and terminal sides, so one is reached from the other after whole complete turns. Each complete turn is 360° (or 2π in radians), so they differ by a multiple of 360°.

mcqs.q: A positive coterminal angle of 55° is:
mcqs.why: Add one complete turn: positive coterminal angle = 55° + 360° = 415°. Adding 360° does not change the terminal side, so 415° is coterminal with 55°.

mcqs.q: A negative coterminal angle of 55° is:
mcqs.why: Subtract one complete turn: negative coterminal angle = 55° - 360° = -305°. Subtracting 360° does not change the terminal side, so -305° is coterminal with 55°.

mcqs.q: The coterminal angles of -45° found in the exercise are:
mcqs.why: Add 360° for the positive one: -45° + 360° = 315°. Subtract 360° for the negative one: -45° - 360° = -405°. So the pair is 315° and -405°.

mcqs.q: A positive coterminal angle of π/6 is:
mcqs.why: In radians add one complete turn 2π: π/6 + 2π = π/6 + 12π/6 = 13π/6. Adding 2π does not change the terminal side, so 13π/6 is coterminal with π/6.

mcqs.q: A negative coterminal angle of -3π/4 is:
mcqs.why: In radians subtract one complete turn 2π: -3π/4 - 2π = -3π/4 - 8π/4 = -11π/4. Subtracting 2π does not change the terminal side, so -11π/4 is coterminal with -3π/4.

mcqs.q: The angle 8π/5 lies in which quadrant?
mcqs.why: Convert to degrees: (8π/5) × (180°/π) = (8 × 180°)/5 = 288°. Since 270° < 288° < 360°, the terminal side is in the range of the 4th quadrant.

mcqs.q: The angle 75° lies in which quadrant?
mcqs.why: Compare with the quadrant ranges: 0° < 75° < 90°. Angles strictly between 0° and 90° have their terminal side in the 1st quadrant, so 75° lies in the 1st quadrant.

mcqs.q: The angle -818° lies in which quadrant?
mcqs.why: Reduce by adding 360° repeatedly: -818° + 360° = -458°; -458° + 360° = -98°; -98° + 360° = 262°. Since 180° < 262° < 270°, the terminal side is in the 3rd quadrant.

mcqs.q: The angle -5π/4 lies in which quadrant?
mcqs.why: Add 2π to bring it into range: -5π/4 + 2π = -5π/4 + 8π/4 = 3π/4. Convert: (3π/4) × (180°/π) = 135°. Since 90° < 135° < 180°, it lies in the 2nd quadrant.

lessons.title: Try This (Section 7.3.5)
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • On the unit circle, sin θ = y and cos θ = x for a point P(x, y) on the terminal side of θ
  • sin θ < 0 means y < 0, which happens in the 3rd and 4th quadrants
  • cos θ < 0 means x < 0, which happens in the 2nd and 3rd quadrants
  • The quadrant common to sin θ < 0 and cos θ < 0 is the 3rd quadrant
  • In the 3rd quadrant both coordinates are negative: x < 0 and y < 0

Solved Exercises

Q: Q1. If sin θ < 0 and cos θ < 0, name the quadrant in which angle θ lies.

Ans: On the unit circle, sin θ = y and cos θ = x, where P(x, y) is the point on the terminal side of θ.
sin θ < 0 means y < 0, so θ lies in the 3rd or 4th quadrant, where only sin θ and cosec θ are negative together with cos θ in one of them.
cos θ < 0 means x < 0, so θ lies in the 2nd or 3rd quadrant.
The quadrant common to both conditions is the 3rd quadrant, where x < 0 and y < 0.
Answer: θ lies in the 3rd quadrant

mcqs.q: If sin θ < 0 and cos θ < 0, in which quadrant does θ lie?
mcqs.why: On the unit circle sin θ = y and cos θ = x. sin θ < 0 gives y < 0 (3rd or 4th quadrant) and cos θ < 0 gives x < 0 (2nd or 3rd quadrant). The only quadrant satisfying both is the 3rd quadrant.

mcqs.q: On the unit circle, sin θ is equal to which coordinate of P(x, y)?
mcqs.why: For a point P(x, y) on the terminal side on the unit circle, the source defines sin θ = y and cos θ = x. So sin θ is the y-coordinate of the point.

mcqs.q: On the unit circle, cos θ is equal to which coordinate of P(x, y)?
mcqs.why: For a point P(x, y) on the terminal side on the unit circle, the source defines cos θ = x and sin θ = y. So cos θ is the x-coordinate of the point.

mcqs.q: sin θ < 0 tells us that the y-coordinate of P is:
mcqs.why: Since sin θ = y on the unit circle, the inequality sin θ < 0 is the same as y < 0. A negative y places the point below the x-axis, in the 3rd or 4th quadrant.

mcqs.q: cos θ < 0 tells us that the x-coordinate of P is:
mcqs.why: Since cos θ = x on the unit circle, the inequality cos θ < 0 is the same as x < 0. A negative x places the point to the left of the y-axis, in the 2nd or 3rd quadrant.

mcqs.q: sin θ < 0 on its own is possible in which pair of quadrants?
mcqs.why: sin θ = y, and y < 0 below the x-axis. The quadrants below the x-axis are the 3rd quadrant (x < 0, y < 0) and the 4th quadrant (x > 0, y < 0), so sin θ < 0 in the 3rd and 4th quadrants.

mcqs.q: cos θ < 0 on its own is possible in which pair of quadrants?
mcqs.why: cos θ = x, and x < 0 to the left of the y-axis. The quadrants to the left of the y-axis are the 2nd quadrant (x < 0, y > 0) and the 3rd quadrant (x < 0, y < 0), so cos θ < 0 in the 2nd and 3rd quadrants.

mcqs.q: In the 3rd quadrant, the signs of x and y are:
mcqs.why: The 3rd quadrant is the region to the left of the y-axis and below the x-axis. Left gives x < 0 and below gives y < 0, which is exactly why both sin θ = y and cos θ = x are negative there.

mcqs.q: Which quadrant is common to the conditions y < 0 and x < 0?
mcqs.why: y < 0 holds in the 3rd and 4th quadrants, while x < 0 holds in the 2nd and 3rd quadrants. Comparing the two lists, the single common quadrant is the 3rd quadrant.

mcqs.q: If θ is in the 3rd quadrant, then sin θ and cos θ are both:
mcqs.why: In the 3rd quadrant x < 0 and y < 0. Since cos θ = x and sin θ = y on the unit circle, both ratios take negative values for a 3rd-quadrant angle.

lessons.title: Try This (Section 7.3.6)
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • For P(x, y) on the terminal side with r = OP: sin θ = y/r, cos θ = x/r, tan θ = y/x, cot θ = x/y, sec θ = r/x and cosec θ = r/y
  • Given sin θ = 1/2, take y = 1 and r = 2
  • By Pythagoras, x² = r² - y² = 4 - 1 = 3, so x = ±√3
  • In the 2nd quadrant x < 0, so x = -√3 is chosen
  • For sin θ = 1/2 in the 2nd quadrant: cos θ = -√3/2, tan θ = -1/√3, cot θ = -√3, sec θ = -2/√3 and cosec θ = 2

Solved Exercises

Q: Q1. If sin θ = 1/2 and θ lies in 2nd Quadrant, find the other trigonometric ratios.

Ans: For a point P(x, y) on the terminal side of θ, with r = OP, the ratios are sin θ = y/r, cos θ = x/r, tan θ = y/x, cot θ = x/y, sec θ = r/x and cosec θ = r/y.
Given sin θ = (y)/(r) = 1/2, take y = 1 and r = 2.
By Pythagoras' theorem: r² = x² + y²
x² = r² - y²
x² = (2)² - (1)² = 4 - 1 = 3
x = ±√(3)
θ lies in the 2nd quadrant, where x < 0, so x = -√(3).
cos θ = (x)/(r) = (-√(3))/2
tan θ = (y)/(x) = 1/(-√(3)) = -(1/√(3))
cot θ = (x)/(y) = (-√(3))/1 = -√(3)
sec θ = (r)/(x) = 2/(-√(3)) = -(2/√(3))
cosec θ = (r)/(y) = 2/1 = 2
Answer: cos θ = -(√(3))/2, tan θ = -(1/√(3)), cot θ = -√(3), sec θ = -(2/√(3)), cosec θ = 2

mcqs.q: If sin θ = 1/2 with y = 1 and r = 2, the value of x² by Pythagoras' theorem is:
mcqs.why: Use r² = x² + y², so x² = r² - y². Substitute r = 2 and y = 1: x² = (2)² - (1)² = 4 - 1 = 3, which then gives x = ±√3 before the quadrant sign is applied.

mcqs.q: For sin θ = 1/2 in the 2nd quadrant, the correct value of x is:
mcqs.why: Pythagoras gives x = ±√3 from x² = 3. The angle lies in the 2nd quadrant, where x < 0, so the negative root is chosen: x = -√3.

mcqs.q: If sin θ = 1/2 and θ is in the 2nd quadrant, cos θ is:
mcqs.why: Use cos θ = x/r. Substitute x = -√3 (2nd quadrant) and r = 2: cos θ = (-√3)/2 = -√3/2. The sign is negative because x is negative in the 2nd quadrant.

mcqs.q: If sin θ = 1/2 and θ is in the 2nd quadrant, tan θ is:
mcqs.why: Use tan θ = y/x. Substitute y = 1 and x = -√3: tan θ = 1/(-√3) = -(1/√3). The result is negative because y and x have opposite signs in the 2nd quadrant.

mcqs.q: If sin θ = 1/2 and θ is in the 2nd quadrant, cot θ is:
mcqs.why: Use cot θ = x/y. Substitute x = -√3 and y = 1: cot θ = (-√3)/1 = -√3. This is also the reciprocal of tan θ = -1/√3.

mcqs.q: If sin θ = 1/2 and θ is in the 2nd quadrant, sec θ is:
mcqs.why: Use sec θ = r/x. Substitute r = 2 and x = -√3: sec θ = 2/(-√3) = -(2/√3). The sign is negative because sec θ follows the sign of cos θ in the 2nd quadrant.

mcqs.q: If sin θ = 1/2 and θ is in the 2nd quadrant, cosec θ is:
mcqs.why: Use cosec θ = r/y. Substitute r = 2 and y = 1: cosec θ = 2/1 = 2. This is the reciprocal of sin θ = 1/2, and it is positive in the 2nd quadrant.

mcqs.q: The definitions used give sin θ as which ratio?
mcqs.why: For a point P(x, y) on the terminal side with r = OP, the source defines sin θ = y/r, cos θ = x/r and tan θ = y/x. So sin θ is the ratio y/r.

mcqs.q: The definitions used give tan θ as which ratio?
mcqs.why: For a point P(x, y) on the terminal side with r = OP, the source defines tan θ = y/x, while cot θ = x/y is its reciprocal. So tan θ is the ratio y/x.

mcqs.q: Why is the positive root x = +√3 rejected in this problem?
options: Because y must be negative in the 2nd quadrant
Because x is positive in the 2nd quadrant
mcqs.why: Pythagoras gives two possible roots, x = ±√3. In the 2nd quadrant the terminal side lies to the left of the y-axis, where x < 0, so only x = -√3 is consistent with the given quadrant.

lessons.title: Exercise 7.4
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Signs by quadrant: 1st all positive; 2nd only sin θ and cosec θ positive; 3rd only tan θ and cot θ positive; 4th only cos θ and sec θ positive
  • sin 98°, sin 160° and sin 460° are positive (2nd quadrant); sec 120° is negative (2nd quadrant); tan 200° is positive and cosec 198° is negative (3rd quadrant)
  • For quadrantal angles use the unit-circle point: -180° gives P(-1, 0), -270° is coterminal with 90° giving P(0, 1), and 720° is coterminal with 0° giving P(1, 0)
  • Ratios with a zero denominator are undefined, e.g. cosec(-180°) and cot(-180°) are undefined
  • 1470° is coterminal with 30°, so its ratios are the standard 30° ratios: sin = 1/2, cos = √3/2, tan = 1/√3, cosec = 2, sec = 2/√3, cot = √3
  • Given one ratio and the quadrant, find x or y from r² = x² + y² and choose its sign from the quadrant, e.g. sec θ = 2 in the 4th quadrant gives sin θ = -√3/2, and sin θ = 4/5 in the 2nd quadrant gives cos θ = -3/5
  • Standard values: sin 30° = 1/2, cos 30° = √3/2, tan 30° = 1/√3; sin 45° = cos 45° = 1/√2, tan 45° = 1; sin 60° = √3/2, cos 60° = 1/2, tan 60° = √3
  • In a right triangle sin θ = opposite/hypotenuse and tan θ = opposite/adjacent, used for the missing sides and the lake distance 333.92 yd

Solved Exercises

Q: Q1(i). Find the sign of sin 98° and tell in which quadrant it lies.

Ans: The signs of the trigonometric ratios depend on the quadrant of the terminal side: in the 1st quadrant all ratios are positive; in the 2nd quadrant only sin θ and cosec θ are positive; in the 3rd quadrant only tan θ and cot θ are positive; in the 4th quadrant only cos θ and sec θ are positive.
90° < 98° < 180°, so 98° lies in the 2nd quadrant.
In the 2nd quadrant sin θ is positive.
Answer: sin 98° is positive (+ve), in the 2nd (II) quadrant

Q: Q1(ii). Find the sign of sin 160° and tell in which quadrant it lies.

Ans: The signs of the trigonometric ratios depend on the quadrant of the terminal side: in the 1st quadrant all ratios are positive; in the 2nd quadrant only sin θ and cosec θ are positive; in the 3rd quadrant only tan θ and cot θ are positive; in the 4th quadrant only cos θ and sec θ are positive.
90° < 160° < 180°, so 160° lies in the 2nd quadrant.
In the 2nd quadrant sin θ is positive.
Answer: sin 160° is positive (+ve), in the 2nd (II) quadrant

Q: Q1(iii). Find the sign of tan 200° and tell in which quadrant it lies.

Ans: The signs of the trigonometric ratios depend on the quadrant of the terminal side: in the 1st quadrant all ratios are positive; in the 2nd quadrant only sin θ and cosec θ are positive; in the 3rd quadrant only tan θ and cot θ are positive; in the 4th quadrant only cos θ and sec θ are positive.
180° < 200° < 270°, so 200° lies in the 3rd quadrant.
In the 3rd quadrant tan θ is positive.
Answer: tan 200° is positive (+ve), in the 3rd (III) quadrant

Q: Q1(iv). Find the sign of sec 120° and tell in which quadrant it lies.

Ans: The signs of the trigonometric ratios depend on the quadrant of the terminal side: in the 1st quadrant all ratios are positive; in the 2nd quadrant only sin θ and cosec θ are positive; in the 3rd quadrant only tan θ and cot θ are positive; in the 4th quadrant only cos θ and sec θ are positive.
90° < 120° < 180°, so 120° lies in the 2nd quadrant.
In the 2nd quadrant only sin θ and cosec θ are positive, so sec θ is negative.
Answer: sec 120° is negative (-ve), in the 2nd (II) quadrant

Q: Q1(v). Find the sign of cosec 198° and tell in which quadrant it lies.

Ans: The signs of the trigonometric ratios depend on the quadrant of the terminal side: in the 1st quadrant all ratios are positive; in the 2nd quadrant only sin θ and cosec θ are positive; in the 3rd quadrant only tan θ and cot θ are positive; in the 4th quadrant only cos θ and sec θ are positive.
180° < 198° < 270°, so 198° lies in the 3rd quadrant.
In the 3rd quadrant only tan θ and cot θ are positive, so cosec θ is negative.
Answer: cosec 198° is negative (-ve), in the 3rd (III) quadrant

Q: Q1(vi). Find the sign of sin 460° and tell in which quadrant it lies.

Ans: The signs of the trigonometric ratios depend on the quadrant of the terminal side: in the 1st quadrant all ratios are positive; in the 2nd quadrant only sin θ and cosec θ are positive; in the 3rd quadrant only tan θ and cot θ are positive; in the 4th quadrant only cos θ and sec θ are positive.
460° = 360° + 100°, so 460° is coterminal with 100°.
90° < 100° < 180°, so the terminal side lies in the 2nd quadrant.
In the 2nd quadrant sin θ is positive.
Answer: sin 460° is positive (+ve), in the 2nd (II) quadrant

Q: Q2(i). Find the trigonometric ratios of the angle -180°.

Ans: For an angle in standard position, if P(x, y) is the point where the terminal side meets the unit circle (r = 1), then sin θ = y/r, cos θ = x/r, tan θ = y/x, cot θ = x/y, sec θ = r/x and cosec θ = r/y.
The angle -180° is coterminal with 180°, whose terminal side lies on the negative x-axis, so P = (-1, 0), that is x = -1, y = 0 and r = 1.
sin(-180°) = (y)/(r) = 0/1 = 0
cos(-180°) = (x)/(r) = -1/1 = -1
tan(-180°) = (y)/(x) = 0/(-1) = 0
cosec(-180°) = (r)/(y) = 1/0 = undefined
sec(-180°) = (r)/(x) = 1/(-1) = -1
cot(-180°) = (x)/(y) = -1/0 = undefined
Answer: sin(-180°) = 0, cos(-180°) = -1, tan(-180°) = 0, cosec(-180°) = undefined, sec(-180°) = -1, cot(-180°) = undefined

Q: Q2(ii). Find the trigonometric ratios of the angle -270°.

Ans: For an angle in standard position, if P(x, y) is the point where the terminal side meets the unit circle (r = 1), then sin θ = y/r, cos θ = x/r, tan θ = y/x, cot θ = x/y, sec θ = r/x and cosec θ = r/y.
The angle -270° is coterminal with 90° (-270° + 360° = 90°), whose terminal side lies on the positive y-axis, so P = (0, 1), that is x = 0, y = 1 and r = 1.
sin(-270°) = (y)/(r) = 1/1 = 1
cos(-270°) = (x)/(r) = 0/1 = 0
tan(-270°) = (y)/(x) = 1/0 = undefined
cosec(-270°) = (r)/(y) = 1/1 = 1
sec(-270°) = (r)/(x) = 1/0 = undefined
cot(-270°) = (x)/(y) = 0/1 = 0
Answer: sin(-270°) = 1, cos(-270°) = 0, tan(-270°) = undefined, cosec(-270°) = 1, sec(-270°) = undefined, cot(-270°) = 0

Q: Q2(iii). Find the trigonometric ratios of the angle 720°.

Ans: For an angle in standard position, if P(x, y) is the point where the terminal side meets the unit circle (r = 1), then sin θ = y/r, cos θ = x/r, tan θ = y/x, cot θ = x/y, sec θ = r/x and cosec θ = r/y.
720° = 2 × 360°, so 720° is coterminal with 0° (and 360°), whose terminal side lies on the positive x-axis, so P = (1, 0), that is x = 1, y = 0 and r = 1.
sin 720° = (y)/(r) = 0/1 = 0
cos 720° = (x)/(r) = 1/1 = 1
tan 720° = (y)/(x) = 0/1 = 0
cosec 720° = (r)/(y) = 1/0 = undefined
sec 720° = (r)/(x) = 1/1 = 1
cot 720° = (x)/(y) = 1/0 = undefined
Answer: sin 720° = 0, cos 720° = 1, tan 720° = 0, cosec 720° = undefined, sec 720° = 1, cot 720° = undefined

Q: Q2(iv). Find the trigonometric ratios of the angle 1470°.

Ans: For an angle in standard position, if P(x, y) is the point where the terminal side meets the unit circle (r = 1), then sin θ = y/r, cos θ = x/r, tan θ = y/x, cot θ = x/y, sec θ = r/x and cosec θ = r/y.
1470° = 4 × 360° + 30° = 1440° + 30°, so 1470° is coterminal with 30°, which lies in the 1st quadrant, where all ratios are positive.
Use the standard values for 30°: sin 30° = 1/2 and cos 30° = √(3)/2.
sin 1470° = sin 30° = 1/2
cos 1470° = cos 30° = √(3)/2
tan 1470° = tan 30° = 1/√(3)
cosec 1470° = 1/(sin 30°) = 2
sec 1470° = 1/(cos 30°) = 2/√(3)
cot 1470° = 1/(tan 30°) = √(3)
Answer: sin 1470° = 1/2, cos 1470° = √(3)/2, tan 1470° = 1/√(3), cosec 1470° = 2, sec 1470° = 2/√(3), cot 1470° = √(3)

Q: Q3. If sec θ = 2 where θ lies in 4th quadrant, find the other values of trigonometric ratios.

Ans: For a point P(x, y) on the terminal side of θ, with r = OP, the ratios are sin θ = y/r, cos θ = x/r, tan θ = y/x, cot θ = x/y, sec θ = r/x and cosec θ = r/y.
Given sec θ = (r)/(x) = 2/1, take r = 2 and x = 1, so cos θ = (x)/(r) = 1/2.
By Pythagoras' theorem: r² = x² + y²
y² = r² - x²
y² = (2)² - (1)² = 4 - 1 = 3
y = ±√(3)
θ lies in the 4th quadrant, where y < 0, so y = -√(3).
sin θ = (y)/(r) = (-√(3))/2
tan θ = (y)/(x) = (-√(3))/1 = -√(3)
cot θ = (x)/(y) = 1/(-√(3)) = -(1/√(3))
cosec θ = (r)/(y) = 2/(-√(3)) = -(2/√(3))
Answer: cos θ = 1/2, sin θ = -(√(3))/2, tan θ = -√(3), cot θ = -(1/√(3)), cosec θ = -(2/√(3))

Q: Q4. If sin θ = 4/5 and (π/2) < θ < π then find other trigonometric ratios.

Ans: The condition (π/2) < θ < π means θ lies in the 2nd quadrant, where x < 0 and y > 0.
For a point P(x, y) on the terminal side of θ, with r = OP, the ratios are sin θ = y/r, cos θ = x/r, tan θ = y/x, cot θ = x/y, sec θ = r/x and cosec θ = r/y.
Given sin θ = (y)/(r) = 4/5, take y = 4 and r = 5.
By Pythagoras' theorem: r² = x² + y²
x² = r² - y²
x² = (5)² - (4)² = 25 - 16 = 9
x = ±3
θ lies in the 2nd quadrant, where x < 0, so x = -3.
cos θ = (x)/(r) = -3/5
tan θ = (y)/(x) = 4/(-3) = -(4/3)
cot θ = (x)/(y) = -3/4
sec θ = (r)/(x) = 5/(-3) = -(5/3)
cosec θ = (r)/(y) = 5/4
Answer: cos θ = -3/5, tan θ = -(4/3), cot θ = -3/4, sec θ = -5/3, cosec θ = 5/4

Q: Q5(i). Find the value of 2 sin 45° cos 45°.

Ans: Use the standard values of trigonometric ratios for 30°, 45° and 60°: sin 30° = 1/2, cos 30° = √(3)/2, tan 30° = 1/√(3); sin 45° = cos 45° = 1/√(2), tan 45° = 1; sin 60° = √(3)/2, cos 60° = 1/2, tan 60° = √(3). Also (π/3) radians = 60° and (π/6) radians = 30°.
2 sin 45° cos 45° = 2 × (1/√(2)) × (1/√(2))
= 2 × (1/2)
Answer: 2 sin 45° cos 45° = 1

Q: Q5(ii). Find the value of (tan 60° - tan 30°)/(1 + tan 60° tan 30°).

Ans: Use the standard values of trigonometric ratios for 30°, 45° and 60°: sin 30° = 1/2, cos 30° = √(3)/2, tan 30° = 1/√(3); sin 45° = cos 45° = 1/√(2), tan 45° = 1; sin 60° = √(3)/2, cos 60° = 1/2, tan 60° = √(3). Also (π/3) radians = 60° and (π/6) radians = 30°.
(tan 60° - tan 30°)/(1 + tan 60° tan 30°) = (√(3) - 1/√(3))/(1 + √(3) × (1/√(3)))
Numerator: √(3) - 1/√(3) = (3 - 1)/√(3) = 2/√(3)
Denominator: 1 + 1 = 2
= (2/√(3))/2
Answer: (tan 60° - tan 30°)/(1 + tan 60° tan 30°) = 1/√(3)

Q: Q5(iii). Find the value of (cos 45°)/(sin 45° + tan 45°).

Ans: Use the standard values of trigonometric ratios for 30°, 45° and 60°: sin 30° = 1/2, cos 30° = √(3)/2, tan 30° = 1/√(3); sin 45° = cos 45° = 1/√(2), tan 45° = 1; sin 60° = √(3)/2, cos 60° = 1/2, tan 60° = √(3). Also (π/3) radians = 60° and (π/6) radians = 30°.
(cos 45°)/(sin 45° + tan 45°) = (1/√(2))/((1/√(2)) + 1)
Multiply numerator and denominator by √(2).
= 1/(1 + √(2))
Answer: (cos 45°)/(sin 45° + tan 45°) = 1/(1 + √(2)) ≈ 0.4142

Q: Q5(iv). Find the value of tan 30° tan 60° + tan 45°.

Ans: Use the standard values of trigonometric ratios for 30°, 45° and 60°: sin 30° = 1/2, cos 30° = √(3)/2, tan 30° = 1/√(3); sin 45° = cos 45° = 1/√(2), tan 45° = 1; sin 60° = √(3)/2, cos 60° = 1/2, tan 60° = √(3). Also (π/3) radians = 60° and (π/6) radians = 30°.
tan 30° tan 60° + tan 45° = (1/√(3)) × √(3) + 1
= 1 + 1
Answer: tan 30° tan 60° + tan 45° = 2

Q: Q5(v). Find the value of cos (π/3) cos (π/6) - sin (π/3) sin (π/6).

Ans: Use the standard values of trigonometric ratios for 30°, 45° and 60°: sin 30° = 1/2, cos 30° = √(3)/2, tan 30° = 1/√(3); sin 45° = cos 45° = 1/√(2), tan 45° = 1; sin 60° = √(3)/2, cos 60° = 1/2, tan 60° = √(3). Also (π/3) radians = 60° and (π/6) radians = 30°.
(π/3) radians = 60° and (π/6) radians = 30°.
cos (π/3) = cos 60° = 1/2
cos (π/6) = cos 30° = √(3)/2
sin (π/3) = sin 60° = √(3)/2
sin (π/6) = sin 30° = 1/2
cos (π/3) cos (π/6) - sin (π/3) sin (π/6) = (1/2) × (√(3)/2) - (√(3)/2) × (1/2)
= √(3)/4 - √(3)/4
Answer: cos (π/3) cos (π/6) - sin (π/3) sin (π/6) = 0

Q: Q6(i). In which quadrant does θ lie if sin θ > 0, tan θ > 0?

Ans: The signs of the trigonometric ratios by quadrant are: 1st quadrant - all positive; 2nd quadrant - sin θ and cosec θ positive only; 3rd quadrant - tan θ and cot θ positive only; 4th quadrant - cos θ and sec θ positive only.
sin θ > 0 in the 1st and 2nd quadrants.
tan θ > 0 in the 1st and 3rd quadrants.
The quadrant common to both conditions is the 1st quadrant.
Answer: θ lies in the 1st quadrant

Q: Q6(ii). In which quadrant does θ lie if sin θ < 0, cot θ > 0?

Ans: The signs of the trigonometric ratios by quadrant are: 1st quadrant - all positive; 2nd quadrant - sin θ and cosec θ positive only; 3rd quadrant - tan θ and cot θ positive only; 4th quadrant - cos θ and sec θ positive only.
sin θ < 0 in the 3rd and 4th quadrants.
cot θ > 0 in the 1st and 3rd quadrants.
The quadrant common to both conditions is the 3rd quadrant.
Answer: θ lies in the 3rd quadrant

Q: Q6(iii). In which quadrant does θ lie if sin θ > 0, cos θ < 0?

Ans: The signs of the trigonometric ratios by quadrant are: 1st quadrant - all positive; 2nd quadrant - sin θ and cosec θ positive only; 3rd quadrant - tan θ and cot θ positive only; 4th quadrant - cos θ and sec θ positive only.
sin θ > 0 in the 1st and 2nd quadrants.
cos θ < 0 in the 2nd and 3rd quadrants.
The quadrant common to both conditions is the 2nd quadrant.
Answer: θ lies in the 2nd quadrant

Q: Q6(iv). In which quadrant does θ lie if cos θ > 0, cosec θ < 0?

Ans: The signs of the trigonometric ratios by quadrant are: 1st quadrant - all positive; 2nd quadrant - sin θ and cosec θ positive only; 3rd quadrant - tan θ and cot θ positive only; 4th quadrant - cos θ and sec θ positive only.
cos θ > 0 in the 1st and 4th quadrants.
cosec θ < 0 where sin θ < 0, that is in the 3rd and 4th quadrants.
The quadrant common to both conditions is the 4th quadrant.
Answer: θ lies in the 4th quadrant

Q: Q6(v). In which quadrant does θ lie if tan θ < 0, sec θ > 0?

Ans: The signs of the trigonometric ratios by quadrant are: 1st quadrant - all positive; 2nd quadrant - sin θ and cosec θ positive only; 3rd quadrant - tan θ and cot θ positive only; 4th quadrant - cos θ and sec θ positive only.
tan θ < 0 in the 2nd and 4th quadrants.
sec θ > 0 where cos θ > 0, that is in the 1st and 4th quadrants.
The quadrant common to both conditions is the 4th quadrant.
Answer: θ lies in the 4th quadrant

Q: Q6(vi). In which quadrant does θ lie if cos θ < 0, tan θ < 0?

Ans: The signs of the trigonometric ratios by quadrant are: 1st quadrant - all positive; 2nd quadrant - sin θ and cosec θ positive only; 3rd quadrant - tan θ and cot θ positive only; 4th quadrant - cos θ and sec θ positive only.
cos θ < 0 in the 2nd and 3rd quadrants.
tan θ < 0 in the 2nd and 4th quadrants.
The quadrant common to both conditions is the 2nd quadrant.
Answer: θ lies in the 2nd quadrant

Q: Q7(i). For the given right triangle, find the missing measure x to two decimal places.

Ans: Diagram: a right triangle with the right angle at the top-left vertex; the angle at the bottom vertex is 53°; the hypotenuse, joining the bottom vertex to the right-hand vertex, is 32; the side marked x is the top side, joining the top-left vertex to the right-hand vertex, opposite the 53° angle.
In a right triangle, sin θ = (opposite side)/(hypotenuse).
For the 53° angle, the opposite side is x and the hypotenuse is 32.
sin 53° = x/32
x = 32 × sin 53°
sin 53° ≈ 0.7986
x ≈ 32 × 0.7986
x ≈ 25.56
Answer: x ≈ 25.56

Q: Q7(ii). For the given right triangle, find the missing measure x to two decimal places.

Ans: Diagram: a right triangle with the right angle at the top-right vertex; the angle at the top-left vertex is 21°; the hypotenuse, joining the top-left vertex to the bottom vertex, is 73; the side marked x is the vertical right side, joining the top-right vertex to the bottom vertex, opposite the 21° angle.
In a right triangle, sin θ = (opposite side)/(hypotenuse).
For the 21° angle, the opposite side is x and the hypotenuse is 73.
sin 21° = x/73
x = 73 × sin 21°
sin 21° ≈ 0.3584
x ≈ 73 × 0.3584
x ≈ 26.16
Answer: x ≈ 26.16

Q: Q7(iii). For the given right triangle, find the missing measure x to two decimal places.

Ans: Diagram: a right triangle with the right angle at the bottom-left vertex; the angle at the right-hand vertex is 33°; the base, joining the bottom-left vertex to the right-hand vertex, is 12; the side marked x is the vertical left side, opposite the 33° angle.
In a right triangle, tan θ = (opposite side)/(adjacent side).
For the 33° angle, the opposite side is x and the adjacent side is 12.
tan 33° = x/12
x = 12 × tan 33°
tan 33° ≈ 0.6494
x ≈ 12 × 0.6494
x ≈ 7.79
Answer: x ≈ 7.79

Q: Q8. The irregular blue shape in the diagram represents a lake. The distance across the lake, a, is unknown. To find this distance, a surveyor took the measurements shown in the figure. What is the distance across the lake?

Ans: Diagram: a right triangle ABC with the right angle at C; A is the surveyor's point on the left; C is on the shore directly below B; the horizontal distance AC = 750 yd; the vertical side BC = a is the distance across the lake; the angle at A between AC and the line of sight AB is 24°.
In a right triangle, tan θ = (opposite side)/(adjacent side).
For the 24° angle at A, the opposite side is a and the adjacent side is 750 yd.
tan 24° = a/750
a = 750 × tan 24°
tan 24° ≈ 0.4452
a ≈ 750 × 0.4452
a ≈ 333.92
Answer: the distance across the lake is ≈ 333.92 yd

mcqs.q: The sign of sin 98° is:
mcqs.why: First locate the angle: 90° < 98° < 180°, so 98° is in the 2nd quadrant. In the 2nd quadrant only sin θ and cosec θ are positive, so sin 98° is positive.

mcqs.q: The sign of sec 120° is:
mcqs.why: First locate the angle: 90° < 120° < 180°, so 120° is in the 2nd quadrant. There only sin θ and cosec θ are positive; sec θ is not one of them, so sec 120° is negative.

mcqs.q: The sign of tan 200° is:
mcqs.why: First locate the angle: 180° < 200° < 270°, so 200° is in the 3rd quadrant. In the 3rd quadrant only tan θ and cot θ are positive, so tan 200° is positive.

mcqs.q: The sign of cosec 198° is:
mcqs.why: First locate the angle: 180° < 198° < 270°, so 198° is in the 3rd quadrant. There only tan θ and cot θ are positive; cosec θ is not one of them, so cosec 198° is negative.

mcqs.q: sin 460° is positive because 460° is coterminal with:
mcqs.why: Subtract one complete turn: 460° - 360° = 100°. Since 90° < 100° < 180°, the terminal side is in the 2nd quadrant, where sin θ is positive, so sin 460° is positive.

mcqs.q: For the angle -180°, cos(-180°) is:
mcqs.why: -180° is coterminal with 180°, whose terminal side meets the unit circle at P(-1, 0), so x = -1, y = 0, r = 1. Then cos θ = x/r = -1/1 = -1.

mcqs.q: For the angle -180°, cosec(-180°) is:
mcqs.why: -180° meets the unit circle at P(-1, 0), so y = 0 and r = 1. Then cosec θ = r/y = 1/0, and division by zero is not possible, so cosec(-180°) is undefined.

mcqs.q: For the angle -270°, sin(-270°) is:
mcqs.why: Add 360°: -270° + 360° = 90°, whose terminal side meets the unit circle at P(0, 1), so y = 1 and r = 1. Then sin θ = y/r = 1/1 = 1.

mcqs.q: For the angle 720°, cos 720° is:
mcqs.why: 720° = 2 × 360°, so 720° is coterminal with 0°, meeting the unit circle at P(1, 0), so x = 1 and r = 1. Then cos θ = x/r = 1/1 = 1.

mcqs.q: sin 1470° is:
mcqs.why: Reduce the angle: 1470° = 4 × 360° + 30° = 1440° + 30°, so 1470° is coterminal with 30°. Using the standard value sin 30° = 1/2 gives sin 1470° = 1/2.

mcqs.q: If sec θ = 2 and θ lies in the 4th quadrant, then sin θ is:
mcqs.why: sec θ = r/x = 2/1 gives r = 2, x = 1. Then y² = r² - x² = 4 - 1 = 3, so y = ±√3; in the 4th quadrant y < 0, so y = -√3. Hence sin θ = y/r = (-√3)/2 = -√3/2.

mcqs.q: If sin θ = 4/5 and (π/2) < θ < π, then cos θ is:
mcqs.why: sin θ = y/r = 4/5 gives y = 4, r = 5. Then x² = r² - y² = 25 - 16 = 9, so x = ±3; the condition (π/2) < θ < π is the 2nd quadrant, where x < 0, so x = -3. Hence cos θ = x/r = -3/5.

mcqs.q: The value of 2 sin 45° cos 45° is:
mcqs.why: Use the standard value sin 45° = cos 45° = 1/√2. Substitute: 2 sin 45° cos 45° = 2 × (1/√2) × (1/√2) = 2 × (1/2) = 1.

mcqs.q: The value of tan 30° tan 60° + tan 45° is:
mcqs.why: Use the standard values tan 30° = 1/√3, tan 60° = √3 and tan 45° = 1. Substitute: (1/√3) × √3 + 1 = 1 + 1 = 2.

mcqs.q: In which quadrant does θ lie if sin θ > 0 and cos θ < 0?
mcqs.why: sin θ > 0 in the 1st and 2nd quadrants, and cos θ < 0 in the 2nd and 3rd quadrants. The quadrant appearing in both lists is the 2nd quadrant, so θ lies there.

lessons.title: Exercise 7.5
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • The fundamental identity sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 gives 1 - sin²θ = cos²θ and 1 - cos²θ = sin²θ
  • From 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ, sec²θ - 1 = tan²θ; from 1 + cot²θ = cosec²θ
  • Reciprocal and quotient relations used: tan θ = sin θ/cos θ, cot θ = cos θ/sin θ, sec θ = 1/cos θ and cosec θ = 1/sin θ
  • (sec²θ - 1) cos²θ = sin²θ follows by replacing sec²θ - 1 with tan²θ = sin²θ/cos²θ
  • tan θ + cot θ = sec θ cosec θ follows from (sin²θ + cos²θ)/(sin θ cos θ) = 1/(sin θ cos θ)
  • Multiplying (1 - sin θ)/cos θ above and below by (1 + sin θ) uses (a - b)(a + b) = a² - b² and 1 - sin²θ = cos²θ to give cos θ/(1 + sin θ)
  • sin θ √(1 + tan²θ) = tan θ follows from 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ, so the root is sec θ and sin θ sec θ = sin θ/cos θ
  • cos⁴b - sin⁴b = 1 - 2 sin²b follows by factorising as a difference of squares and using cos²b + sin²b = 1

Solved Exercises

Q: Q1. Prove the following trigonometric identity: (sec²θ - 1) cos²θ = sin²θ

Ans: Take the left-hand side.
L.H.S = (sec²θ - 1) cos²θ
Using the identity 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ, so sec²θ - 1 = tan²θ.
L.H.S = tan²θ × cos²θ
Using tan θ = (sin θ)/(cos θ), so tan²θ = (sin²θ)/(cos²θ).
L.H.S = (sin²θ)/(cos²θ) × cos²θ
L.H.S = sin²θ
L.H.S = R.H.S
Answer: (sec²θ - 1) cos²θ = sin²θ, proved

Q: Q2. Prove the following trigonometric identity: tan θ + sec θ = (1 + sin θ)/(cos θ)

Ans: Take the left-hand side.
L.H.S = tan θ + sec θ
Using tan θ = (sin θ)/(cos θ) and sec θ = 1/(cos θ).
L.H.S = (sin θ)/(cos θ) + 1/(cos θ)
L.H.S = (sin θ + 1)/(cos θ)
L.H.S = (1 + sin θ)/(cos θ)
L.H.S = R.H.S
Answer: tan θ + sec θ = (1 + sin θ)/(cos θ), proved

Q: Q3. Prove the following trigonometric identity: (cos θ - sin θ)² = 1 - 2 sin θ cos θ

Ans: Take the left-hand side.
L.H.S = (cos θ - sin θ)²
Expanding the square, (a - b)² = a² - 2ab + b².
L.H.S = cos²θ - 2 sin θ cos θ + sin²θ
L.H.S = (sin²θ + cos²θ) - 2 sin θ cos θ
Using the identity sin²θ + cos²θ = 1.
L.H.S = 1 - 2 sin θ cos θ
L.H.S = R.H.S
Answer: (cos θ - sin θ)² = 1 - 2 sin θ cos θ, proved

Q: Q4. Prove the following trigonometric identity: cos²θ - sin²θ = 2 cos²θ - 1

Ans: Take the left-hand side.
L.H.S = cos²θ - sin²θ
Using the identity sin²θ + cos²θ = 1, so sin²θ = 1 - cos²θ.
L.H.S = cos²θ - (1 - cos²θ)
L.H.S = cos²θ - 1 + cos²θ
L.H.S = 2 cos²θ - 1
L.H.S = R.H.S
Answer: cos²θ - sin²θ = 2 cos²θ - 1, proved

Q: Q5. Prove the following trigonometric identity: tan θ + cot θ = sec θ cosec θ

Ans: Take the left-hand side.
L.H.S = tan θ + cot θ
Using tan θ = (sin θ)/(cos θ) and cot θ = (cos θ)/(sin θ).
L.H.S = (sin θ)/(cos θ) + (cos θ)/(sin θ)
Taking the common denominator sin θ cos θ.
L.H.S = (sin²θ + cos²θ)/(sin θ cos θ)
Using the identity sin²θ + cos²θ = 1.
L.H.S = 1/(sin θ cos θ)
L.H.S = (1/(sin θ)) × (1/(cos θ))
Using cosec θ = 1/(sin θ) and sec θ = 1/(cos θ).
L.H.S = cosec θ × sec θ
L.H.S = R.H.S
Answer: tan θ + cot θ = sec θ cosec θ, proved

Q: Q6. Prove the following trigonometric identity: (1 - sin θ)/(cos θ) = (cos θ)/(1 + sin θ)

Ans: Take the left-hand side.
L.H.S = (1 - sin θ)/(cos θ)
Multiply numerator and denominator by (1 + sin θ).
L.H.S = ((1 - sin θ)(1 + sin θ))/((cos θ)(1 + sin θ))
Using (a - b)(a + b) = a² - b² in the numerator.
L.H.S = (1 - sin²θ)/((cos θ)(1 + sin θ))
Using the identity sin²θ + cos²θ = 1, so 1 - sin²θ = cos²θ.
L.H.S = (cos²θ)/((cos θ)(1 + sin θ))
Cancelling cos θ.
L.H.S = (cos θ)/(1 + sin θ)
L.H.S = R.H.S
Answer: (1 - sin θ)/(cos θ) = (cos θ)/(1 + sin θ), proved

Q: Q7. Prove the following trigonometric identity: sin θ √(1 + tan²θ) = tan θ

Ans: Take the left-hand side.
L.H.S = sin θ √(1 + tan²θ)
Using the identity 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ.
L.H.S = sin θ √(sec²θ)
L.H.S = sin θ × sec θ
Using sec θ = 1/(cos θ).
L.H.S = (sin θ)/(cos θ)
Using tan θ = (sin θ)/(cos θ).
L.H.S = tan θ
L.H.S = R.H.S
Answer: sin θ √(1 + tan²θ) = tan θ, proved

Q: Q8. Prove the following trigonometric identity: cos θ = √(1 - sin²θ)

Ans: Using the identity sin²θ + cos²θ = 1.
cos²θ = 1 - sin²θ
Taking the square root of both sides.
cos θ = √(1 - sin²θ)
Answer: cos θ = √(1 - sin²θ), proved

Q: Q9. Prove the following trigonometric identity: (1 + cos θ)(1 - cos θ) = 1/(cosec²θ)

Ans: Take the left-hand side.
L.H.S = (1 + cos θ)(1 - cos θ)
Using (a + b)(a - b) = a² - b².
L.H.S = 1 - cos²θ
Using the identity sin²θ + cos²θ = 1, so 1 - cos²θ = sin²θ.
L.H.S = sin²θ
Now the right-hand side: using cosec θ = 1/(sin θ), so 1/(cosec²θ) = sin²θ.
R.H.S = sin²θ
L.H.S = R.H.S
Answer: (1 + cos θ)(1 - cos θ) = 1/(cosec²θ), proved

Q: Q10. Prove the following trigonometric identity: cos x - cos x sin²x = cos³x

Ans: Take the left-hand side.
L.H.S = cos x - cos x sin²x
Taking cos x as a common factor.
L.H.S = cos x (1 - sin²x)
Using the identity sin²x + cos²x = 1, so 1 - sin²x = cos²x.
L.H.S = cos x × cos²x
L.H.S = cos³x
L.H.S = R.H.S
Answer: cos x - cos x sin²x = cos³x, proved

Q: Q11. Prove the following trigonometric identity: (sin x)/(1 + cos x) + (1 + cos x)/(sin x) = 2 cosec x

Ans: Take the left-hand side.
L.H.S = (sin x)/(1 + cos x) + (1 + cos x)/(sin x)
Taking the common denominator sin x (1 + cos x).
L.H.S = (sin²x + (1 + cos x)²)/(sin x (1 + cos x))
Expanding (1 + cos x)² = 1 + 2 cos x + cos²x.
L.H.S = (sin²x + 1 + 2 cos x + cos²x)/(sin x (1 + cos x))
Grouping sin²x + cos²x in the numerator.
L.H.S = ((sin²x + cos²x) + 1 + 2 cos x)/(sin x (1 + cos x))
Using the identity sin²x + cos²x = 1.
L.H.S = (1 + 1 + 2 cos x)/(sin x (1 + cos x))
L.H.S = (2 + 2 cos x)/(sin x (1 + cos x))
Taking 2 as a common factor in the numerator.
L.H.S = (2(1 + cos x))/(sin x (1 + cos x))
Cancelling (1 + cos x).
L.H.S = 2/(sin x)
Using cosec x = 1/(sin x).
L.H.S = 2 cosec x
L.H.S = R.H.S
Answer: (sin x)/(1 + cos x) + (1 + cos x)/(sin x) = 2 cosec x, proved

Q: Q12. Prove the following trigonometric identity: (sin x)/(1 + cos x) = (1 - cos x)/(sin x)

Ans: Take the left-hand side.
L.H.S = (sin x)/(1 + cos x)
Multiply numerator and denominator by (1 - cos x).
L.H.S = ((sin x)(1 - cos x))/((1 + cos x)(1 - cos x))
Using (a + b)(a - b) = a² - b² in the denominator.
L.H.S = ((sin x)(1 - cos x))/(1 - cos²x)
Using the identity sin²x + cos²x = 1, so 1 - cos²x = sin²x.
L.H.S = ((sin x)(1 - cos x))/(sin²x)
Cancelling sin x.
L.H.S = (1 - cos x)/(sin x)
L.H.S = R.H.S
Answer: (sin x)/(1 + cos x) = (1 - cos x)/(sin x), proved

Q: Q13. Prove the following trigonometric identity: 1/(1 + cos a) + 1/(1 - cos a) = 2 + 2 cot²a

Ans: Take the left-hand side.
L.H.S = 1/(1 + cos a) + 1/(1 - cos a)
Taking the common denominator (1 + cos a)(1 - cos a).
L.H.S = ((1 - cos a) + (1 + cos a))/((1 + cos a)(1 - cos a))
L.H.S = 2/((1 + cos a)(1 - cos a))
Using (a + b)(a - b) = a² - b² in the denominator.
L.H.S = 2/(1 - cos²a)
Using the identity sin²a + cos²a = 1, so 1 - cos²a = sin²a.
L.H.S = 2/(sin²a)
Using cosec a = 1/(sin a), so 1/(sin²a) = cosec²a.
L.H.S = 2 cosec²a
Using the identity 1 + cot²a = cosec²a.
L.H.S = 2(1 + cot²a)
L.H.S = 2 + 2 cot²a
L.H.S = R.H.S
Answer: 1/(1 + cos a) + 1/(1 - cos a) = 2 + 2 cot²a, proved

Q: Q14. Prove the following trigonometric identity: cos⁴b - sin⁴b = 1 - 2 sin²b

Ans: Take the left-hand side.
L.H.S = cos⁴b - sin⁴b
Factorising as a difference of squares, a² - b² = (a - b)(a + b), with a = cos²b and b = sin²b.
L.H.S = (cos²b - sin²b)(cos²b + sin²b)
Using the identity sin²b + cos²b = 1, so cos²b + sin²b = 1.
L.H.S = (cos²b - sin²b) × 1
L.H.S = cos²b - sin²b
Using the identity sin²b + cos²b = 1 again, so cos²b = 1 - sin²b.
L.H.S = (1 - sin²b) - sin²b
L.H.S = 1 - 2 sin²b
L.H.S = R.H.S
Answer: cos⁴b - sin⁴b = 1 - 2 sin²b, proved

Q: Q15. Prove the following trigonometric identity: (sin y + cos y)/(sin y) + (cos y - sin y)/(cos y) = sec y cosec y

Ans: Note: as printed, with the denominators in this order, the two sides are not equal; the denominators of the two fractions appear interchanged in printing. The evident intended identity, proved here, is (sin y + cos y)/(cos y) + (cos y - sin y)/(sin y) = sec y cosec y.
Take the left-hand side of the intended identity.
L.H.S = (sin y + cos y)/(cos y) + (cos y - sin y)/(sin y)
Splitting each fraction.
L.H.S = (sin y)/(cos y) + (cos y)/(cos y) + (cos y)/(sin y) - (sin y)/(sin y)
L.H.S = tan y + 1 + cot y - 1, using tan y = (sin y)/(cos y) and cot y = (cos y)/(sin y).
L.H.S = tan y + cot y
Using tan y = (sin y)/(cos y) and cot y = (cos y)/(sin y) again, with common denominator sin y cos y.
L.H.S = (sin²y + cos²y)/(sin y cos y)
Using the identity sin²y + cos²y = 1.
L.H.S = 1/(sin y cos y)
L.H.S = (1/(sin y)) × (1/(cos y))
Using cosec y = 1/(sin y) and sec y = 1/(cos y).
L.H.S = cosec y × sec y
L.H.S = R.H.S
Answer: (sin y + cos y)/(cos y) + (cos y - sin y)/(sin y) = sec y cosec y, proved (see the note above about the printed denominators)

Q: Q16. Prove the following trigonometric identity: (sec x - tan x)² = (1 - sin x)/(1 + sin x)

Ans: Take the left-hand side.
L.H.S = (sec x - tan x)²
Using sec x = 1/(cos x) and tan x = (sin x)/(cos x).
L.H.S = (1/(cos x) - (sin x)/(cos x))²
L.H.S = ((1 - sin x)/(cos x))²
L.H.S = (1 - sin x)²/(cos²x)
Using the identity sin²x + cos²x = 1, so cos²x = 1 - sin²x.
L.H.S = (1 - sin x)²/(1 - sin²x)
Factorising 1 - sin²x = (1 - sin x)(1 + sin x).
L.H.S = (1 - sin x)²/((1 - sin x)(1 + sin x))
Cancelling (1 - sin x).
L.H.S = (1 - sin x)/(1 + sin x)
L.H.S = R.H.S
Answer: (sec x - tan x)² = (1 - sin x)/(1 + sin x), proved

Q: Q17. Prove the following trigonometric identity: sin x tan x + cos x = sec x

Ans: Take the left-hand side.
L.H.S = sin x tan x + cos x
Using tan x = (sin x)/(cos x).
L.H.S = sin x × (sin x)/(cos x) + cos x
L.H.S = (sin²x)/(cos x) + cos x
Taking the common denominator cos x.
L.H.S = (sin²x + cos²x)/(cos x)
Using the identity sin²x + cos²x = 1.
L.H.S = 1/(cos x)
Using sec x = 1/(cos x).
L.H.S = sec x
L.H.S = R.H.S
Answer: sin x tan x + cos x = sec x, proved

mcqs.q: The identity sin²θ + cos²θ is equal to:
mcqs.why: This is the fundamental trigonometric identity used repeatedly in the exercise: for any angle θ, sin²θ + cos²θ = 1. It is the step that turns sin²θ + cos²θ in a numerator into 1.

mcqs.q: From 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ, the expression sec²θ - 1 is equal to:
mcqs.why: Start with 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ and subtract 1 from both sides: tan²θ = sec²θ - 1. So sec²θ - 1 = tan²θ, the first replacement used in proving Q1 of the exercise.

mcqs.q: In the proof of (sec²θ - 1) cos²θ = sin²θ, after replacing sec²θ - 1 by tan²θ, tan²θ is written as:
mcqs.why: Use tan θ = sin θ/cos θ and square both sides: tan²θ = sin²θ/cos²θ. Then tan²θ × cos²θ = (sin²θ/cos²θ) × cos²θ = sin²θ after cancelling cos²θ.

mcqs.q: tan θ + sec θ, written with denominator cos θ, is equal to:
mcqs.why: Write each term over cos θ: tan θ = sin θ/cos θ and sec θ = 1/cos θ. Adding fractions with the same denominator: (sin θ + 1)/(cos θ) = (1 + sin θ)/(cos θ).

mcqs.q: Expanding (cos θ - sin θ)² gives, after using sin²θ + cos²θ = 1:
mcqs.why: Expand with (a - b)² = a² - 2ab + b²: (cos θ - sin θ)² = cos²θ - 2 sin θ cos θ + sin²θ. Group the squares: (sin²θ + cos²θ) - 2 sin θ cos θ = 1 - 2 sin θ cos θ.

mcqs.q: cos²θ - sin²θ can be rewritten, using sin²θ = 1 - cos²θ, as:
mcqs.why: Substitute sin²θ = 1 - cos²θ into the expression: cos²θ - sin²θ = cos²θ - (1 - cos²θ) = cos²θ - 1 + cos²θ = 2 cos²θ - 1.

mcqs.q: tan θ + cot θ simplifies, over the common denominator sin θ cos θ, to:
options: (sin θ + cos θ)/(sin θ cos θ)
mcqs.why: Write tan θ + cot θ = sin θ/cos θ + cos θ/sin θ = (sin²θ + cos²θ)/(sin θ cos θ). Using sin²θ + cos²θ = 1, this becomes 1/(sin θ cos θ), which equals sec θ cosec θ.

mcqs.q: To prove (1 - sin θ)/(cos θ) = (cos θ)/(1 + sin θ), the numerator and denominator of the left side are multiplied by:
mcqs.why: Multiply above and below by (1 + sin θ): the numerator becomes (1 - sin θ)(1 + sin θ) = 1 - sin²θ = cos²θ, and cancelling one cos θ from cos²θ/(cos θ(1 + sin θ)) leaves cos θ/(1 + sin θ).

mcqs.q: sin θ √(1 + tan²θ) simplifies to tan θ because √(1 + tan²θ) is equal to:
mcqs.why: Use the identity 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ under the root: √(1 + tan²θ) = √(sec²θ) = sec θ. Then sin θ × sec θ = sin θ × (1/cos θ) = sin θ/cos θ = tan θ.

mcqs.q: The product (1 + cos θ)(1 - cos θ) is equal to:
mcqs.why: Use (a + b)(a - b) = a² - b²: (1 + cos θ)(1 - cos θ) = 1 - cos²θ = sin²θ, by sin²θ + cos²θ = 1. Also 1/(cosec²θ) = sin²θ since cosec θ = 1/sin θ, so the product equals 1/(cosec²θ).

lessons.title: Exercise 7.6
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Heights and distances are modelled as right triangles with tan θ = opposite/adjacent for the angle of elevation or depression
  • The angle of depression from a top point equals the angle of elevation at the lower point, by alternate interior angles
  • A 21 m building with a 25 m shadow gives tan θ = 21/25 = 0.84, so the sun's angle of elevation is ≈ 40°
  • From a 150 m lighthouse with angle of depression 60°, the boat distance is 150/√3 = 50√3 ≈ 86.60 m
  • A 50 m tree seen from 100 m away gives tan θ = 0.5, so the angle of elevation is ≈ 26.56°
  • Two-step problems use tan with two angles: the 240 m hill with depressions 30° and 60° gives a minaret of height 160 m, and walking 210 m towards a cliff changing the elevation from 30° to 45° gives a cliff height of ≈ 286.87 m
  • Boats on opposite sides of a 300 m lighthouse at depressions 45° and 30° are 300 + 300√3 = 300(√3 + 1) ≈ 819.6 m apart

Solved Exercises

Q: Q1. A building that is 21 metres tall casts a shadow 25 metres long. Find the angle of elevation of the sun to the nearest degree.

Ans: Diagram: the building is the vertical side of a right triangle, of height 21 m; its shadow is the horizontal side, of length 25 m, on the ground; the line from the tip of the shadow to the top of the building is the hypotenuse; the angle of elevation of the sun, θ, is the angle at the tip of the shadow between the shadow and the line to the top of the building.
In a right triangle, tan θ = (opposite side)/(adjacent side).
For the angle θ, the opposite side is the height of the building, 21 m, and the adjacent side is the shadow, 25 m.
tan θ = 21/25
tan θ = 0.84
