θ = tan⁻¹(0.84)
θ ≈ 40.03°
Answer: the angle of elevation of the sun is ≈ 40°

Q: Q2. A light house is 150 m above the sea level. Angle of depression of a boat from its top is 60°. Find the distance between the boat and the lighthouse.

Ans: Diagram: the lighthouse is the vertical side AB of a right triangle, with A at the foot on sea level and B at the top, AB = 150 m; the boat is at point C on the sea; AC is the horizontal distance to be found; the angle of depression from B to the boat is 60°, which equals the angle of elevation at C, ∠BCA = 60°, by alternate interior angles.
In a right triangle, tan θ = (opposite side)/(adjacent side).
In △ABC, for the angle 60° at C, the opposite side is AB = 150 m and the adjacent side is AC.
tan 60° = 150/(AC)
Using tan 60° = √(3).
√(3) = 150/(AC)
AC = 150/√(3)
AC = (150√(3))/3 = 50√(3)
AC ≈ 86.60
Answer: the distance between the boat and the lighthouse is 50√(3) m ≈ 86.60 m

Q: Q3. A tree is 50 m high. Find the angle of elevation of its top to a point, on the ground 100 m away from the foot of tree.

Ans: Diagram: the tree is the vertical side of a right triangle, of height 50 m; the point on the ground is 100 m horizontally from the foot of the tree; the angle of elevation θ is the angle at that point between the ground and the line of sight to the top of the tree.
In a right triangle, tan θ = (opposite side)/(adjacent side).
For the angle θ, the opposite side is the height of the tree, 50 m, and the adjacent side is 100 m.
tan θ = 50/100
tan θ = 0.5
θ = tan⁻¹(0.5)
θ ≈ 26.565°
Answer: the angle of elevation is ≈ 26.56°

Q: Q4. From the top of hill 240 m high, measure of the angles of depression of the top and bottom of minaret are 30° and 60° respectively. Find the height of minaret.

Ans: Diagram: the hill is a vertical side of height 240 m with its top at T and foot at F; the minaret stands vertically at a horizontal distance d from the hill, with its top at M and bottom at N on the same level as F; the angle of depression from T to N (the bottom of the minaret) is 60°, and the angle of depression from T to M (the top of the minaret) is 30°; by alternate interior angles these equal the angles of elevation at N and M in the right triangles.
Let the height of the minaret be h metres and the horizontal distance between the hill and the minaret be d metres.
In a right triangle, tan θ = (opposite side)/(adjacent side).
First use the angle of depression 60° to the bottom of the minaret.
In the right triangle with vertical side TF = 240 m and horizontal side d:
tan 60° = 240/d
Using tan 60° = √(3).
√(3) = 240/d
d = 240/√(3) = 80√(3) ≈ 138.56 m
Now use the angle of depression 30° to the top of the minaret.
The top of the minaret is h metres above the ground, so it is (240 - h) metres below the top of the hill.
tan 30° = (240 - h)/d
Using tan 30° = 1/√(3) and d = 80√(3).
1/√(3) = (240 - h)/(80√(3))
240 - h = (80√(3))/√(3)
240 - h = 80
h = 240 - 80
Answer: the height of the minaret is 160 m

Q: Q5. A police helicopter is flying at 800 feet. A stolen car is sighted at an angle of depression of 72°. Find the distance of the stolen car, to the nearest foot, from a point directly below the helicopter.

Ans: Diagram: the helicopter is at point H, 800 ft vertically above the point G on the ground directly below it, so HG = 800 ft; the stolen car is at point C on the ground; the distance to be found is GC = d; the angle of depression from H to the car is 72°, which equals the angle of elevation at C, ∠HCG = 72°, by alternate interior angles; HGC is a right angle.
In a right triangle, tan θ = (opposite side)/(adjacent side).
In △HGC, for the angle 72° at C, the opposite side is HG = 800 ft and the adjacent side is d.
tan 72° = 800/d
d = 800/(tan 72°)
tan 72° ≈ 3.0777
d ≈ 800/3.0777
d ≈ 259.94
Answer: the distance of the stolen car from the point directly below the helicopter is ≈ 260 feet

Q: Q6. A light house is 300 m above the sea level. The angle of depression of two boats from the top of light house are 30° and 45° respectively. If the line of joining of the boats passes through the foot of light house, find the distance between two boats when they are on the opposite side of the light house.

Ans: Diagram: the lighthouse is the vertical side AB of height 300 m, with A at the foot and B at the top; one boat is at point C on one side of the lighthouse and the other boat is at point D on the opposite side, with A between C and D on the same straight line; the angle of depression from B to the nearer boat C is 45° and to the farther boat D is 30°; by alternate interior angles these equal the angles of elevation at C and D.
In a right triangle, tan θ = (opposite side)/(adjacent side).
First find AC, using the boat with angle of depression 45°.
In △ABC, tan 45° = 300/(AC)
Using tan 45° = 1.
1 = 300/(AC)
AC = 300 m
Now find AD, using the boat with angle of depression 30°.
In △ABD, tan 30° = 300/(AD)
Using tan 30° = 1/√(3).
1/√(3) = 300/(AD)
AD = 300√(3) m
The boats are on opposite sides of the lighthouse, so the distance between them is CD = AC + AD.
CD = 300 + 300√(3)
CD = 300(√(3) + 1)
CD ≈ 819.6 m
Answer: the distance between the two boats is 300(√(3) + 1) m ≈ 819.6 m

Q: Q7. The angle of elevation of the top of a cliff is 30°. Walking 210 metre from the point towards the cliff, the angle of elevation becomes 45°. Find the height of cliff.

Ans: Diagram: the cliff is the vertical side of height h, with foot at F and top at T; the first observation point is P, at distance (x + 210) m from F, where the angle of elevation of T is 30°; after walking 210 m towards the cliff the observer is at Q, at distance x from F, where the angle of elevation of T is 45°; PQ = 210 m and Q lies between P and F.
In a right triangle, tan θ = (opposite side)/(adjacent side).
From the nearer point Q, with angle of elevation 45°:
tan 45° = h/x
Using tan 45° = 1.
1 = h/x, so x = h
From the farther point P, with angle of elevation 30°:
tan 30° = h/(x + 210)
Using tan 30° = 1/√(3) and x = h.
1/√(3) = h/(h + 210)
h + 210 = h√(3)
210 = h√(3) - h
210 = h(√(3) - 1)
h = 210/(√(3) - 1)
h ≈ 286.87
Answer: the height of the cliff is 210/(√(3) - 1) m ≈ 286.87 m

mcqs.q: A building 21 m tall casts a shadow 25 m long. The angle of elevation θ of the sun satisfies:
mcqs.why: In the right triangle, the building is the side opposite θ and the shadow is the side adjacent to θ. Use tan θ = opposite/adjacent and substitute: tan θ = 21/25 = 0.84.

mcqs.q: A building 21 m tall casts a shadow 25 m long. The angle of elevation of the sun, to the nearest degree, is:
mcqs.why: Use tan θ = opposite/adjacent = 21/25 = 0.84. Then θ = tan⁻¹(0.84) ≈ 40.03°, which to the nearest degree is 40°.

mcqs.q: A lighthouse is 150 m above sea level and the angle of depression of a boat is 60°. The distance of the boat from the lighthouse is:
mcqs.why: The depression 60° equals the elevation at the boat. Use tan 60° = opposite/adjacent = 150/AC, with tan 60° = √3: AC = 150/√3 = (150√3)/3 = 50√3 ≈ 86.60 m.

mcqs.q: A tree is 50 m high. The angle of elevation of its top from a point 100 m from its foot is approximately:
mcqs.why: Use tan θ = opposite/adjacent with the tree as opposite and the ground distance as adjacent: tan θ = 50/100 = 0.5. Then θ = tan⁻¹(0.5) ≈ 26.565°, approximately 26.56°.

mcqs.q: From the top of a 240 m hill, the angles of depression of the bottom and top of a minaret are 60° and 30°. The height of the minaret is:
A helicopter at 800 feet sights a car at an angle of depression of 72°. The distance of the car from the point directly below the helicopter, to the nearest foot, is:
mcqs.why: The depression 72° equals the elevation at the car. Use tan 72° = 800/d, so d = 800/(tan 72°) = 800/3.0777 ≈ 259.94 feet, which to the nearest foot is 260 feet.

mcqs.q: Two boats on opposite sides of a 300 m lighthouse have angles of depression 45° and 30°. The distance between the boats is approximately:
The angle of elevation of a cliff top is 30°; after walking 210 m towards the cliff it is 45°. The height of the cliff is approximately:
mcqs.why: From the nearer point tan 45° = h/x gives x = h. From the farther point tan 30° = h/(x + 210), so 1/√3 = h/(h + 210), giving h + 210 = h√3 and h = 210/(√3 - 1) ≈ 286.87 m.

mcqs.q: In these problems, the angle of depression from the top of an object is used as the angle of elevation at the lower point because they are:
mcqs.why: The horizontal line through the top and the horizontal ground line are parallel, cut by the line of sight. The angle of depression and the angle of elevation are alternate interior angles, so they are equal, as used in the lighthouse and helicopter solutions.

mcqs.q: For an angle of elevation problem in this exercise, the ratio used with the vertical height and the horizontal distance is:
mcqs.why: The known or required sides are the vertical height (opposite the angle) and the horizontal distance (adjacent to the angle), with no hypotenuse involved. The ratio connecting opposite and adjacent is tan θ = opposite/adjacent.

lessons.title: Review Exercise 7
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • The angle of elevation is the angle between the horizontal line and the line of sight to an object above the observer's level
  • cot θ = cos θ/sin θ and 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ
  • 45° = π/4 radians; a minute hand turns through 3π/2 radians in 45 minutes and 2π radians in one hour
  • Coterminal angles: 190° gives 550° and -170°; -250° gives 110° and -610°
  • 390° is coterminal with 30° and -240° with 120°, giving the standard-ratio values for both angles
  • sec θ = 2 with θ not in the 1st quadrant places θ in the 4th quadrant, giving cos θ = 1/2, sin θ = -√3/2, tan θ = -√3, cot θ = -1/√3 and cosec θ = -2/√3
  • 45°35'30" ≈ 45.5917° and 216.67° = 216°40'12"
  • From 125 feet with an angle of elevation of 57.2°, a tower's height is 125 × tan 57.2° ≈ 194 feet

Solved Exercises

Q: Q1(i). If an object is above the level of observer then the angle formed between the horizontal line and observer's line of sight is called ______.

Options: (a) angle of depression (b) angle of elevation (c) obtuse angle (d) none of the above

Correct answer: angle of elevation

Q: Q1(ii). cot θ = ______.

Options: (a) (sin θ)/(cos θ) (b) 1/(cos θ) (c) (cos θ)/(sin θ) (d) 1/(sin θ)

Correct answer: (cos θ)/(sin θ)

Q: Q1(iii). 1 + tan²θ = ______.

Options: (a) sin²θ (b) cos²θ (c) cosec²θ (d) sec²θ

Correct answer: sec²θ

Q: Q1(iv). If tan θ = 1 then sin θ = ______ when θ lies in 3rd quadrant.

Options: (a) 1/2 (b) -1/2 (c) -(1/√(2)) (d) 1/√(2)

Correct answer: -(1/√(2))

Q: Q1(v). Sin (-350°) lies in ______.

Options: (a) 1st quadrant (b) 2nd quadrant (c) 3rd quadrant (d) 4th quadrant

Correct answer: 1st quadrant

Q: Q1(vi). 45° = ______ radian.

Options: (a) π/3 (b) π/4 (c) π/6 (d) π/2

Correct answer: π/4

Q: Q1(vii). If the measure of the hypotenuse of a right triangle is 5 feet and m∠B = 58°, what is the measure of the leg adjacent to ∠B?

Options: (a) 4.2402 (b) 8.0017 (c) 0.10060 (d) 2.6496

Correct answer: 2.6496

Q: Q1(viii). Find the value of tan P to the nearest tenth. (In the diagram, △MNP is right-angled at N, MN = 8 cm, NP = 21 cm and the angle at P is marked 20°.)

Options: (a) 2.6 (b) 0.5 (c) 0.4 (d) 0.1

Correct answer: 0.4

Q: Q1(ix). In the diagram, △QRS has vertex R at the top, RT is drawn from R perpendicular to QS at T, QR = 4 and QT = 2. RT is equal to TS. What is RT? (Question printed as: "RT is equal to TS. What is ∠S?", with length options.)

Options: (a) 2√(6) (b) 2√(3) (c) 4√(3) (d) 2√(2)

Correct answer: 2√(3)

Q: Q1(x). In the same diagram (△QRS, RT perpendicular to QS at T, QR = 4, QT = 2), RT is equal to TS. What is ∠S?

Options: (a) 25° (b) 30° (c) 45° (d) 60°

Correct answer: 45°

Q: Q2. Convert 45°35'30" into decimal form.

Ans: In the sexagesimal system, 1' = (1/60)° and 1" = (1/3600)°.
45°35'30" = [45 + 35 × (1/60) + 30 × (1/3600)]°
35 × (1/60) = 0.58333
30 × (1/3600) = 0.00833
45°35'30" = [45 + 0.58333 + 0.00833]°
Answer: 45°35'30" ≈ 45.5917°

Q: Q3. Convert 216.67° into D°M'S" form.

Ans: In the sexagesimal system, 1° = 60' and 1' = 60".
216.67° = 216° + (0.67)°
(0.67)° = (0.67 × 60)' = (40.2)'
216.67° = 216° + 40' + (0.2)'
(0.2)' = (0.2 × 60)" = 12"
Answer: 216.67° = 216°40'12"

Q: Q4(i). Through how many radians does a minute hand of a clock turn through in 45 minutes?

Ans: The minute hand makes one complete revolution in 60 minutes.
One complete revolution = 2π radians.
In 1 minute the minute hand turns through (2π/60) radians.
In 45 minutes it turns through 45 × (2π/60) radians.
45 × (2π/60) = (90π/60) = (3π/2)
Answer: the minute hand turns through (3π/2) radians in 45 minutes

Q: Q4(ii). Through how many radians does a minute hand of a clock turn through in one hour?

Ans: The minute hand makes one complete revolution in one hour (60 minutes).
One complete revolution = 360° = 2π radians.
Answer: the minute hand turns through 2π radians in one hour

Q: Q5(i). Find coterminal angle of 190°.

Ans: Coterminal angles differ by a multiple of 360°; add 360° for a positive coterminal angle and subtract 360° for a negative coterminal angle.
190° + 360° = 550°
190° - 360° = -170°
Answer: the coterminal angles of 190° are 550° and -170°

Q: Q5(ii). Find coterminal angle of -250°.

Ans: Coterminal angles differ by a multiple of 360°; add 360° for a positive coterminal angle and subtract 360° for a negative coterminal angle.
-250° + 360° = 110°
-250° - 360° = -610°
Answer: the coterminal angles of -250° are 110° and -610°

Q: Q6(i). Find trigonometric ratios of 390°.

Ans: 390° = 360° + 30°, so 390° is coterminal with 30°, which lies in the 1st quadrant, where all ratios are positive.
Use the standard values for 30°: sin 30° = 1/2 and cos 30° = √(3)/2.
sin 390° = sin 30° = 1/2
cos 390° = cos 30° = √(3)/2
tan 390° = tan 30° = 1/√(3)
cosec 390° = 1/(sin 30°) = 2
sec 390° = 1/(cos 30°) = 2/√(3)
cot 390° = 1/(tan 30°) = √(3)
Answer: sin 390° = 1/2, cos 390° = √(3)/2, tan 390° = 1/√(3), cosec 390° = 2, sec 390° = 2/√(3), cot 390° = √(3)

Q: Q6(ii). Find trigonometric ratios of -240°.

Ans: -240° + 360° = 120°, so -240° is coterminal with 120°, which lies in the 2nd quadrant, where only sin θ and cosec θ are positive.
120° = 180° - 60°, so its ratios have the magnitudes of the 60° ratios: sin 60° = √(3)/2 and cos 60° = 1/2.
sin(-240°) = sin 120° = √(3)/2
cos(-240°) = cos 120° = -1/2
tan(-240°) = (sin 120°)/(cos 120°) = (√(3)/2)/(-1/2) = -√(3)
cosec(-240°) = 1/(sin 120°) = 2/√(3)
sec(-240°) = 1/(cos 120°) = -2
cot(-240°) = 1/(tan 120°) = -(1/√(3))
Answer: sin(-240°) = √(3)/2, cos(-240°) = -1/2, tan(-240°) = -√(3), cosec(-240°) = 2/√(3), sec(-240°) = -2, cot(-240°) = -(1/√(3))

Q: Q7(i). Prove that √((1 - sin θ)/(1 + sin θ)) = sec θ - tan θ.

Ans: Take the left-hand side.
L.H.S = √((1 - sin θ)/(1 + sin θ))
Multiply numerator and denominator inside the root by (1 - sin θ).
L.H.S = √(((1 - sin θ)(1 - sin θ))/((1 + sin θ)(1 - sin θ)))
L.H.S = √((1 - sin θ)²/(1 - sin²θ))
Using the identity sin²θ + cos²θ = 1, so 1 - sin²θ = cos²θ.
L.H.S = √((1 - sin θ)²/(cos²θ))
Taking the square root.
L.H.S = (1 - sin θ)/(cos θ)
L.H.S = 1/(cos θ) - (sin θ)/(cos θ)
Using sec θ = 1/(cos θ) and tan θ = (sin θ)/(cos θ).
L.H.S = sec θ - tan θ
L.H.S = R.H.S
Answer: √((1 - sin θ)/(1 + sin θ)) = sec θ - tan θ, proved

Q: Q7(ii). Prove that 2 cos θ sec θ - tan θ cot θ = 1.

Ans: Take the left-hand side.
L.H.S = 2 cos θ sec θ - tan θ cot θ
Using sec θ = 1/(cos θ).
2 cos θ sec θ = 2 cos θ × (1/(cos θ)) = 2
Using cot θ = 1/(tan θ).
tan θ cot θ = tan θ × (1/(tan θ)) = 1
L.H.S = 2 - 1
L.H.S = 1
L.H.S = R.H.S
Answer: 2 cos θ sec θ - tan θ cot θ = 1, proved

Q: Q8. If sec θ = 2 and θ does not lie in first quadrant. Find remaining trigonometric ratios.

Ans: sec θ = 2 is positive; sec θ is positive in the 1st and 4th quadrants.
θ does not lie in the 1st quadrant, so θ lies in the 4th quadrant, where x > 0 and y < 0.
For a point P(x, y) on the terminal side of θ, with r = OP, the ratios are sin θ = y/r, cos θ = x/r, tan θ = y/x, cot θ = x/y, sec θ = r/x and cosec θ = r/y.
Given sec θ = (r)/(x) = 2/1, take r = 2 and x = 1, so cos θ = (x)/(r) = 1/2.
By Pythagoras' theorem: r² = x² + y²
y² = r² - x²
y² = (2)² - (1)² = 4 - 1 = 3
y = ±√(3)
θ lies in the 4th quadrant, where y < 0, so y = -√(3).
sin θ = (y)/(r) = (-√(3))/2
tan θ = (y)/(x) = (-√(3))/1 = -√(3)
cot θ = (x)/(y) = 1/(-√(3)) = -(1/√(3))
cosec θ = (r)/(y) = 2/(-√(3)) = -(2/√(3))
Answer: cos θ = 1/2, sin θ = -(√(3))/2, tan θ = -√(3), cot θ = -(1/√(3)), cosec θ = -(2/√(3))

Q: Q9. Refer to the diagram shown. What is the height of the building?

Ans: Diagram: an observer's instrument, 1.6 m high, stands on the ground at a horizontal distance of 85 m from a building; from the top of the instrument the angle of elevation of the top of the building is 28.8°; the horizontal line from the instrument meets the building at a height of 1.6 m.
Let h be the height of the top of the building above the level of the instrument.
In a right triangle, tan θ = (opposite side)/(adjacent side).
For the angle 28.8°, the opposite side is h and the adjacent side is 85 m.
tan 28.8° = h/85
h = 85 × tan 28.8°
tan 28.8° ≈ 0.5498
h ≈ 85 × 0.5498
h ≈ 46.73 m
Total height of the building = h + height of the instrument
Total height ≈ 46.73 + 1.6
Answer: the height of the building is ≈ 48.3 m
Note: the book's printed answer key gives 44 m (approximately), which does not follow from the diagram values as they appear in the scan (28.8°, 85 m, 1.6 m); one of the faint digits in the diagram may be misread in the scan.

Q: Q10. From a point on level ground 125 feet from the base of a tower, the angle of elevation is 57.2°. Approximate the height of the tower to the nearest foot.

Ans: Diagram: the tower is the vertical side of a right triangle, of height h (marked a in the book's figure); the observation point is on level ground 125 ft horizontally from the base of the tower; the angle of elevation from that point to the top of the tower is 57.2°, and the line of sight is the hypotenuse.
In a right triangle, tan θ = (opposite side)/(adjacent side).
For the angle 57.2°, the opposite side is the height h and the adjacent side is 125 ft.
tan 57.2° = h/125
h = 125 × tan 57.2°
tan 57.2° ≈ 1.5517
h ≈ 125 × 1.5517
h ≈ 193.96
Answer: the height of the tower is ≈ 194 feet

mcqs.q: If an object is above the level of observer then the angle formed between the horizontal line and observer's line of sight is called ______.
mcqs.why: An object above the observer's level is viewed by looking upward, and the angle between the horizontal line and the upward line of sight is defined as the angle of elevation. (The book's fourth option was a none-type option; it has been replaced here with the explicit option 'right angle', keeping the book's keyed answer.)

By definition cot θ is the reciprocal of tan θ = sin θ/cos θ, and the solved items define cot θ = x/y = (cos θ)/(sin θ) since cos θ = x/r and sin θ = y/r. So cot θ = (cos θ)/(sin θ), the book's keyed answer.
This is the Pythagorean identity 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ, used in Exercise 7.5 in the form sec²θ - 1 = tan²θ. So the expression equals sec²θ, the book's keyed answer.

mcqs.q: If tan θ = 1 then sin θ = ______ when θ lies in 3rd quadrant.
mcqs.why: tan θ = 1 with θ in the 3rd quadrant gives the reference angle 45° at 225°, where x and y are equal in magnitude and both negative. Hence sin θ = y/r = -1/√2, i.e. -(1/√(2)), the book's keyed answer.
Reduce the angle: -350° + 360° = 10°, so -350° is coterminal with 10°. Since 0° < 10° < 90°, the angle lies in the 1st quadrant, the book's keyed answer.
Use radians = degrees × (π/180). Substitute: 45 × (π/180) = 45π/180 = π/4 after dividing numerator and denominator by 45. So 45° = π/4 radian, the book's keyed answer.

mcqs.q: If the measure of the hypotenuse of a right triangle is 5 feet and m∠B = 58°, what is the measure of the leg adjacent to ∠B?
mcqs.why: Use cos B = adjacent/hypotenuse, so adjacent = hypotenuse × cos B. Substitute: adjacent = 5 × cos 58° = 5 × 0.52992 ≈ 2.6496 feet, the book's keyed answer.

mcqs.q: Find the value of tan P to the nearest tenth. (In the diagram, △MNP is right-angled at N, MN = 8 cm, NP = 21 cm and the angle at P is marked 20°.)
mcqs.why: For angle P, the opposite side is MN = 8 cm and the adjacent side is NP = 21 cm. Use tan P = opposite/adjacent = 8/21 ≈ 0.381, which to the nearest tenth is 0.4, the book's keyed answer.

mcqs.q: In the diagram, △QRS has vertex R at the top, RT is drawn from R perpendicular to QS at T, QR = 4 and QT = 2. RT is equal to TS. What is RT?
mcqs.why: In right triangle QRT, use Pythagoras: RT² = QR² - QT². Substitute QR = 4 and QT = 2: RT² = 16 - 4 = 12, so RT = √12 = 2√3, the book's keyed answer.

mcqs.q: In the same diagram (△QRS, RT perpendicular to QS at T, QR = 4, QT = 2), RT is equal to TS. What is ∠S?
mcqs.why: From the previous part RT = 2√3, and RT is equal to TS, so in right triangle RTS, tan S = opposite/adjacent = RT/TS = (2√3)/(2√3) = 1. The angle whose tangent is 1 is 45°, so ∠S = 45°, the book's keyed answer.

mcqs.q: 45°35'30" in decimal form is approximately:
216.67° in D°M'S" form is:
Through how many radians does the minute hand of a clock turn in 45 minutes?
mcqs.why: The minute hand makes one revolution (2π radians) in 60 minutes, so in 1 minute it turns (2π/60) radians. In 45 minutes: 45 × (2π/60) = 90π/60 = 3π/2 radians.

mcqs.q: A coterminal angle pair for 190° (positive and negative) is:
mcqs.why: Add one complete turn for the positive angle: 190° + 360° = 550°. Subtract one complete turn for the negative angle: 190° - 360° = -170°. So the pair is 550° and -170°.
Add 360°: -240° + 360° = 120°, which is 180° - 60° in the 2nd quadrant, where sin is positive with the magnitude of sin 60°. So sin(-240°) = sin 120° = sin 60° = √3/2.

chapters.title: Unit 8: Projection of a Side of a Triangle

lessons.title: Exercise 8.1
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Theorem 8.1: in an obtuse-angled triangle, the square on the side opposite the obtuse angle equals the sum of the squares on the sides containing the obtuse angle plus twice one containing side times the projection of the other on it.
  • Theorem 8.2: the square on the side opposite an acute angle equals the sum of the squares on the sides containing that acute angle diminished by twice one containing side times the projection of the other on it.
  • An angle is obtuse when the square on the opposite side is greater than the sum of the squares on the containing sides, and acute when it is less (converse of Pythagoras).
  • With mAB = 6 cm, mBC = 10 cm, angle B = 120 degrees and projection of BC on AB = 5 cm, Theorem 8.1 gives mAC = 14 cm.
  • With mAB = 3 cm, mBC = 5 cm and mAC = 7 cm, angle B is obtuse and the projection of BC on AB is 2.5 cm.
  • With a = 7, b = 11 and c = 8, angle A is acute and the projection of AC on AB is 8.5.
  • In parallelogram ABCD with mAB = 4 cm, mAD = 5 cm and diagonal mAC = 7 cm, angles B and D are obtuse and angles A and C are acute.

Solved Exercises

Q: Q1. In △ABC, mAB = 6cm, mBC = 10cm, m∠B = 120°. The projection of BC on AB is 5 cm. Find mAC.

Ans: Diagram: △ABC with vertex B at the left, base BC = 10 cm going to the right, side BA = 6 cm going up from B, vertex A at the top, side AC closing the triangle on the right, and ∠B = 120° marked obtuse at B; the projection of BC on AB is 5 cm.
∠B = 120° is an obtuse angle, so AC is the side opposite the obtuse angle.
By Theorem 8.1 (in an obtuse-angled triangle, the square on the side opposite the obtuse angle is equal to the sum of the squares on the sides containing the obtuse angle together with twice the rectangle contained by one of those sides and the projection on it of the other):
(mAC)² = (mAB)² + (mBC)² + 2(mAB)(projection of BC on AB)
Substitute mAB = 6 cm, mBC = 10 cm and projection = 5 cm:
(mAC)² = 6² + 10² + 2(6)(5)
(mAC)² = 36 + 100 + 60
(mAC)² = 196
Taking the square root of both sides:
mAC = 14 cm
Answer: mAC = 14 cm

Q: Q2. In △ABC, mAB = 3cm, mBC = 5cm, mAC = 7cm. Find the projection of BC on AB.

Ans: Diagram: △ABC with side AB = 3 cm, side BC = 5 cm and side AC = 7 cm; the perpendicular from C falls on AB produced beyond B, and its foot segment on the line of AB is the projection of BC on AB.
First check the angle at B, which is contained by AB and BC.
By the converse of Pythagoras' theorem, compare (mAC)² with (mAB)² + (mBC)²:
(mAB)² + (mBC)² = 3² + 5² = 9 + 25 = 34
(mAC)² = 7² = 49
Since 49 > 34, ∠B is obtuse, so Theorem 8.1 applies at B.
By Theorem 8.1 (square on the side opposite the obtuse angle = sum of squares on the containing sides + twice one containing side × projection of the other on it):
(mAC)² = (mAB)² + (mBC)² + 2(mAB)(projection of BC on AB)
Let the required projection be p. Substitute mAC = 7 cm, mAB = 3 cm, mBC = 5 cm:
49 = 9 + 25 + 2(3)(p)
49 = 34 + 6p
6p = 49 - 34 = 15
p = 15/6 = 2.5 cm
Answer: The projection of BC on AB is 2.5 cm

Q: Q3. In △ABC, a = 7, b = 11, c = 8. Calculate the projection of AC on AB.

Ans: Diagram: △ABC with the book's notation mBC = a = 7 opposite A, mAC = b = 11 opposite B and mAB = c = 8 opposite C; the perpendicular from C meets AB at a foot inside the segment, and the segment from A to that foot is the projection of AC on AB.
The projection of AC on AB is found from the angle at A, contained by AB and AC.
First check whether ∠A is acute, using the side opposite it, a = 7:
b² + c² = 11² + 8² = 121 + 64 = 185
Since a² = 49 < 185, ∠A is acute, so Theorem 8.2 applies at A.
By Theorem 8.2 (in any triangle, the square on the side opposite an acute angle is equal to the sum of the squares on the sides containing that acute angle diminished by twice the rectangle contained by one of those sides and the projection on it of the other):
a² = b² + c² - 2(c)(projection of AC on AB)
Let the required projection be p. Substitute a = 7, b = 11, c = 8:
49 = 121 + 64 - 2(8)(p)
49 = 185 - 16p
16p = 185 - 49 = 136
p = 136/16 = 8.5
Answer: The projection of AC on AB is 8.5

Q: Q4. In a parallelogram ABCD, mAB = 4cm, mAC = 7cm, mAD = 5cm. Find which of the angles of the parallelogram are obtuse.

Ans: Diagram: Parallelogram ABCD in order, with AB = 4 cm along the bottom, AD = 5 cm up the left side, DC = AB = 4 cm along the top, BC = AD = 5 cm up the right side, and diagonal AC = 7 cm drawn from bottom-left A to top-right C.
In a parallelogram, opposite sides are equal, so mBC = mAD = 5 cm and mDC = mAB = 4 cm.
Consider △ABC, in which the diagonal AC = 7 cm is opposite ∠B.
Compare (mAC)² with (mAB)² + (mBC)²:
(mAB)² + (mBC)² = 4² + 5² = 16 + 25 = 41
(mAC)² = 7² = 49
Since 49 > 41, by the converse of Pythagoras' theorem ∠B is obtuse.
Consider △ADC, in which the diagonal AC = 7 cm is opposite ∠D.
(mAD)² + (mDC)² = 5² + 4² = 25 + 16 = 41 < 49 = (mAC)²
So ∠D is also obtuse.
In a parallelogram opposite angles are equal and adjacent angles are supplementary, so ∠A = ∠C = 180° - ∠B are acute.
Answer: ∠B and ∠D are obtuse (and ∠A and ∠C are acute)

mcqs.q: According to Theorem 8.1, for the side opposite an obtuse angle, (side opposite)² is equal to:
options: sum of squares on the containing sides minus twice one side times the projection
sum of squares on the containing sides plus twice one side times the projection of the other on it
the product of the two containing sides only
the sum of the two containing sides plus the projection
mcqs.why: Theorem 8.1 states the square on the side opposite the obtuse angle equals the sum of the squares on the containing sides together with twice the rectangle of one containing side and the projection of the other.

mcqs.q: In triangle ABC, mAB = 6 cm, mBC = 10 cm, angle B = 120° and the projection of BC on AB is 5 cm. Find mAC.
mcqs.why: By Theorem 8.1: (mAC)² = (mAB)² + (mBC)² + 2(mAB)(projection) = 6² + 10² + 2(6)(5) = 36 + 100 + 60 = 196, so mAC = √196 = 14 cm.

mcqs.q: In triangle ABC, mAB = 3 cm, mBC = 5 cm and mAC = 7 cm. The projection of BC on AB is:
mcqs.why: Since 7² = 49 > 3² + 5² = 34, angle B is obtuse. By Theorem 8.1: 49 = 9 + 25 + 2(3)p = 34 + 6p, so 6p = 15 and p = 2.5 cm.

mcqs.q: In triangle ABC, a = 7, b = 11 and c = 8. The projection of AC on AB is:
mcqs.why: Angle A is acute because a² = 49 < b² + c² = 121 + 64 = 185. By Theorem 8.2: 49 = 121 + 64 − 2(8)p = 185 − 16p, so 16p = 136 and p = 8.5.

mcqs.q: In triangle ABC with mAB = 3 cm, mBC = 5 cm and mAC = 7 cm, angle B is obtuse because:
options: mAC is the shortest side of the triangle
mcqs.why: Compare the squares: (mAB)² + (mBC)² = 9 + 25 = 34 while (mAC)² = 49. Since 49 > 34, by the converse of Pythagoras the angle B opposite AC is obtuse.

mcqs.q: In triangle ABC with a = 7, b = 11 and c = 8, angle A is acute because:
options: a² = 49 is greater than b² + c² = 185
a² = 49 is equal to b² + c² = 185
a² = 49 is less than b² + c² = 185
a is the longest side of the triangle
mcqs.why: Compute b² + c² = 11² + 8² = 121 + 64 = 185 and a² = 7² = 49. Since 49 < 185, the angle A opposite side a is acute, so Theorem 8.2 applies at A.

mcqs.q: In parallelogram ABCD, mAB = 4 cm, mAC = 7 cm and mAD = 5 cm. Which angles are obtuse?
mcqs.why: In triangle ABC, (mAB)² + (mBC)² = 16 + 25 = 41 < 49 = (mAC)², so angle B is obtuse; likewise angle D is obtuse in triangle ADC, and opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal.

mcqs.q: According to Theorem 8.2, for the side a opposite an acute angle A contained by sides b and c, with p the projection of AC on AB:
mcqs.why: Theorem 8.2 says the square on the side opposite an acute angle equals the sum of the squares on the containing sides diminished by twice one containing side times the projection, giving a² = b² + c² − 2cp.

mcqs.q: In the question with mAB = 6 cm, mBC = 10 cm and projection 5 cm, the value of (mAC)² before taking the square root is:
mcqs.why: By Theorem 8.1: (mAC)² = 6² + 10² + 2(6)(5). Step by step: 36 + 100 = 136, then 136 + 60 = 196, and only then mAC = √196 = 14 cm.

mcqs.q: In parallelogram ABCD with angles B and D obtuse, angles A and C must be:
mcqs.why: Adjacent angles of a parallelogram are supplementary, so angle A = 180° − angle B. Since angle B is obtuse (greater than 90°), angle A is less than 90°, that is acute, and angle C equals angle A.

lessons.title: Exercise 8.2
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Apollonius theorem: the sum of the squares on any two sides of a triangle equals twice the square on half the third side plus twice the square on the median which bisects the third side.
  • For a median m to a side a with other sides b and c: m² = (2b² + 2c² − a²)/4.
  • The medians of the triangle with sides 10 cm, 12 cm and 16 cm are 5√7 cm, √142 cm and √58 cm.
  • In triangle ABC with mAB = 4 cm, mBC = 5 cm, mAC = 6 cm and D the midpoint of BC, the median mAD = √79/2 cm.
  • In triangle ABC with mBC = 4 cm, mAC = 12 cm and angle C = 120°, mCD = 6 cm, mAD = 6√3 cm and mAB = 4√13 cm, where CD is the projection of AC on BC produced.
  • Right-triangle projection theorem: the square on a leg equals the rectangle contained by the hypotenuse and the projection of that leg on the hypotenuse.
  • In the right triangle with angle B = 90°, mAB = 6 cm and mBC = 5 cm, mAC = √61 cm, mAD = 36/√61 cm and mCD = 25/√61 cm.

Solved Exercises

Q: Q1. Using Apollonius theorem find the length of the medians of a triangle having sides 10 cm, 12 cm and 16 cm respectively.

Ans: Diagram: A triangle whose three sides measure 10 cm, 12 cm and 16 cm, with a median drawn from a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side in each of the three cases.
By Apollonius' theorem: if a median of length m is drawn to a side of length a in a triangle with other sides b and c, then b² + c² = 2m² + 2(a/2)², that is, m² = (2b² + 2c² - a²)/4.
Median to the side of length 10 cm (here a = 10, b = 12, c = 16):
m² = (2(12)² + 2(16)² - (10)²)/4
m² = (288 + 512 - 100)/4 = 700/4 = 175
m = √175 = 5√7 cm
Median to the side of length 12 cm (here a = 12, b = 10, c = 16):
m² = (2(10)² + 2(16)² - (12)²)/4
m² = (200 + 512 - 144)/4 = 568/4 = 142
m = √142 cm
Median to the side of length 16 cm (here a = 16, b = 10, c = 12):
m² = (2(10)² + 2(12)² - (16)²)/4
m² = (200 + 288 - 256)/4 = 232/4 = 58
m = √58 cm
Answer: The three medians are 5√7 cm, √142 cm and √58 cm

Q: Q2. In △ABC, D is the mid-point of BC. Find the length of the median if mAB = 4cm, mBC = 5cm and mAC = 6cm.

Ans: Diagram: △ABC with A at the top, BC = 5 cm as the base, AB = 4 cm on the left, AC = 6 cm on the right, D the midpoint of BC, and median AD drawn from A down to D.
D is the midpoint of BC, so mBD = mDC = 5/2 = 2.5 cm.
By Apollonius' theorem (the sum of the squares on any two sides is equal to twice the square on half the third side together with twice the square on the median which bisects the third side):
(mAB)² + (mAC)² = 2(mBD)² + 2(mAD)²
Substitute mAB = 4 cm, mAC = 6 cm, mBD = 2.5 cm:
16 + 36 = 2(2.5)² + 2(mAD)²
52 = 12.5 + 2(mAD)²
2(mAD)² = 52 - 12.5 = 39.5
(mAD)² = 19.75 = 79/4
Taking the square root of both sides:
mAD = √79/2 cm
Answer: The length of the median is √79/2 cm

Q: Q3. △ABC is given with mBC = 4cm, mAC = 12cm and m∠C = 120°. Find mCD, mAD, mAB and then verify Apollonius theorem. (In the figure, AD is perpendicular to BC produced, meeting it at D, and CD = p.)

Ans: Diagram: B at the left and C to its right on a horizontal line with BC = 4 cm, the line produced beyond C to D, A above D, AC = 12 cm slanting from A down-left to C with ∠ACB = 120° marked obtuse at C, AD vertical with a right-angle mark at D, and CD labelled p.
∠ACB = 120°, so its supplementary angle at C on the straight line BD is:
m∠ACD = 180° - 120° = 60°
In the right-angled △ADC, by the trigonometric ratio cos in △ADC:
cos 60° = mCD/mAC
(1)/(2) = mCD/12
mCD = 12 × (1)/(2) = 6 cm
By Pythagoras' theorem in △ADC:
(mAC)² = (mCD)² + (mAD)²
144 = 36 + (mAD)²
(mAD)² = 108
mAD = √108 = 6√3 cm
Now ∠C = 120° is obtuse in △ABC, and CD is the projection of AC on BC produced.
By Theorem 8.1 (obtuse-angle projection theorem):
(mAB)² = (mBC)² + (mAC)² + 2(mBC)(mCD)
(mAB)² = 4² + 12² + 2(4)(6) = 16 + 144 + 48 = 208
mAB = √208 = 4√13 cm
Verification of Apollonius' theorem: Take △ABD, in which BD = BC + CD = 4 + 6 = 10 cm. Let M be the midpoint of BD, so mBM = 5 cm, and AM is a median of △ABD. M lies 5 cm from B, that is 1 cm beyond C, so mMD = 5 cm and the horizontal distance from M to D is 5 cm while mAD = 6√3 cm.
By Pythagoras' theorem in the right triangle with vertex A, foot D and horizontal leg MD:
(mAM)² = (mAD)² + (mMD)² = 108 + 25 = 133
By Apollonius' theorem applied to △ABD with median AM:
(mAB)² + (mAD)² should equal 2(mAM)² + 2(mBM)²
Left side: 208 + 108 = 316
Right side: 2(133) + 2(25) = 266 + 50 = 316
The two sides are equal, so Apollonius' theorem is verified.
Answer: mCD = 6 cm, mAD = 6√3 cm, mAB = 4√13 cm, and Apollonius' theorem is verified

Q: Q4. △ABC is a right triangle with m∠B = 90° and BD ⊥ AC. If mAB = 6cm and mBC = 5cm, find mAD and mCD. Verify your answer with Pythagorean theorem.

Ans: Diagram: △ABC right-angled at B, with AB = 6 cm, BC = 5 cm, hypotenuse AC slanting across, and D the foot of the perpendicular from B onto AC, so BD ⊥ AC and D divides AC into AD and CD.
By Pythagoras' theorem in △ABC:
(mAC)² = (mAB)² + (mBC)² = 6² + 5² = 36 + 25 = 61
mAC = √61 cm
In a right triangle, the square on a leg is equal to the rectangle contained by the hypotenuse and the projection of that leg on the hypotenuse (projection theorem for a right triangle).
For leg AB, whose projection on AC is AD:
(mAB)² = (mAD)(mAC)
36 = (mAD)(√61)
mAD = 36/√61 cm
For leg BC, whose projection on AC is CD:
(mBC)² = (mCD)(mAC)
25 = (mCD)(√61)
mCD = 25/√61 cm
Check: mAD + mCD = (36 + 25)/√61 = 61/√61 = √61 = mAC, as required.
Verification with Pythagoras' theorem: First find BD from the area of △ABC written in two ways:
(1)/(2)(mAB)(mBC) = (1)/(2)(mAC)(mBD)
(6)(5) = (√61)(mBD)
mBD = 30/√61 cm
By Pythagoras' theorem in △ABD:
(mAD)² + (mBD)² = (36/√61)² + (30/√61)² = (1296 + 900)/61 = 2196/61 = 36 = (mAB)², which checks.
By Pythagoras' theorem in △CBD:
(mCD)² + (mBD)² = (25/√61)² + (30/√61)² = (625 + 900)/61 = 1525/61 = 25 = (mBC)², which checks.
Answer: mAD = 36/√61 cm and mCD = 25/√61 cm, verified by Pythagoras' theorem

mcqs.q: Apollonius theorem states that if D is the midpoint of BC in triangle ABC, then:
mcqs.why: Apollonius theorem: the sum of the squares on any two sides equals twice the square on half the third side together with twice the square on the median bisecting that side, i.e. (mAB)² + (mAC)² = 2(mBD)² + 2(mAD)².

mcqs.q: Using Apollonius theorem, the median to the side of length 10 cm in a triangle with sides 10 cm, 12 cm and 16 cm is:
Using Apollonius theorem, the median to the side of length 16 cm in a triangle with sides 10 cm, 12 cm and 16 cm is:
In triangle ABC, D is the midpoint of BC, mAB = 4 cm, mBC = 5 cm and mAC = 6 cm. The median mAD is:
mcqs.why: mBD = 5/2 = 2.5 cm. By Apollonius: 4² + 6² = 2(2.5)² + 2(mAD)², so 52 = 12.5 + 2(mAD)², giving (mAD)² = 19.75 = 79/4 and mAD = √79/2 cm.

mcqs.q: In triangle ABC, mBC = 4 cm, mAC = 12 cm, angle C = 120°, and AD is perpendicular to BC produced at D. Then mCD is:
mcqs.why: Angle ACD = 180° − 120° = 60°. In right-angled triangle ADC, cos 60° = mCD/mAC, so 1/2 = mCD/12 and mCD = 12 × 1/2 = 6 cm.

mcqs.q: In the same triangle (mBC = 4 cm, mAC = 12 cm, angle C = 120°, mCD = 6 cm), mAD is:
mcqs.why: By Pythagoras in right-angled triangle ADC: (mAD)² = (mAC)² − (mCD)² = 144 − 36 = 108, so mAD = √108 = 6√3 cm.

mcqs.q: In the same triangle (mBC = 4 cm, mAC = 12 cm, angle C = 120°, mCD = 6 cm), mAB is:
mcqs.why: Angle C is obtuse and CD is the projection of AC on BC produced. By Theorem 8.1: (mAB)² = 4² + 12² + 2(4)(6) = 16 + 144 + 48 = 208, so mAB = √208 = 4√13 cm.

mcqs.q: Triangle ABC is right-angled at B with mAB = 6 cm and mBC = 5 cm. The hypotenuse mAC is:
mcqs.why: By Pythagoras theorem in triangle ABC: (mAC)² = (mAB)² + (mBC)² = 6² + 5² = 36 + 25 = 61, so mAC = √61 cm.

mcqs.q: In that right triangle (angle B = 90°, mAB = 6 cm, mAC = √61 cm, BD perpendicular to AC), mAD is:
mcqs.why: By the right-triangle projection theorem, (mAB)² = (mAD)(mAC). Substitute: 36 = (mAD)(√61), so mAD = 36/√61 cm.

mcqs.q: In that right triangle, the altitude mBD found from the two area expressions is:
mcqs.why: Area in two ways: (1/2)(mAB)(mBC) = (1/2)(mAC)(mBD), so (6)(5) = (√61)(mBD), giving 30 = √61 × mBD and mBD = 30/√61 cm.

lessons.title: Review Exercise 8
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Pythagoras was a Greek mathematician and Apollonius was a mathematician born in Perga.
  • For a triangle with sides 10, 17 and 21 units, the angle between the sides 10 and 17 is obtuse and the projection of the 10-unit side upon the 17-unit side is 26/17, about 1.53 units.
  • In the right triangle with angle A = 90°, mAB = 5 cm and mAC = 8 cm: mBC = √89 cm, mAD = 40/√89 cm and mBD = 25/√89 cm, where AD is perpendicular to BC.
  • The median BE to side AC in that triangle has length √41 cm, found both by Pythagoras theorem and by Apollonius theorem.
  • For the triangle with sides 10 and 17 on a base of 19 split by a perpendicular h into x and y: x = 86/19, y = 275/19 and h = (4√1794)/19.

Solved Exercises

Q: Q1(i). Pythagoras was a /an ______ mathematician.

Options: (a) Indian (b) Greek (c) Pakistani (d) Chinese

Correct answer: Greek

Q: Q1(ii). Apollonius was born in ______.

Options: (a) Perga (b) Istanbul (c) Islamabad (d) Kabul

Correct answer: Perga

Q: Q1(iii). Apollonius is the name of a ______.

Options: (a) City (b) Town (c) Country (d) Mathematician

Correct answer: Mathematician

Q: Q2. Find the projection of the side of measure 10 units upon the side of measure 17 units in a triangle whose sides respectively have measures 10, 17 and 21 units.

Ans: Diagram: A triangle with sides 10 units, 17 units and 21 units; the side of 21 units is opposite the angle contained by the sides of 10 and 17 units, and the perpendicular from the opposite vertex falls outside the side of 17 units, giving the projection of the 10-unit side upon the 17-unit side.
The angle between the sides of 10 and 17 units is opposite the side of 21 units.
Compare 21² with 10² + 17²:
10² + 17² = 100 + 289 = 389
21² = 441
Since 441 > 389, this angle is obtuse, so Theorem 8.1 applies.
Let p be the projection of the side of measure 10 units upon the side of measure 17 units.
By Theorem 8.1 (obtuse-angle projection theorem):
21² = 10² + 17² + 2(17)(p)
441 = 389 + 34p
34p = 441 - 389 = 52
p = 52/34 = 26/17 ≈ 1.53 units
Answer: The projection is approximately 1.53 units

Q: Q3. △ABC is a right-triangle with m∠A = 90°. From the vertex A perpendicular AD is drawn on BC. If mAB = 5 cm, mAC = 8 cm. Find mBC, mAD and mBD.

Ans: Diagram: △ABC right-angled at A, with AB = 5 cm on one side, AC = 8 cm on the other side, BC as the hypotenuse, and D the foot of the perpendicular from A onto BC, dividing BC into BD and DC.
By Pythagoras' theorem in △ABC:
(mBC)² = (mAB)² + (mAC)² = 5² + 8² = 25 + 64 = 89
mBC = √89 cm
Find AD by writing the area of △ABC in two ways:
(1)/(2)(mAB)(mAC) = (1)/(2)(mBC)(mAD)
(5)(8) = (√89)(mAD)
mAD = 40/√89 cm
In a right triangle, the square on a leg equals the rectangle of the hypotenuse and the projection of that leg on the hypotenuse.
For leg AB, whose projection on BC is BD:
(mAB)² = (mBD)(mBC)
25 = (mBD)(√89)
mBD = 25/√89 cm
Answer: mBC = √89 cm, mAD = 40/√89 cm and mBD = 25/√89 cm

Q: Q4(a). In the above question (△ABC right-angled at A with mAB = 5 cm, mAC = 8 cm and mBC = √89 cm), BE is a median. Find mBE using Pythagoras theorem.

Ans: Diagram: The same right triangle △ABC, right-angled at A, with AB = 5 cm, AC = 8 cm, BC = √89 cm, and E the midpoint of AC, with median BE drawn from B to E.
BE is a median from B, so E is the midpoint of AC.
Therefore mAE = (1)/(2)(mAC) = (1)/(2)(8) = 4 cm.
Since ∠A = 90°, △BAE is right-angled at A.
By Pythagoras' theorem in △BAE:
(mBE)² = (mAB)² + (mAE)²
(mBE)² = 5² + 4² = 25 + 16 = 41
mBE = √41 cm
Answer: mBE = √41 cm

Q: Q4(b). In the above question (△ABC right-angled at A with mAB = 5 cm, mAC = 8 cm and mBC = √89 cm), BE is a median. Find mBE using Apollonius theorem.

Ans: Diagram: The same right triangle △ABC, right-angled at A, with AB = 5 cm, AC = 8 cm, BC = √89 cm, and E the midpoint of AC, with median BE drawn from B to E.
E is the midpoint of AC, so mAE = (1)/(2)(8) = 4 cm.
By Apollonius' theorem, applied to △ABC with median BE to side AC:
(mAB)² + (mBC)² = 2(mAE)² + 2(mBE)²
Substitute mAB = 5 cm, mBC = √89 cm, mAE = 4 cm:
25 + 89 = 2(16) + 2(mBE)²
114 = 32 + 2(mBE)²
2(mBE)² = 114 - 32 = 82
(mBE)² = 41
mBE = √41 cm
This agrees with the value found by Pythagoras' theorem.
Answer: mBE = √41 cm

Q: Q5. Find h, x and y in the figure. (The figure shows a triangle with left side 10, right side 17, base 19, and a perpendicular of length h drawn to the base, dividing the base into x on the left and y on the right.)

Ans: Diagram: A triangle with vertex at the top, left side 10, right side 17, base 19 along the bottom, and a perpendicular from the top vertex down to the base with length h, its foot dividing the base into a left part x (under the side 10) and a right part y (under the side 17).
The two parts of the base add up to the whole base:
x + y = 19, so y = 19 - x ... (i)
By Pythagoras' theorem in the left right-angled triangle (hypotenuse 10, base x, height h):
h² = 10² - x² = 100 - x² ... (ii)
By Pythagoras' theorem in the right right-angled triangle (hypotenuse 17, base y, height h):
h² = 17² - y² = 289 - y² ... (iii)
Equate (ii) and (iii):
100 - x² = 289 - y²
Substitute y = 19 - x from (i):
100 - x² = 289 - (19 - x)²
100 - x² = 289 - (361 - 38x + x²)
100 - x² = -72 + 38x - x²
100 = -72 + 38x
38x = 172
x = 172/38 = 86/19 ≈ 4.53
From (i): y = 19 - 86/19 = (361 - 86)/19 = 275/19 ≈ 14.47
From (ii): h² = 100 - (86/19)² = 100 - 7396/361 = (36100 - 7396)/361 = 28704/361
h = √28704/19 = (4√1794)/19 ≈ 8.92
Answer: x = 86/19 ≈ 4.53, y = 275/19 ≈ 14.47 and h = (4√1794)/19 ≈ 8.92

mcqs.q: Q1(i). Pythagoras was a /an ______ mathematician.
mcqs.why: Pythagoras was a Greek mathematician, as keyed in the book and consistent with the history given in this unit on the projection theorems.

mcqs.q: Q1(ii). Apollonius was born in ______.
mcqs.why: Apollonius, the mathematician whose median theorem is used in this unit, was born in Perga, as keyed in the book's review exercise.

mcqs.q: Find the projection of the side of measure 10 units upon the side of measure 17 units in a triangle whose sides are 10, 17 and 21 units.
mcqs.why: Since 21² = 441 > 10² + 17² = 389, the angle is obtuse. By Theorem 8.1: 441 = 389 + 2(17)p = 389 + 34p, so 34p = 52 and p = 26/17 ≈ 1.53 units.

mcqs.q: Triangle ABC is right-angled at A with mAB = 5 cm and mAC = 8 cm. Then mBC is:
mcqs.why: By Pythagoras theorem: (mBC)² = (mAB)² + (mAC)² = 5² + 8² = 25 + 64 = 89, so mBC = √89 cm.

mcqs.q: In that right triangle, AD is perpendicular to BC. Then mAD is:
mcqs.why: Area in two ways: (1/2)(mAB)(mAC) = (1/2)(mBC)(mAD), so (5)(8) = (√89)(mAD), giving 40 = √89 × mAD and mAD = 40/√89 cm.

mcqs.q: In that right triangle, mBD, the projection of AB on BC, is:
mcqs.why: By the right-triangle projection theorem, (mAB)² = (mBD)(mBC). Substitute: 25 = (mBD)(√89), so mBD = 25/√89 cm.

mcqs.q: In that right triangle, BE is a median to AC. Its length, by both Pythagoras and Apollonius, is:
mcqs.why: E is the midpoint of AC, so mAE = 4 cm. By Pythagoras in triangle BAE: (mBE)² = 5² + 4² = 41. By Apollonius: 25 + 89 = 2(16) + 2(mBE)² also gives (mBE)² = 41, so mBE = √41 cm.

lessons.title: Exercise 9.1
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Theorem 9.3: the perpendicular from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects the chord, so each half-chord, the distance from the centre and the radius form a right triangle.
  • Radius 30 cm with a chord 10 cm from the centre gives half-chord 20√2 cm and chord 40√2 cm.
  • A chord of 48 cm at distance 18 cm from the centre gives radius 30 cm and diameter 60 cm.
  • A circle of diameter 5 units has radius 2.5 units, and its chord of 4 units lies 1.5 units from the centre.
  • A chord of 8 cm at distance 5 cm from the centre gives radius √41 cm; radius 8 cm with distance 5 cm gives chord 2√39 cm.
  • Theorem 9.5: two chords of a circle which are equidistant from the centre are congruent; in circle Q, QW = QT = 5 and YT = 12 give YZ = 24 and XY = 24.

Solved Exercises

Q: Q1. If the radius of a circle is 30 cm, find the length of a chord which is 10 cm from the centre.

Ans: Diagram: A circle with centre O and radius 30 cm, a chord AB inside it, and the perpendicular from O to AB meeting AB at its midpoint M, with OM = 10 cm and radius OA = 30 cm drawn to one end of the chord.
The perpendicular from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects the chord (Theorem 9.3), so M is the midpoint of AB and AM is half the chord.
△OMA is right-angled at M.
By Pythagoras' theorem in △OMA:
(OA)² = (OM)² + (AM)²
Substitute OA = 30 cm and OM = 10 cm:
900 = 100 + (AM)²
(AM)² = 900 - 100 = 800
AM = √800 = 20√2 cm
The chord is twice its half:
AB = 2 × AM = 2 × 20√2 = 40√2 cm
Answer: The length of the chord is 40√2 cm

Q: Q2. If a chord of a circle is 48 cm long and its distance from the centre is 18 cm. Find the diameter of the circle.

Ans: Diagram: A circle with centre O, a chord AB = 48 cm, the perpendicular from O to AB meeting it at its midpoint M with OM = 18 cm, and radius OA drawn to one end of the chord.
The perpendicular from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects the chord (Theorem 9.3), so:
AM = (1)/(2)(AB) = (1)/(2)(48) = 24 cm
△OMA is right-angled at M, and OA is the radius.
By Pythagoras' theorem in △OMA:
(OA)² = (OM)² + (AM)²
(OA)² = 18² + 24² = 324 + 576 = 900
OA = 30 cm
The diameter is twice the radius:
Diameter = 2 × 30 = 60 cm
Answer: The diameter of the circle is 60 cm

Q: Q3. The diameter of a circle is 5 units long. How far from the centre is a chord which is 4 units in length.

Ans: Diagram: A circle with centre O and diameter 5 units, a chord AB = 4 units, the perpendicular from O to AB meeting it at its midpoint M, and radius OA drawn to one end of the chord; OM is the distance to be found.
The radius is half the diameter:
OA = 5/2 = 2.5 units
The perpendicular from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects the chord (Theorem 9.3), so:
AM = (1)/(2)(AB) = (1)/(2)(4) = 2 units
△OMA is right-angled at M.
By Pythagoras' theorem in △OMA:
(OA)² = (OM)² + (AM)²
(2.5)² = (OM)² + 2²
6.25 = (OM)² + 4
(OM)² = 2.25
OM = 1.5 units = 3/2 units
Answer: The chord is 3/2 = 1.5 units from the centre

Q: Q4. A chord of a circle is 8 cm in length is drawn 5 cm from the centre. Find the length of the radius.

Ans: Diagram: A circle with centre O, a chord AB = 8 cm, the perpendicular from O to AB meeting it at its midpoint M with OM = 5 cm, and radius OA drawn to one end of the chord.
The perpendicular from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects the chord (Theorem 9.3), so:
AM = (1)/(2)(AB) = (1)/(2)(8) = 4 cm
△OMA is right-angled at M, and OA is the radius.
By Pythagoras' theorem in △OMA:
(OA)² = (OM)² + (AM)²
(OA)² = 5² + 4² = 25 + 16 = 41
OA = √41 cm
Answer: The length of the radius is √41 cm

Q: Q5. Find the length of a chord that is at a distance of 5cm from the centre of a circle with radius 8cm.

Ans: Diagram: A circle with centre O and radius OA = 8 cm, a chord AB, and the perpendicular from O to AB meeting it at its midpoint M, with OM = 5 cm.
The perpendicular from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects the chord (Theorem 9.3), so AM is half the chord.
△OMA is right-angled at M.
By Pythagoras' theorem in △OMA:
(OA)² = (OM)² + (AM)²
Substitute OA = 8 cm and OM = 5 cm:
64 = 25 + (AM)²
(AM)² = 64 - 25 = 39
AM = √39 cm
The chord is twice its half:
AB = 2 × √39 = 2√39 cm
Answer: The length of the chord is 2√39 cm

Q: Q6. In circle Q, QW ⊥ XY, QT ⊥ YZ, QW = 5, QT = 5 and YT = 12. Find XY. (In the figure, Y is a point on the circle, X and Z are two other points on the circle, W is the foot of the perpendicular from centre Q on chord XY, and T is the foot of the perpendicular from Q on chord YZ.)

Ans: Diagram: Circle with centre Q inside, points X (lower left), Y (top) and Z (lower right) on the circle, chords XY and YZ forming two sides from Y, segment QW perpendicular to XY at W, and segment QT perpendicular to YZ at T, with QW = 5, QT = 5 and YT = 12 marked on the figure.
The perpendicular from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects the chord (Theorem 9.3).
QT ⊥ YZ, so T is the midpoint of YZ.
Therefore YZ = 2 × YT = 2 × 12 = 24.
The distances of the chords XY and YZ from the centre are QW = 5 and QT = 5, which are equal.
Two chords of a circle which are equidistant from the centre are congruent (Theorem 9.5).
Therefore XY = YZ = 24.
Answer: XY = 24

mcqs.q: Theorem 9.3 states that the perpendicular from the centre of a circle to a chord:
options: passes through an end of the chord only
mcqs.why: Theorem 9.3, used in every question of this exercise, states that the perpendicular from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects the chord, so the foot of the perpendicular is the midpoint of the chord.

mcqs.q: The radius of a circle is 30 cm. The length of a chord which is 10 cm from the centre is:
mcqs.why: By Pythagoras in triangle OMA: (AM)² = (OA)² − (OM)² = 30² − 10² = 900 − 100 = 800, so AM = 20√2 cm and the chord AB = 2 × 20√2 = 40√2 cm.

mcqs.q: A chord of a circle is 48 cm long and its distance from the centre is 18 cm. The diameter of the circle is:
mcqs.why: Half the chord is 24 cm. By Pythagoras: (OA)² = 18² + 24² = 324 + 576 = 900, so radius OA = 30 cm and diameter = 2 × 30 = 60 cm.

mcqs.q: The diameter of a circle is 5 units. How far from the centre is a chord of 4 units?
mcqs.why: Radius = 5/2 = 2.5 units and half the chord = 2 units. By Pythagoras: (OM)² = (2.5)² − 2² = 6.25 − 4 = 2.25, so OM = 1.5 units = 3/2 units.

mcqs.q: A chord of a circle is 8 cm long and is drawn 5 cm from the centre. The radius is:
mcqs.why: Half the chord is 4 cm. By Pythagoras in triangle OMA: (OA)² = (OM)² + (AM)² = 5² + 4² = 25 + 16 = 41, so the radius OA = √41 cm.

mcqs.q: Find the length of a chord at a distance of 5 cm from the centre of a circle with radius 8 cm.
mcqs.why: By Pythagoras: (AM)² = (OA)² − (OM)² = 8² − 5² = 64 − 25 = 39, so AM = √39 cm and the chord AB = 2 × √39 = 2√39 cm.

mcqs.q: In circle Q, QT is perpendicular to chord YZ and YT = 12. Then YZ is:
mcqs.why: The perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects the chord (Theorem 9.3), so T is the midpoint of YZ and YZ = 2 × YT = 2 × 12 = 24.

mcqs.q: In circle Q, QW is perpendicular to XY with QW = 5, QT is perpendicular to YZ with QT = 5, and YZ = 24. Then XY is:
mcqs.why: The distances of chords XY and YZ from the centre are equal, both 5. By Theorem 9.5, chords equidistant from the centre are congruent, so XY = YZ = 24.

mcqs.q: For the circle of radius 30 cm with a chord 10 cm from the centre, the half-chord AM is:
mcqs.why: By Pythagoras in right triangle OMA: (AM)² = 900 − 100 = 800, so AM = √800 = 20√2 cm; the full chord is then twice this value, 40√2 cm.

mcqs.q: For the chord of 48 cm at distance 18 cm from the centre, the half-chord AM is:
mcqs.why: The perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord (Theorem 9.3), so AM = (1/2)(AB) = (1/2)(48) = 24 cm, which is then used with OM = 18 cm to find the radius 30 cm.

lessons.title: Exercise 9.2
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • In a circle of radius 5 cm, the chord of 8 cm is 3 cm from the centre and the chord of 6 cm is 4 cm from the centre, by Pythagoras with the half-chords 4 cm and 3 cm.
  • Two parallel chords of 8 cm and 6 cm in that circle are 7 cm apart when on opposite sides of the centre and 1 cm apart when on the same side.
  • Parallel chords PQ = 7 cm and MN = 14 cm, 3 cm apart on the same side, give distance x = 4.625 cm for MN and radius about 8.39 cm.
  • In circle C of radius 10, chord QT at distance 5 has length 10√3, about 17.32 units, and chord PR at distance 8 has length 12 units.
  • The chord nearer the centre is the longer chord: QT is longer than PR, and PR is farther from C than QT.

Solved Exercises

Q: Q1. In a circle of radius 5cm, there are two parallel chords of length 8cm and 6cm respectively. Calculate the distance between the chords.

Ans: Diagram: A circle with centre O and radius 5 cm, with two parallel chords, one of length 8 cm and one of length 6 cm, and perpendiculars drawn from O to each chord.
The perpendicular from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects the chord (Theorem 9.3), so the halves of the chords are 4 cm and 3 cm.
Distance of the 8 cm chord from O: by Pythagoras' theorem in the right triangle with hypotenuse = radius 5 cm and one leg = half-chord 4 cm:
d₁² = 5² - 4² = 25 - 16 = 9
d₁ = 3 cm
Distance of the 6 cm chord from O: by Pythagoras' theorem in the right triangle with hypotenuse = radius 5 cm and one leg = half-chord 3 cm:
d₂² = 5² - 3² = 25 - 9 = 16
d₂ = 4 cm
Case 1: the chords are on opposite sides of the centre. The distance between them is:
d₁ + d₂ = 3 + 4 = 7 cm
Case 2: the chords are on the same side of the centre. The distance between them is:
d₂ - d₁ = 4 - 3 = 1 cm
Answer: The distance between the chords is 1 cm or 7 cm

Q: Q2. Two Parallel chords PQ and MN are 3cm apart on the same side of a circle where PQ = 7cm and MN = 14 cm. Calculate the radius of the circle.

Ans: Diagram: A circle with centre C, two parallel chords PQ = 7 cm (the shorter, farther from the centre) and MN = 14 cm on the same side of the centre, 3 cm apart, with perpendiculars from the centre to both chords lying on one straight line.
The perpendicular from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects the chord (Theorem 9.3), so the half-chords are (7)/(2) = 3.5 cm and (14)/(2) = 7 cm.
The longer chord MN is nearer the centre. Let the distance of MN from the centre be x cm; then the distance of PQ from the centre is (x + 3) cm, since the chords are 3 cm apart on the same side.
Let the radius be r. By Pythagoras' theorem for chord MN:
r² = 7² + x² = 49 + x² ... (i)
By Pythagoras' theorem for chord PQ:
r² = (3.5)² + (x + 3)² = 12.25 + (x + 3)² ... (ii)
Equate (i) and (ii):
49 + x² = 12.25 + x² + 6x + 9
49 = 21.25 + 6x
6x = 27.75
x = 4.625 cm
Substitute in (i):
r² = 49 + (4.625)² = 49 + 21.390625 = 70.390625
r = √70.390625 ≈ 8.39 cm
Answer: The radius of the circle is approximately 8.39 cm

Q: Q3(i). Circle C has a radius of 10. Chord QT is 5 units from C and chord PR is 8 units from C. Compare the lengths of PR and QT. (In the figure, C is the centre, PR is a chord whose perpendicular distance from C is 8, and QT is a chord whose perpendicular distance from C is 5.)

Ans: Diagram: Circle with centre C and radius 10, chord PR on the upper side with the perpendicular from C to PR marked 8, radii CR and CT marked 10, and chord QT on the lower side with the perpendicular from C to QT marked 5.
The perpendicular from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects the chord (Theorem 9.3), so each half-chord is found by Pythagoras' theorem.
Half of QT: the right triangle has hypotenuse = radius 10 and one leg = distance 5:
(half of QT)² = 10² - 5² = 100 - 25 = 75
QT = 2√75 = 10√3 ≈ 17.32 units
Half of PR: the right triangle has hypotenuse = radius 10 and one leg = distance 8:
(half of PR)² = 10² - 8² = 100 - 64 = 36
half of PR = 6, so PR = 12 units
Comparing: 17.32 > 12, so QT is longer than PR. This also follows because the chord nearer the centre is the longer chord.
Answer: QT > PR, that is, chord QT is longer than chord PR

Q: Q3(ii). Circle C has a radius of 10. Chord QT is 5 units from C and chord PR is 8 units from C. Compare the distances of PR and QT from C.

Ans: Diagram: Circle with centre C and radius 10, chord PR on the upper side with the perpendicular from C to PR marked 8, and chord QT on the lower side with the perpendicular from C to QT marked 5.
The distance of a chord from the centre is the length of the perpendicular from the centre to the chord.
Distance of QT from C = 5 units (given).
Distance of PR from C = 8 units (given).
Since 8 > 5, PR is farther from C than QT.
This agrees with Q3(i): the longer chord QT is nearer the centre, and the shorter chord PR is farther from the centre.
Answer: PR is farther from C than QT

mcqs.q: In a circle of radius 5 cm, the distance of a chord of length 8 cm from the centre is:
mcqs.why: Half the chord is 4 cm. By Pythagoras: d₁² = 5² − 4² = 25 − 16 = 9, so d₁ = 3 cm.

mcqs.q: In a circle of radius 5 cm, the distance of a chord of length 6 cm from the centre is:
mcqs.why: Half the chord is 3 cm. By Pythagoras: d₂² = 5² − 3² = 25 − 9 = 16, so d₂ = 4 cm.

mcqs.q: The two parallel chords of 8 cm and 6 cm in the radius-5 cm circle lie on opposite sides of the centre. The distance between them is:
mcqs.why: The distances from the centre are d₁ = 3 cm and d₂ = 4 cm. On opposite sides they add: distance = d₁ + d₂ = 3 + 4 = 7 cm.

mcqs.q: The same two parallel chords lie on the same side of the centre. The distance between them is:
mcqs.why: On the same side the distances subtract: distance = d₂ − d₁ = 4 − 3 = 1 cm, using d₁ = 3 cm for the 8 cm chord and d₂ = 4 cm for the 6 cm chord.

mcqs.q: Parallel chords PQ = 7 cm and MN = 14 cm are 3 cm apart on the same side of the centre, with MN at distance x from the centre. Then x is:
mcqs.why: Equate r² from both chords: 49 + x² = 12.25 + (x + 3)² = 12.25 + x² + 6x + 9, so 49 = 21.25 + 6x, 6x = 27.75 and x = 4.625 cm.

mcqs.q: For those parallel chords (PQ = 7 cm, MN = 14 cm, 3 cm apart), the radius of the circle is about:
Circle C has radius 10. Chord QT is 5 units from C. The length of QT is:
mcqs.why: Half of QT satisfies (half)² = 10² − 5² = 100 − 25 = 75, so half = √75 and QT = 2√75 = 10√3 ≈ 17.32 units.

mcqs.q: Circle C has radius 10. Chord PR is 8 units from C. The length of PR is:
mcqs.why: Half of PR satisfies (half)² = 10² − 8² = 100 − 64 = 36, so half of PR = 6 units and PR = 2 × 6 = 12 units.

mcqs.q: Comparing chords QT (5 units from C) and PR (8 units from C) in the radius-10 circle:
mcqs.why: QT = 10√3 ≈ 17.32 units while PR = 12 units, and 17.32 > 12. This agrees with the fact used in the solution that the chord nearer the centre is the longer chord.

mcqs.q: Comparing the distances of PR and QT from centre C:
options: QT is farther from C than PR
Both are equally far from C
PR is farther from C than QT
QT is 8 units and PR is 5 units from C
mcqs.why: The distance of a chord from the centre is the perpendicular length: QT is 5 units from C and PR is 8 units from C. Since 8 > 5, PR is farther from C than QT.

lessons.title: Review Exercise 9
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Theorem 9.5: chords equidistant from the centre are congruent, and the longer chord is closer to the centre.
  • A chord 5 cm from the centre of a circle of radius 13 cm has half-length 12 cm and length 24 cm.
  • A chord of 40 units in a circle of radius 25 lies 15 units from the centre; a chord of 8√3 units at distance 4 units gives radius 8 units.
  • With radius 5 cm and distance 4 cm the chord is 6 cm; with radius 5, CE = 2 and diameter AC perpendicular to chord BD, BD = 8.
  • In circle O with OA = 13 m and OC = 5 m, AC = 12 m and AB = 24 m; a chord of 30 cm in a circle of diameter 34 cm lies 8 cm from the centre.
  • The perpendicular bisector of chord XY = 16 cm with NP = 2 cm gives radius 17 cm.

Solved Exercises

Q: Q1(i). In a circle, two chords are equally distant from the centre of the circle. The chords are

Options: (a) congruent (b) not congruent (c) parallel (d) non parallel

Correct answer: congruent

Q: Q1(ii). AB and CD are two chords of the same circle ⊙O and AB < CD. Then

Options: (a) AB is closer to O (b) AB must be parallel to CD (c) CD is closer to O (d) Can't decide

Correct answer: CD is closer to O

Q: Q1(iii). A chord is 5 cm from the centre of a circle of radius 13cm. The length of the chord is

Options: (a) 6 centimeters (b) 12 centimeters (c) 24 centimeters (d) 30 centimeters

Correct answer: 24 centimeters

Q: Q1(iv). A chord 40 units long is contained in a circle of radius 25. The distance of the chord from the centre of the circle is

Options: (a) 15 units (b) 31.2 units (c) 47.1 units (d) 50.1 units

Correct answer: 15 units

Q: Q1(v). A chord 8√3 units long is 4 units from the centre of a circle. The length of the radius of the circle is

Options: (a) 14.4 units (b) 8 units (c) 8√2 units (d) 2√8 units

Correct answer: 8 units

Q: Q1(vi). In the adjacent circular figure with centre O and radius 5cm, the length of the chord intercepted at 4cm away from the centre of this circle is: (Figure: circle with centre O, chord AB across the upper part, radii OA = 5 cm and OD = 5 cm marked, and the perpendicular distance from O to chord AB marked 4 cm.)

Options: (a) 4 cm (b) 6 cm (c) 7 cm (d) 9 cm

Correct answer: 6 cm

Q: Q1(vii). In the diagram, circle O has a radius of 5, and CE = 2. Diameter AC is perpendicular to chord BD at E. What is the length of BD? (Figure: circle with centre O, vertical diameter CA with C at the top and A at the bottom, horizontal chord BD crossing CA at E with a right-angle mark at E, CE = 2 marked near the top, and radius OD = 5 marked.)

Options: (a) 12 (b) 8 (c) 10 (d) 4

Correct answer: 8

Q: Q2(i). In circle O, AB is a chord, OA is a radius and AB ⊥ OC. (Leave radicals in your answers in simplest form). If AO = 13m and OC = 5m, find AC and AB. (In the figure, C is the foot of the perpendicular from O on AB.)

Ans: Diagram: Circle with centre O, chord AB along the bottom, C the foot of the perpendicular from O onto AB, radius OA = 13 m drawn from O down-left to A, and OC = 5 m drawn vertically from O to C.
OC ⊥ AB, and the perpendicular from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects the chord (Theorem 9.3), so C is the midpoint of AB.
△OCA is right-angled at C.
By Pythagoras' theorem in △OCA:
(OA)² = (OC)² + (AC)²
Substitute OA = 13 m and OC = 5 m:
169 = 25 + (AC)²
(AC)² = 144
AC = 12 m
Since C bisects AB:
AB = 2 × AC = 2 × 12 = 24 m
Answer: AC = 12 m and AB = 24 m

Q: Q2(ii). In circle O, AB is a chord, OA is a radius and AB ⊥ OC. (Leave radicals in your answers in simplest form). If AB is 16 cm long and is 6 cm from O. Find the radius and diameter of the circle. (In the figure, C is the foot of the perpendicular from O on AB, so OC = 6 cm.)

Ans: Diagram: Circle with centre O, chord AB = 16 cm along the bottom, C the midpoint of AB where the perpendicular from O meets AB, OC = 6 cm, and radius OA drawn from O to A.
The perpendicular from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects the chord (Theorem 9.3), so:
AC = (1)/(2)(AB) = (1)/(2)(16) = 8 cm
△OCA is right-angled at C, and OA is the radius.
By Pythagoras' theorem in △OCA:
(OA)² = (OC)² + (AC)² = 6² + 8² = 36 + 64 = 100
OA = 10 cm
The diameter is twice the radius:
Diameter = 2 × 10 = 20 cm
Answer: Radius = 10 cm and diameter = 20 cm

Q: Q2(iii). In circle O, AB is a chord, OA is a radius and AB ⊥ OC. (Leave radicals in your answers in simplest form). If the diameter of circle O is 34 cm, how far from the centre is a chord 30 cm long? (In the figure, C is the foot of the perpendicular from O on the chord.)

Ans: Diagram: Circle with centre O and diameter 34 cm, a chord of length 30 cm, C the midpoint of the chord where the perpendicular from O meets it, and a radius drawn from O to one end of the chord.
The radius is half the diameter:
Radius = 34/2 = 17 cm
The perpendicular from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects the chord (Theorem 9.3), so half the chord is:
30/2 = 15 cm
Let the distance from the centre be d. By Pythagoras' theorem in the right triangle formed by the radius, half the chord and the distance:
17² = 15² + d²
289 = 225 + d²
d² = 64
d = 8 cm
Answer: The chord is 8 cm from the centre

Q: Q2(iv). In circle O, AB is a chord, OA is a radius and AB ⊥ OC. (Leave radicals in your answers in simplest form). The radius of circle O is 25 units long. How long is AB if it is 7 units from point O? (In the figure, C is the foot of the perpendicular from O on AB, so OC = 7 units.)

Ans: Diagram: Circle with centre O and radius OA = 25 units, chord AB at the bottom, C the midpoint of AB where the perpendicular from O meets AB, with OC = 7 units.
The perpendicular from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects the chord (Theorem 9.3), so AC is half of AB.
△OCA is right-angled at C.
By Pythagoras' theorem in △OCA:
(OA)² = (OC)² + (AC)²
625 = 49 + (AC)²
(AC)² = 576
AC = 24 units
Therefore AB = 2 × AC = 2 × 24 = 48 units.
Answer: AB = 48 units

Q: Q2(v). In circle O, AB is a chord, OA is a radius and AB ⊥ OC. (Leave radicals in your answers in simplest form). Chord AB is 10 m long and is 5 m from O. Find OA. (In the figure, C is the foot of the perpendicular from O on AB, so OC = 5 m.)

Ans: Diagram: Circle with centre O, chord AB = 10 m at the bottom, C the midpoint of AB where the perpendicular from O meets AB, with OC = 5 m, and radius OA drawn from O to A.
The perpendicular from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects the chord (Theorem 9.3), so:
AC = (1)/(2)(AB) = (1)/(2)(10) = 5 m
△OCA is right-angled at C, and OA is the radius.
By Pythagoras' theorem in △OCA:
(OA)² = (OC)² + (AC)² = 5² + 5² = 25 + 25 = 50
OA = √50 = 5√2 m
Answer: OA = 5√2 m

Q: Q3. The perpendicular bisector of a chord XY cuts XY at N and the circle at P. If XY = 16cm and NP = 2cm, calculate the radius of the circle.

Ans: Diagram: A circle with chord XY = 16 cm across it, N the midpoint of XY where its perpendicular bisector crosses it, the perpendicular bisector continued to meet the circle at P on the near side with NP = 2 cm, and the centre O lying on the line PN produced, with radius OX drawn to X.
The perpendicular bisector of a chord passes through the centre of the circle, so the centre O lies on the line through N and P.
N is the midpoint of XY, so:
XN = (1)/(2)(XY) = (1)/(2)(16) = 8 cm
Let the radius be r. Then OP = r, and since NP = 2 cm and O is on the opposite side of N from P:
ON = OP - NP = r - 2
△ONX is right-angled at N, with hypotenuse OX = r.
By Pythagoras' theorem in △ONX:
(OX)² = (ON)² + (XN)²
r² = (r - 2)² + 8²
r² = r² - 4r + 4 + 64
4r = 68
r = 17 cm
Answer: The radius of the circle is 17 cm

mcqs.q: Q1(i). In a circle, two chords are equally distant from the centre of the circle. The chords are
mcqs.why: By Theorem 9.5, two chords of a circle which are equidistant from the centre are congruent, which is the book's keyed answer and is also used in Exercise 9.1 Q6.

mcqs.q: Q1(ii). AB and CD are two chords of the same circle ⊙O and AB < CD. Then
options: AB must be parallel to CD
mcqs.why: The longer chord is nearer the centre, as shown in Exercise 9.2 Q3 where the longer chord QT is nearer C. Since CD is longer than AB, CD is closer to O, the book's keyed answer.

mcqs.q: Q1(iii). A chord is 5 cm from the centre of a circle of radius 13cm. The length of the chord is
mcqs.why: Half-chord: h² = 13² − 5² = 169 − 25 = 144, so h = 12 cm and the chord = 2 × 12 = 24 centimeters, confirming the book's keyed answer.

mcqs.q: Q1(iv). A chord 40 units long is contained in a circle of radius 25. The distance of the chord from the centre of the circle is
mcqs.why: Half the chord is 20 units. By Pythagoras: d² = 25² − 20² = 625 − 400 = 225, so d = 15 units, confirming the book's keyed answer.

mcqs.q: Q1(v). A chord 8√3 units long is 4 units from the centre of a circle. The length of the radius of the circle is
mcqs.why: Half the chord is 4√3 units. By Pythagoras: r² = (4√3)² + 4² = 48 + 16 = 64, so r = 8 units, confirming the book's keyed answer.

mcqs.q: Q1(vi). In the adjacent circular figure with centre O and radius 5cm, the length of the chord intercepted at 4cm away from the centre of this circle is: (Figure: circle with centre O, chord AB across the upper part, radii OA = 5 cm and OD = 5 cm marked, and the perpendicular distance from O to chord AB marked 4 cm.)
mcqs.why: Half-chord: h² = 5² − 4² = 25 − 16 = 9, so h = 3 cm and the chord = 2 × 3 = 6 cm, confirming the book's keyed answer.

mcqs.q: Q1(vii). In the diagram, circle O has a radius of 5, and CE = 2. Diameter AC is perpendicular to chord BD at E. What is the length of BD? (Figure: circle with centre O, vertical diameter CA with C at the top and A at the bottom, horizontal chord BD crossing CA at E with a right-angle mark at E, CE = 2 marked near the top, and radius OD = 5 marked.)
mcqs.why: OC = 5 and CE = 2, so OE = 5 − 2 = 3. By Pythagoras: BE² = 5² − 3² = 16, BE = 4, and since the perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord, BD = 2 × 4 = 8, confirming the book's key.

mcqs.q: In circle O, OA = 13 m and OC = 5 m, where C is the foot of the perpendicular from O on chord AB. Then AC and AB are:
mcqs.why: By Pythagoras in triangle OCA: (AC)² = 13² − 5² = 169 − 25 = 144, so AC = 12 m. C bisects AB by Theorem 9.3, so AB = 2 × 12 = 24 m.

mcqs.q: The diameter of circle O is 34 cm. How far from the centre is a chord 30 cm long?
mcqs.why: Radius = 34/2 = 17 cm and half the chord = 15 cm. By Pythagoras: 17² = 15² + d², so d² = 289 − 225 = 64 and d = 8 cm.

mcqs.q: The perpendicular bisector of chord XY = 16 cm cuts XY at N and the circle at P, with NP = 2 cm. The radius of the circle is:
mcqs.why: XN = 8 cm and ON = r − 2. By Pythagoras: r² = (r − 2)² + 8² = r² − 4r + 4 + 64, so 4r = 68 and r = 17 cm.

lessons.title: Exercise 10.1
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Theorem 10.1: a line drawn perpendicular to a radial segment at its outer end point is tangent to the circle at that point; verified with 3-4-5 and 6-8-10 right triangles.
  • Theorem 10.2: the tangent to a circle and the radial segment joining the point of contact and the centre are perpendicular to each other.
  • Theorem 10.3: the two tangents drawn to a circle from a point outside it are equal in length; OP bisects the angle between the tangents and the angles the tangents subtend at the centre are equal.
  • A tangent from a point 10 cm from the centre of a circle of radius 6 cm has length 8 cm; a tangent of 8 cm from a point 9 cm from the centre gives radius √17 cm.
  • With radius 8 cm and a 60° angle between the two tangents, OP = 16 cm because OP bisects the angle and sin 30° = 8/OP.
  • Alternate segment result proved in Q3: for chord AC produced to P with tangent PB, angle PBC equals angle BAP.
  • For tangents AD, DE and BE touching at A, C and B: DA = DC and EB = EC, so AD + BE = DE.

Solved Exercises

Q: Q1. Find the length of a tangent drawn to a circle of radius 6 cm from a point at a distance of 10 cm from the centre of the circle.

Ans: Diagram: A circle with centre O and radius 6 cm, an external point P with OP = 10 cm, and a tangent from P touching the circle at T, with radius OT drawn to the point of contact T.
The tangent to a circle and the radial segment joining the point of contact and the centre are perpendicular to each other (Theorem 10.2), so OT ⊥ PT and △OTP is right-angled at T.
Let the length of the tangent PT be t.
By Pythagoras' theorem in △OTP:
(OP)² = (OT)² + (PT)²
Substitute OP = 10 cm and OT = 6 cm:
100 = 36 + t²
t² = 100 - 36 = 64
t = 8 cm
Answer: The length of the tangent is 8 cm

Q: Q2. Find the radius of a circle if the length of the tangent drawn is 8 cm and distance from the centre of the circle to the point outside the circle is 9 cm.

Ans: Diagram: A circle with centre O, an external point P with OP = 9 cm, a tangent from P touching the circle at T with PT = 8 cm, and radius OT drawn to the point of contact T.
The tangent to a circle and the radial segment joining the point of contact and the centre are perpendicular to each other (Theorem 10.2), so OT ⊥ PT and △OTP is right-angled at T.
Let the radius be r.
By Pythagoras' theorem in △OTP:
(OP)² = (OT)² + (PT)²
Substitute OP = 9 cm and PT = 8 cm:
81 = r² + 64
r² = 81 - 64 = 17
r = √17 cm
Answer: The radius of the circle is √17 cm

Q: Q3. A chord AC of a circle is produced to P. From P a tangent PB to the circle is drawn. Prove that m∠PBC = m∠BAP.

Ans: Diagram: A circle, a chord AC with A on the left of the circle and C on the right, the chord produced beyond C to an external point P, and a tangent from P touching the circle at B at the top, with chord BC and chord BA also drawn.
Given: AC is a chord of the circle produced to P, so A, C and P are collinear with C between A and P. PB is a tangent to the circle at B.
To Prove: m∠PBC = m∠BAP
Construction: Draw the diameter through B and the centre O, meeting the circle again at Q. Join Q to C.
Proof:
1. PB is a tangent at B and OB is the radial segment, so OB ⊥ PB (the tangent to a circle is perpendicular to the radial segment at the point of contact, Theorem 10.2)
2. Q lies on the line OB, so ∠PBQ = 90°, that is, m∠PBC + m∠CBQ = 90° (angle addition at B on the line PQ side)
3. ∠BCQ = 90° (angle in a semicircle, since BQ is a diameter)
4. In △BQC, m∠CBQ + m∠BQC = 180° - 90° = 90° (angle sum of a triangle)
5. From steps 2 and 4, m∠PBC = m∠BQC (both are complements of m∠CBQ)
6. m∠BQC = m∠BAC (angles in the same segment of a circle, both subtending chord BC)
7. m∠BAC = m∠BAP (P lies on the production of AC, so the two angles are the same angle)
8. Therefore m∠PBC = m∠BAP (from steps 5, 6 and 7)
Hence proved.

Q: Q4(i). In the following figure AB intersects the circle, find a. Figure (i): the circle has centre O; a line through B and A is tangent to the circle at A; OA = 3 is a radius; the tangent segment from A to B is 4; the segment OB crosses the circle at C, and CB = a.

Ans: Diagram: A circle with centre O, radius OA = 3 drawn down-right to the point of contact A, a tangent line through A running down-left to the external point B with tangent segment AB = 4, and segment OB drawn from O down-left through the circle boundary at C to B, with the outside part CB labelled a.
The tangent to a circle and the radial segment joining the point of contact and the centre are perpendicular to each other (Theorem 10.2), so OA ⊥ AB and △OAB is right-angled at A.
By Pythagoras' theorem in △OAB:
(OB)² = (OA)² + (AB)²
(OB)² = 3² + 4² = 9 + 16 = 25
OB = 5
OC is a radius, so OC = OA = 3.
C lies on OB between O and B, so by segment addition:
a = CB = OB - OC = 5 - 3 = 2
Answer: a = 2

Q: Q4(ii). In the following figure AB intersects the circle, find a. Figure (ii): the circle has centre O; AB is a tangent to the circle at A with AB = 24; OA = a is a radius; the segment OB is made up of a radius part of length a (from O to the circle) and an outside part of length 13 (from the circle to B).

Ans: Diagram: A circle with centre O at the upper left, radius OA labelled a drawn vertically down to the point of contact A, tangent segment AB = 24 drawn horizontally from A to the external point B at the right, and segment OB slanting from O to B, its part inside the circle (a radius) labelled a and its part outside the circle labelled 13.
The tangent to a circle and the radial segment joining the point of contact and the centre are perpendicular to each other (Theorem 10.2), so OA ⊥ AB and △OAB is right-angled at A.
OB is the hypotenuse, and by segment addition OB = a + 13.
By Pythagoras' theorem in △OAB:
(OB)² = (OA)² + (AB)²
(a + 13)² = a² + 24²
Expand the left side:
a² + 26a + 169 = a² + 576
26a = 576 - 169 = 407
a = 407/26 ≈ 15.65
Answer: a ≈ 15.65

Q: Q4(iii). In the following figure AB intersects the circle, find a. Figure (iii): the circle has centre O; DA is a vertical diameter with D at the top of the circle and A at the bottom; DO = 4; BC is a horizontal line tangent to the circle at A, with B on the left, C on the right and BA = 6; D is joined to B and to C, A is the midpoint of BC, and the side marked a in the figure is equal to DC.

Ans: Diagram: A circle with centre O in the middle, vertical diameter DA with D at the top and A at the bottom of the circle, the upper radius DO labelled 4, horizontal tangent line BC touching the circle at A with B at the lower left and C at the lower right, BA labelled 6, A the midpoint of BC, straight segments DB and DC from D down to B and C, and a parallelogram drawn outside the circle on the right whose side labelled a is equal to DC.
DO is a radius, so the radius is 4 and the diameter is:
DA = 2 × 4 = 8
BC is tangent to the circle at A, and OA is the radial segment to the point of contact, so OA ⊥ BC (Theorem 10.2); hence the diameter DA is also perpendicular to BC.
A is the midpoint of BC in the figure, so:
AC = BA = 6
△DAC is right-angled at A.
By Pythagoras' theorem in △DAC:
(DC)² = (DA)² + (AC)²
(DC)² = 8² + 6² = 64 + 36 = 100
DC = 10
The side marked a is equal to DC.
Answer: a = 10

Q: Q5. If the radius of a circle is 8 cm. Tangents drawn from an external point P make an angle of 60°. Find the distance between the centre of the circle and the point P.

Ans: Diagram: A circle with centre O and radius 8 cm, an external point P, two tangents from P touching the circle at A and B with ∠APB = 60° between them, radii OA and OB drawn to the points of contact, and segment OP joining the centre to P.
The two tangents from P subtend equal angles at the centre and OP bisects the angle between the tangents (corollaries of Theorem 10.3), so:
m∠APO = (1)/(2)(60°) = 30°
The tangent is perpendicular to the radial segment at the point of contact (Theorem 10.2), so OA ⊥ PA and △OAP is right-angled at A.
In △OAP, by the trigonometric ratio sin in △OAP:
sin 30° = (opposite)/(hypotenuse) = OA/OP
(1)/(2) = 8/OP
OP = 2 × 8 = 16 cm
Answer: The distance between the centre of the circle and the point P is 16 cm

Q: Q6(i). Given that PA and PB are tangents to the circle, with centre O, find the values of x and y in the following figure. Figure (i): PB = y cm, PA = 14 cm, ∠BOP = 49°, and x° is ∠AOP.
