Ans: Diagram: A circle with centre O on the left, external point P on the right, tangents PB (upper) and PA (lower) touching the circle at B and A, radii OB and OA drawn to B and A, segment OP drawn horizontally, PB labelled y cm, PA labelled 14 cm, the angle between OB and OP marked 49°, and the angle between OA and OP marked x°.
The two tangents drawn to a circle from a point outside it are equal in length (Theorem 10.3).
Therefore PB = PA, so:
y = 14
The two tangents subtend equal angles at the centre (corollary of Theorem 10.3), so ∠AOP = ∠BOP.
Therefore x = 49.
Answer: x = 49 and y = 14

Q: Q6(ii). Given that PA and PB are tangents to the circle, with centre O, find the values of x and y in the following figure. Figure (ii): PB = 15 cm, PA = y cm, the angle between OP and PB at P is 32°, and x° is ∠AOP.

Ans: Diagram: A circle with centre O on the left, external point P on the right, tangents PB (upper, labelled 15 cm) and PA (lower, labelled y cm) touching the circle at B and A, radii OB and OA drawn, segment OP drawn horizontally, the angle at P between OP and PB marked 32°, and the angle at O between OA and OP marked x°.
The two tangents drawn to a circle from a point outside it are equal in length (Theorem 10.3).
Therefore PA = PB, so:
y = 15
△OPA is congruent to △OPB (Theorem 10.3 proof, H.S congruence), so ∠OPA = ∠OPB = 32°.
OA ⊥ PA (Theorem 10.2), so △OAP is right-angled at A.
By the angle sum of a triangle in △OAP:
x° = 180° - 90° - 32° = 58°
So x = 58.
Answer: x = 58 and y = 15

Q: Q6(iii). Given that PA and PB are tangents to the circle, with centre O, find the values of x and y in the following figure. Figure (iii): the radius OB = 10 cm, ∠AOB = 112°, PB = y cm, and x° is the angle between OP and PA at P.

Ans: Diagram: A circle with centre O on the left, external point P on the right, tangents PB (upper, labelled y cm) and PA (lower) touching the circle at B and A, radii OB (labelled 10 cm) and OA drawn, segment OP drawn horizontally, the angle AOB between the two radii marked 112°, and the angle at P between OP and PA marked x°.
OP joins the external point to the centre, so it bisects the angle between the radii to the points of contact (corollary of Theorem 10.3):
m∠BOP = (1)/(2)(m∠AOB) = (1)/(2)(112°) = 56°
OB ⊥ PB (Theorem 10.2), so △OPB is right-angled at B, and △OPA is congruent to it, giving m∠AOP = 56°.
In right-angled △OPA, by the angle sum of a triangle:
x° = 180° - 90° - 56° = 34°
So x = 34.
In right-angled △OPB, by the trigonometric ratio tan in △OPB:
tan 56° = PB/OB = y/10
y = 10 × tan 56° ≈ 10 × 1.4826 ≈ 14.8 cm
Answer: x = 34 and y ≈ 14.8

Q: Q6(iv). Given that PA and PB are tangents to the circle, with centre O, find the values of x and y in the following figure. Figure (iv): chord AB is drawn joining the points of contact, the angle between OP and PA at P is 35°, x° is ∠ABO inside △OAB, and y° is ∠BAP at A between BA and PA.

Ans: Diagram: A circle with centre O on the left, external point P on the right, tangents PB (upper) and PA (lower) touching the circle at B and A, radii OB and OA drawn, chord BA drawn vertically joining the points of contact, segment OP drawn horizontally, the angle at P between OP and PA marked 35°, the angle at B inside △OAB between AB and OB marked x°, and the angle at A between BA and PA marked y°.
△OPA is congruent to △OPB (H.S congruence, as in the proof of Theorem 10.3), so m∠BPO = m∠APO = 35°.
OB ⊥ PB (Theorem 10.2), so in right-angled △OPB:
m∠BOP = 180° - 90° - 35° = 55°
By congruence m∠AOP = 55°, so:
m∠AOB = 55° + 55° = 110°
In △OAB, OA = OB (radii of the same circle), so △OAB is isosceles and m∠OAB = m∠OBA.
By the angle sum of a triangle in △OAB:
m∠OBA = (180° - 110°)/2 = 70°/2 = 35°
So x = 35.
OA ⊥ PA (Theorem 10.2), so m∠OAP = 90°.
From the figure at A, m∠OAP = m∠OAB + m∠BAP, and m∠OAB = 35°.
Therefore y° = 90° - 35° = 55°.
So y = 55.
Answer: x = 35 and y = 55

Q: Q7(i). In the figure below, VA and VB are tangent to ⊙P, the radius of ⊙P is 3cm, and VA = 6cm. Find VB. (In the figure, V is a point outside the circle on the right, the two tangent lines from V touch the circle at A at the top and B at the bottom, and X is the point where the line from V towards the centre P meets the near side of the circle.)

Ans: Diagram: Circle with centre P, external point V on the right, tangent line from V touching the circle at A at the top with VA = 6 cm, tangent line from V touching the circle at B at the bottom, and point X marked on the near side of the circle on the line from V to P; the radius of the circle is 3 cm.
The two tangents drawn to a circle from a point outside it are equal in length (Theorem 10.3).
VA and VB are the two tangents from the same external point V.
Therefore VB = VA = 6 cm.
Answer: VB = 6 cm

Q: Q7(ii). In the figure below, VA and VB are tangent to ⊙P, the radius of ⊙P is 3cm, and VA = 6cm. Find AP. (In the figure, V is a point outside the circle on the right, the two tangent lines from V touch the circle at A at the top and B at the bottom, and X is the point where the line from V towards the centre P meets the near side of the circle.)

Ans: Diagram: Circle with centre P, external point V on the right, tangent line from V touching the circle at A at the top with VA = 6 cm, tangent line from V touching the circle at B at the bottom, and point X marked on the near side of the circle on the line from V to P; the radius of the circle is 3 cm.
A is a point on the circle and P is the centre.
So AP is a radial segment (radius) of the circle.
The radius is given as 3 cm.
Therefore AP = 3 cm.
Answer: AP = 3 cm

Q: Q7(iii). In the figure below, VA and VB are tangent to ⊙P, the radius of ⊙P is 3cm, and VA = 6cm. Find PV. (In the figure, V is a point outside the circle on the right, the two tangent lines from V touch the circle at A at the top and B at the bottom, and X is the point where the line from V towards the centre P meets the near side of the circle.)

Ans: Diagram: Circle with centre P, external point V on the right, tangent line from V touching the circle at A at the top with VA = 6 cm, tangent line from V touching the circle at B at the bottom, and point X marked on the near side of the circle on the line from V to P; the radius of the circle is 3 cm.
The tangent is perpendicular to the radial segment at the point of contact (Theorem 10.2), so PA ⊥ VA and △PAV is right-angled at A.
PA is the radius, so PA = 3 cm, and VA = 6 cm.
By Pythagoras' theorem in △PAV:
(PV)² = (PA)² + (VA)²
(PV)² = 3² + 6² = 9 + 36 = 45
PV = √45 = 3√5 cm ≈ 6.71 cm
Answer: PV = 3√5 cm

Q: Q7(iv). In the figure below, VA and VB are tangent to ⊙P, the radius of ⊙P is 3cm, and VA = 6cm. Find XV. (In the figure, V is a point outside the circle on the right, the two tangent lines from V touch the circle at A at the top and B at the bottom, and X is the point where the line from V towards the centre P meets the near side of the circle.)

Ans: Diagram: Circle with centre P, external point V on the right, tangent line from V touching the circle at A at the top with VA = 6 cm, tangent line from V touching the circle at B at the bottom, and point X marked on the near side of the circle on the line from V to P; the radius of the circle is 3 cm.
X lies on the segment PV between P and V, and X is on the circle.
So PX is a radius: PX = 3 cm.
From Q7(iii), PV = 3√5 cm.
By segment addition on PV, PV = PX + XV, so:
XV = PV - PX = 3√5 - 3 = 3(√5 - 1) cm ≈ 3.71 cm
Answer: XV = 3(√5 - 1) cm

Q: Q8. In circle N, verify that line l is a tangent. (In the figure, l is a horizontal line touching the top of the circle; the vertical segment from centre N to the point of contact on l is 3; a point on l at distance 4 from the point of contact is joined to N by a line which crosses the circle, and the part of that line outside the circle is 2.)

Ans: Diagram: Circle with centre N, horizontal line l above the circle touching it at one point at the top, a vertical segment from N up to that point of contact labelled 3, a point on l at distance 4 to the right of the point of contact, and a slanted line from N to that point on l crossing the circle, with the part of the slanted line outside the circle labelled 2.
Let T be the point where l meets the top of the circle, and E the point on l at distance 4 from T.
NT is a segment from the centre to a point on the circle, so NT is the radius: NT = 3.
The slanted line NE passes through the circle, and its part outside the circle is 2, so by segment addition:
NE = (radius) + 2 = 3 + 2 = 5
Now check △NTE with NT = 3, TE = 4 and NE = 5.
By the converse of Pythagoras' theorem:
(NT)² + (TE)² = 3² + 4² = 9 + 16 = 25 = 5² = (NE)²
So △NTE is right-angled at T, that is, NT ⊥ l.
If a line is drawn perpendicular to a radial segment of a circle at its outer end point, it is tangent to the circle at that point (Theorem 10.1).
NT is a radial segment and l ⊥ NT at its outer end T.
Answer: Line l is a tangent to circle N, verified

Q: Q9. Verify that AB is tangent to ⊙C at B. (In the figure, C is the centre of the circle, CB = 8 is drawn vertically down to B on the horizontal line through B, A is a point on that line with AB = 6, and AC = 10.)

Ans: Diagram: Circle with centre C, point B at the bottom of the circle on a horizontal line, radius CB = 8 drawn vertically from C down to B, point A on the horizontal line to the left of B with AB = 6, and segment AC = 10 drawn slanting from A up to C.
Check the sides of △ABC: AB = 6, CB = 8 and AC = 10, with AC the longest side.
By the converse of Pythagoras' theorem:
(AB)² + (CB)² = 6² + 8² = 36 + 64 = 100 = 10² = (AC)²
So △ABC is right-angled at B, that is, CB ⊥ AB.
CB is a radial segment and B is its outer end point on the circle.
If a line is drawn perpendicular to a radial segment of a circle at its outer end point, it is tangent to the circle at that point (Theorem 10.1).
Answer: AB is tangent to ⊙C at B, verified

Q: Q10. If AD, DE and BE are tangents to a circle as shown prove that AD + BE = DE. (In the figure, DE is a straight tangent line touching the circle at C at the top, D is its left end and E its right end; from D a second tangent goes down-left to touch the circle at A, and from E a second tangent goes down-right to touch the circle at B.)

Ans: Diagram: A circle with an unnamed centre, a horizontal tangent line DE across the top touching the circle at C, D at the left end and E at the right end of the line, a tangent from D going down to the left touching the circle at A on the lower left, and a tangent from E going down to the right touching the circle at B on the lower right.
Given: AD, DE and BE are tangents to the circle; DE touches the circle at C, AD touches it at A and BE touches it at B.
To Prove: AD + BE = DE
Proof:
1. DA and DC are the two tangents drawn from the same external point D, so DA = DC (the two tangents drawn to a circle from a point outside it are equal in length, Theorem 10.3)
2. EB and EC are the two tangents drawn from the same external point E, so EB = EC (Theorem 10.3)
3. C lies on the segment DE between D and E, so DE = DC + CE (segment addition postulate)
4. Substitute DC = DA from step 1 and CE = EB from step 2 in step 3: DE = DA + EB
5. That is, AD + BE = DE
Hence proved.

mcqs.q: Theorem 10.2 states that the tangent to a circle and the radial segment to the point of contact are:
mcqs.why: Theorem 10.2, used throughout this exercise, states the tangent and the radial segment joining the point of contact and the centre are perpendicular, so triangle OTP is right-angled at the point of contact T.

mcqs.q: Find the length of a tangent drawn to a circle of radius 6 cm from a point 10 cm from the centre.
mcqs.why: OT is perpendicular to PT by Theorem 10.2. By Pythagoras: (OP)² = (OT)² + (PT)², so 100 = 36 + t², t² = 64 and t = 8 cm.

mcqs.q: The tangent drawn is 8 cm long and the external point is 9 cm from the centre. The radius is:
mcqs.why: By Pythagoras in right triangle OTP: (OP)² = (OT)² + (PT)², so 81 = r² + 64, giving r² = 81 − 64 = 17 and r = √17 cm.

mcqs.q: A tangent at A has AB = 4, radius OA = 3, and OB crosses the circle at C with CB = a. Then a is:
mcqs.why: By Pythagoras in right triangle OAB: (OB)² = 3² + 4² = 25, so OB = 5. Since OC is a radius, OC = 3, and a = CB = OB − OC = 5 − 3 = 2.

mcqs.q: A vertical diameter DA has DO = 4, tangent BC at A has BA = 6 with A the midpoint of BC, and a equals DC. Then a is:
mcqs.why: Diameter DA = 2 × 4 = 8 and AC = BA = 6. By Pythagoras in right triangle DAC: (DC)² = 8² + 6² = 64 + 36 = 100, so DC = 10 and a = 10.

mcqs.q: The radius is 8 cm and tangents from P make an angle of 60°. The distance OP is:
mcqs.why: OP bisects the angle between the tangents, so angle APO = 30°. In right triangle OAP, sin 30° = OA/OP, so 1/2 = 8/OP and OP = 2 × 8 = 16 cm.

mcqs.q: PA and PB are tangents with PA = 14 cm, angle BOP = 49° and x° = angle AOP, PB = y cm. Then x and y are:
mcqs.why: By Theorem 10.3 the two tangents are equal, so y = PB = PA = 14. The tangents subtend equal angles at the centre, so x = angle AOP = angle BOP = 49.

mcqs.q: VA and VB are tangents to circle P, with VA = 6 cm. Then VB is:
mcqs.why: VA and VB are the two tangents drawn from the same external point V. By Theorem 10.3 they are equal in length, so VB = VA = 6 cm.

mcqs.q: For circle P of radius 3 cm with tangent VA = 6 cm, the distance PV is:
mcqs.why: PA is perpendicular to VA by Theorem 10.2. By Pythagoras in triangle PAV: (PV)² = 3² + 6² = 9 + 36 = 45, so PV = √45 = 3√5 cm.

mcqs.q: AB is a line through B on circle C, with CB = 8, AB = 6 and AC = 10. AB is tangent to the circle at B because:
options: 6² + 8² = 10², so CB is perpendicular to AB and Theorem 10.1 applies
AC equals the diameter of the circle
mcqs.why: Check: (AB)² + (CB)² = 36 + 64 = 100 = (AC)², so by the converse of Pythagoras triangle ABC is right-angled at B. CB is a radial segment, so by Theorem 10.1, AB is tangent at B.

lessons.title: Exercise 10.2
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Theorem 10.4(a): if two circles touch externally, the distance between their centres equals the sum of their radii; radii 8 cm and 3 cm give 11 cm.
  • Theorem 10.4(b): if two circles touch internally, the distance between their centres equals the difference of their radii; distance 5 cm with bigger radius 17 cm gives smaller radius 12 cm.
  • A chord of 10 cm at distance 12 cm from the centre gives radius 13 cm, and in that circle a chord at distance 5 cm has length 24 cm.
  • A chord of 18 cm in a circle of radius 15 cm has its midpoint 12 cm from the centre (Theorems 9.2 and 9.3).
  • Radius 10 cm with distance 6 cm gives chord 16 cm; distance 3 cm with chord 8 cm gives diameter 10 cm.
  • Radius 8 cm with chord 12 cm gives distance 2√7 cm; radius 7.5 cm with chord 9 cm gives distance 6 cm.

Solved Exercises

Q: Q1. If two circles with radii 8 cm and 3 cm respectively touch each other externally, then what is the distance between their centres?

Ans: Diagram: Two circles, one of radius 8 cm and one of radius 3 cm, touching each other externally at one point, with their centres joined by a straight line passing through the point of contact.
If two circles touch externally, the distance between their centres is equal to the sum of their radii (Theorem 10.4(a)).
Distance between centres = 8 cm + 3 cm
Distance between centres = 11 cm
Answer: The distance between their centres is 11 cm

Q: Q2. The distance between the centres of two circles touching internally is 5 cm. The radius of the bigger circle is 17 cm. What is the radius of the smaller circle?

Ans: Diagram: A bigger circle of radius 17 cm with a smaller circle inside it touching it internally at one point, the centres of the two circles 5 cm apart on the line through the point of contact.
If two circles touch internally, the distance between their centres is equal to the difference of their radii (Theorem 10.4(b)).
Let the radius of the smaller circle be r.
17 - r = 5
r = 17 - 5 = 12 cm
Answer: The radius of the smaller circle is 12 cm

Q: Q3. In a circle a 10 cm long chord is at a distance of 12 cm from the centre. What is the length of a chord at a distance of 5 cm from the centre?

Ans: Diagram: A circle with centre O, a chord of length 10 cm whose perpendicular distance from O is 12 cm, and a second chord whose perpendicular distance from O is 5 cm.
First find the radius using the given chord. The perpendicular from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects the chord (Theorem 9.3), so half the given chord is 5 cm.
By Pythagoras' theorem in the right triangle with legs 5 cm (half-chord) and 12 cm (distance):
r² = 5² + 12² = 25 + 144 = 169
r = 13 cm
Now take the chord at distance 5 cm from the centre. Its half-length h satisfies, by Pythagoras' theorem:
h² = r² - 5² = 169 - 25 = 144
h = 12 cm
The full chord is twice its half:
Chord = 2 × 12 = 24 cm
Answer: The length of the chord is 24 cm

Q: Q4. A chord is 18 cm long. The radius of the circle is 15 cm. What is the distance of the midpoint of the chord from the centre of the circle?

Ans: Diagram: A circle with centre O and radius 15 cm, a chord of length 18 cm, and the segment from O to the midpoint of the chord, which is perpendicular to the chord.
The line from the centre to the midpoint of a chord is perpendicular to the chord (Theorem 9.2), and the perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord (Theorem 9.3), so half the chord is:
18/2 = 9 cm
Let the required distance be d. By Pythagoras' theorem in the right triangle with hypotenuse = radius 15 cm and one leg = half-chord 9 cm:
d² = 15² - 9² = 225 - 81 = 144
d = 12 cm
Answer: The distance of the midpoint of the chord from the centre is 12 cm

Q: Q5. What is the length of a chord at distance of 6cm from the centre of a circle of radius 10 cm?

Ans: Diagram: A circle with centre O and radius 10 cm, a chord whose perpendicular distance from O is 6 cm, and the perpendicular from O meeting the chord at its midpoint.
The perpendicular from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects the chord (Theorem 9.3), so only the half-chord needs to be found.
Let the half-chord be h. By Pythagoras' theorem in the right triangle with hypotenuse = radius 10 cm and one leg = distance 6 cm:
h² = 10² - 6² = 100 - 36 = 64
h = 8 cm
The full chord is twice its half:
Chord = 2 × 8 = 16 cm
Answer: The length of the chord is 16 cm

Q: Q6. The distance of a chord from the centre of a circle is 3 cm, and the length of the chord is 8 cm. What is the diameter?

Ans: Diagram: A circle with centre O, a chord of length 8 cm, and the perpendicular from O to the chord, of length 3 cm, meeting the chord at its midpoint; a radius is drawn to one end of the chord.
The perpendicular from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects the chord (Theorem 9.3), so half the chord is:
8/2 = 4 cm
Let the radius be r. By Pythagoras' theorem in the right triangle with legs 3 cm (distance) and 4 cm (half-chord):
r² = 3² + 4² = 9 + 16 = 25
r = 5 cm
The diameter is twice the radius:
Diameter = 2 × 5 = 10 cm
Answer: The diameter is 10 cm

Q: Q7. The radius of a circle is 8 cm and one of the chords is of 12 cm. What is the distance of the chord from the centre?

Ans: Diagram: A circle with centre O and radius 8 cm, a chord of length 12 cm, and the perpendicular from O to the chord meeting it at its midpoint.
The perpendicular from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects the chord (Theorem 9.3), so half the chord is:
12/2 = 6 cm
Let the distance be d. By Pythagoras' theorem in the right triangle with hypotenuse = radius 8 cm and one leg = half-chord 6 cm:
d² = 8² - 6² = 64 - 36 = 28
d = √28 = 2√7 cm
Answer: The distance of the chord from the centre is 2√7 cm

Q: Q8. The length of a chord of a circle of radius 7.5 cm is 9 cm. What is its distance from the centre of the circle?

Ans: Diagram: A circle with centre O and radius 7.5 cm, a chord of length 9 cm, and the perpendicular from O to the chord meeting it at its midpoint.
The perpendicular from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects the chord (Theorem 9.3), so half the chord is:
9/2 = 4.5 cm
Let the distance be d. By Pythagoras' theorem in the right triangle with hypotenuse = radius 7.5 cm and one leg = half-chord 4.5 cm:
d² = (7.5)² - (4.5)² = 56.25 - 20.25 = 36
d = 6 cm
Answer: Its distance from the centre of the circle is 6 cm

mcqs.q: Two circles with radii 8 cm and 3 cm touch each other externally. The distance between their centres is:
mcqs.why: By Theorem 10.4(a), for circles touching externally the distance between the centres equals the sum of the radii: 8 cm + 3 cm = 11 cm.

mcqs.q: Two circles touch internally, the distance between their centres is 5 cm and the bigger radius is 17 cm. The smaller radius is:
mcqs.why: By Theorem 10.4(b), for internal touching the centre distance equals the difference of the radii: 17 − r = 5, so r = 17 − 5 = 12 cm.

mcqs.q: A chord 10 cm long is 12 cm from the centre. The radius of the circle is:
mcqs.why: Half the chord is 5 cm. By Pythagoras: r² = 5² + 12² = 25 + 144 = 169, so r = 13 cm.

mcqs.q: In that same circle (radius 13 cm), the length of a chord at a distance of 5 cm from the centre is:
mcqs.why: Half-length h satisfies h² = r² − 5² = 169 − 25 = 144, so h = 12 cm and the full chord = 2 × 12 = 24 cm.

mcqs.q: A chord is 18 cm long and the radius is 15 cm. The distance of the midpoint of the chord from the centre is:
mcqs.why: Half the chord is 9 cm. By Pythagoras: d² = 15² − 9² = 225 − 81 = 144, so d = 12 cm.

mcqs.q: What is the length of a chord at distance 6 cm from the centre of a circle of radius 10 cm?
mcqs.why: Half-chord h satisfies h² = 10² − 6² = 100 − 36 = 64, so h = 8 cm and the chord = 2 × 8 = 16 cm.

mcqs.q: The distance of a chord from the centre is 3 cm and the chord is 8 cm long. The diameter is:
mcqs.why: Half the chord is 4 cm. By Pythagoras: r² = 3² + 4² = 9 + 16 = 25, so r = 5 cm and diameter = 2 × 5 = 10 cm.

mcqs.q: The radius is 8 cm and a chord is 12 cm long. The distance of the chord from the centre is:
mcqs.why: Half the chord is 6 cm. By Pythagoras: d² = 8² − 6² = 64 − 36 = 28, so d = √28 = 2√7 cm.

mcqs.q: The radius is 7.5 cm and a chord is 9 cm long. Its distance from the centre is:
mcqs.why: Half the chord is 4.5 cm. By Pythagoras: d² = (7.5)² − (4.5)² = 56.25 − 20.25 = 36, so d = 6 cm.

mcqs.q: Theorem 10.4(b) states that if two circles touch internally, the distance between their centres equals:
mcqs.why: Theorem 10.4(b), applied in Q2 of this exercise, states that for internally touching circles the distance between the centres is equal to the difference of their radii.

lessons.title: Review Exercise 10
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • ACB from A through C to B is an arc; with radial segment OT and tangent line PTQ, OT is perpendicular to PQ (Theorem 10.2).
  • The two tangents drawn to a circle from a point outside it are equal in length (Theorem 10.3).
  • With tangent AB = 80 ft and AC = 50 + r, Pythagoras gives the radius r = 39 ft.
  • With angle APO = 33° in the tangent figure, angle PBA = 24°, using the isosceles triangle AOP and the right triangle OPB.
  • With angle AOT = 64° and tangent TA at A: angle ATB = 26° and angle TAB = 122°.
  • With OB = 5 m and PB = 12 m: OP = 13 m, the part of OP outside the circle i = 8 m and angle BOP j is about 67.4°.
  • With PB = 15 cm and the part of OP outside the circle 7 cm: the radius k is about 12.6 cm and angle BOP l is about 50.0°.

Solved Exercises

Q: Q1(i). In the figure, ACB is called (Figure: a circle with centre O below the chord AB, A on the left of the circle, B on the right, C at the top of the circle, chord AB drawn across, and ACB denoting the arc from A through C to B.)

Options: (a) an arc (b) a secant (c) a chord (d) a diameter

Correct answer: an arc

Q: Q1(ii). In a circle with centre O, if OT is the radial segment and PTQ is the tangent line, then (Figure: a circle with centre O, radius OT drawn up to the point of contact T on the circle, and the tangent line P-T-Q passing through T.)

Options: (a) OT ⊥ PQ (b) OT is not perpendicular to PQ (c) OT ∥ PQ (d) OT is right bisector of PQ

Correct answer: OT ⊥ PQ

Q: Q1(iii). Two tangents drawn to a circle from a point outside it are of .......... in length.

Options: (a) half (b) equal (c) double (d) triple

Correct answer: equal

Q: Q2. In the diagram, B is a point of tangency. Find the radius r of ⊙C. (In the diagram, A is a point outside the circle on the left, AB = 80 ft is a tangent segment touching the circle at B at the bottom, C is the centre of the circle, CB = r is a radius, and the part of AC from A to the circle is 50 ft, so AC = 50 + r.)

Ans: Diagram: Circle with centre C on the right, external point A on the left, tangent segment AB = 80 ft going from A down-right to the point of tangency B at the bottom of the circle, radius CB = r drawn from C to B, and segment AC from A to C crossing the circle, with the part of AC outside the circle labelled 50 ft.
CB is the radial segment to the point of contact B, so CB ⊥ AB (Theorem 10.2) and △ABC is right-angled at B.
By segment addition on AC, since the part from A to the circle is 50 ft and the part inside, from the circle to C, is a radius r:
AC = 50 + r
By Pythagoras' theorem in △ABC:
(AC)² = (AB)² + (CB)²
(50 + r)² = 80² + r²
Expand the left side:
2500 + 100r + r² = 6400 + r²
100r = 6400 - 2500 = 3900
r = 39 ft
Answer: The radius r of ⊙C is 39 ft

Q: Q3. In the figure, BP is a tangent to the circle with centre O. Given that ∠APO = 33°, find ∠PBA. (In the figure, A is a point on the left of the circle, O is the centre on the line AB produced to B outside the circle on the right, P is the point of tangency at the top of the circle, BP is the tangent line, and AP and OP are drawn.)

Ans: Diagram: A circle with centre O, diameter line running horizontally with A on the circle at the left, O in the middle and B outside the circle at the right, P the point of tangency at the top of the circle, tangent line through P going down to B, chord AP drawn from A to P, radius OP drawn from O to P, and ∠APO = 33° marked at P between AP and OP.
OA and OP are radii of the same circle, so OA = OP and △AOP is isosceles.
Therefore m∠OAP = m∠APO = 33°.
By the angle sum of a triangle in △AOP:
m∠AOP = 180° - 33° - 33° = 114°
A, O and B are on a straight line, so by supplementary angles:
m∠POB = 180° - 114° = 66°
OP is the radial segment to the point of contact P of the tangent BP, so OP ⊥ BP (Theorem 10.2) and △OPB is right-angled at P.
By the angle sum of a triangle in △OPB:
m∠PBA = 180° - 90° - 66° = 24°
Answer: ∠PBA = 24°

Q: Q4(i). In the figure, O is the centre of the circle passing through the points A and B. TA is a tangent to the circle at A and TOB is a straight line. Given that ∠AOT = 64°, find ∠ATB. (In the figure, T is outside the circle on the left, B is on the circle on the right, A is on the circle at the bottom, and the tangent at A goes from T down to A.)

Ans: Diagram: A circle with centre O, T an external point on the left, straight line T-O-B running horizontally with B on the circle at the right, A a point on the circle at the bottom, radius OA drawn from O down to A with ∠AOT = 64° marked at O between OA and OT, chord AB drawn from A to B, and the tangent line at A running from T down through A.
OA is the radial segment to the point of contact A of the tangent TA, so OA ⊥ TA (Theorem 10.2) and △OAT is right-angled at A.
By the angle sum of a triangle in △OAT:
m∠ATB = 180° - 90° - 64° = 26°
(∠ATB is the angle at T in △OAT.)
Answer: ∠ATB = 26°

Q: Q4(ii). In the figure, O is the centre of the circle passing through the points A and B. TA is a tangent to the circle at A and TOB is a straight line. Given that ∠AOT = 64°, find ∠TAB. (In the figure, T is outside the circle on the left, B is on the circle on the right, A is on the circle at the bottom, and the tangent at A goes from T down to A.)

Ans: Diagram: A circle with centre O, T an external point on the left, straight line T-O-B running horizontally with B on the circle at the right, A a point on the circle at the bottom, radius OA drawn from O down to A with ∠AOT = 64° marked at O, radius OB and chord AB drawn, and the tangent line at A running from T down through A.
TOB is a straight line, so by supplementary angles at O:
m∠AOB = 180° - m∠AOT = 180° - 64° = 116°
OA = OB (radii of the same circle), so △OAB is isosceles.
By the angle sum of a triangle in △OAB:
m∠OAB = (180° - 116°)/2 = 64°/2 = 32°
OA ⊥ TA (Theorem 10.2), so m∠OAT = 90°, where ∠OAT is the angle between OA and the tangent TA.
At A, the tangent line TA, the radius OA and the chord AB are in order, so by angle addition:
m∠TAB = m∠TAO + m∠OAB = 90° + 32° = 122°
Answer: ∠TAB = 122°

Q: Q5(a). Given that PA and PB are tangents to each of the following circles with centre O, find the values of the unknowns. Figure (a): OB = 5m, PB = 12m, j° is ∠BOP, and i m is the part of OP outside the circle (from the circle to P).

Ans: Diagram: A circle with centre O on the left, external point P on the right, tangents PB (upper, labelled 12m) and PA (lower) touching the circle at B and A, radius OB labelled 5m drawn to B, radius OA drawn to A, segment OP drawn horizontally, the angle at O between OB and OP marked j°, and a double-headed arrow along OP from the circle to P marked i m.
OB ⊥ PB (Theorem 10.2), so △OPB is right-angled at B.
By Pythagoras' theorem in △OPB:
(OP)² = (OB)² + (PB)² = 5² + 12² = 25 + 144 = 169
OP = 13 m
The part of OP outside the circle is OP minus the radius:
i = OP - OB = 13 - 5 = 8 m
By the trigonometric ratio sin in △OPB, for the angle j at O:
sin j° = (opposite)/(hypotenuse) = PB/OP = 12/13
j = sin⁻¹(12/13) ≈ 67.4
Answer: i = 8 and j ≈ 67.4

Q: Q5(b). Given that PA and PB are tangents to each of the following circles with centre O, find the values of the unknowns. Figure (b): OB = k cm, PB = 15 cm, the part of OP outside the circle (from the circle to P) is 7 cm, and l° is ∠BOP.

Ans: Diagram: A circle with centre O on the left, external point P on the right, tangents PB (upper, labelled 15 cm) and PA (lower) touching the circle at B and A, radius OB labelled k cm drawn to B, radius OA drawn to A, segment OP drawn horizontally, the angle at O between OB and OP marked l°, and a double-headed arrow along OP from the circle to P marked 7 cm.
OB is the radius, so OP = (radius) + (part outside the circle) = k + 7.
OB ⊥ PB (Theorem 10.2), so △OPB is right-angled at B.
By Pythagoras' theorem in △OPB:
(OP)² = (OB)² + (PB)²
(k + 7)² = k² + 15²
Expand the left side:
k² + 14k + 49 = k² + 225
14k = 225 - 49 = 176
k = 176/14 ≈ 12.6 cm
Then OP = k + 7 ≈ 19.6 cm.
By the trigonometric ratio sin in △OPB, for the angle l at O:
sin l° = (opposite)/(hypotenuse) = PB/OP = 15/19.6 ≈ 0.7664
l = sin⁻¹(0.7664) ≈ 50.0
Answer: k ≈ 12.6 and l ≈ 50.0

mcqs.q: Q1(i). In the figure, ACB is called (Figure: a circle with centre O below the chord AB, A on the left of the circle, B on the right, C at the top of the circle, chord AB drawn across, and ACB denoting the arc from A through C to B.)
mcqs.why: ACB goes from A through C on the circle to B, which is part of the circumference, so ACB is an arc, confirming the book's keyed answer.

mcqs.q: Q1(ii). In a circle with centre O, if OT is the radial segment and PTQ is the tangent line, then (Figure: a circle with centre O, radius OT drawn up to the point of contact T on the circle, and the tangent line P-T-Q passing through T.)
options: OT is not perpendicular to PQ
OT is right bisector of PQ
mcqs.why: By Theorem 10.2 the tangent and the radial segment at the point of contact are perpendicular. The tangent line PTQ is the line PQ, so OT ⊥ PQ, confirming the book's keyed answer.

mcqs.q: Q1(iii). Two tangents drawn to a circle from a point outside it are of .......... in length.
mcqs.why: By Theorem 10.3, the two tangents drawn to a circle from a point outside it are equal in length, confirming the book's keyed answer.

mcqs.q: B is a point of tangency, AB = 80 ft is a tangent, CB = r is a radius, and AC = 50 + r. The radius r is:
mcqs.why: CB is perpendicular to AB by Theorem 10.2. By Pythagoras: (50 + r)² = 80² + r², so 2500 + 100r + r² = 6400 + r², giving 100r = 3900 and r = 39 ft.

mcqs.q: BP is a tangent with centre O and angle APO = 33°. Then angle PBA is:
mcqs.why: OA = OP gives angle OAP = 33°, so angle AOP = 114° and angle POB = 66°. Triangle OPB is right-angled at P, so angle PBA = 180° − 90° − 66° = 24°.

mcqs.q: TA is a tangent at A, TOB is a straight line and angle AOT = 64°. Then angle ATB is:
mcqs.why: OA is perpendicular to TA by Theorem 10.2, so triangle OAT is right-angled at A. By the angle sum: angle ATB = 180° − 90° − 64° = 26°.

mcqs.q: In the same figure (angle AOT = 64°), angle TAB is:
mcqs.why: Angle AOB = 180° − 64° = 116°, and isosceles triangle OAB gives angle OAB = (180° − 116°)/2 = 32°. Since angle OAT = 90°, angle TAB = 90° + 32° = 122°.

mcqs.q: PA and PB are tangents with OB = 5 m and PB = 12 m. The part i of OP outside the circle is:
mcqs.why: By Pythagoras in right triangle OPB: (OP)² = 5² + 12² = 169, so OP = 13 m. The part outside the circle is i = OP − radius = 13 − 5 = 8 m.

mcqs.q: In that same figure, angle BOP = j°, where sin j° = 12/13. Then j is about:
mcqs.why: In right triangle OPB, sin j° = opposite/hypotenuse = PB/OP = 12/13. Therefore j = sin⁻¹(12/13) ≈ 67.4, as found in the solved item.

mcqs.q: PA and PB are tangents with PB = 15 cm, OB = k cm and the part of OP outside the circle 7 cm, so OP = k + 7. Then k is about:
mcqs.why: By Pythagoras: (k + 7)² = k² + 15², so k² + 14k + 49 = k² + 225, giving 14k = 176 and k = 176/14 ≈ 12.6 cm.

lessons.title: Exercise 11
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Chords of a circle which are equidistant from the centre are equal in length.
  • The perpendicular from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects the chord.
  • A radius, a half-chord and the perpendicular distance from the centre form a right-angled triangle, so Pythagoras theorem applies.
  • With perpendicular distance 5 and radius 13, the half-chord is 12, from x squared = 13 squared minus 5 squared = 144.
  • With radius 17 and half-chord 13, the perpendicular distance is the square root of 120, about 11.0.
  • Equal arcs subtend equal angles at the centre, so the line from the centre to the midpoint of an arc bisects the chord joining its ends.
  • If arc KL equals arc LM in circle Q, then CK equals CM, giving 2x + 3 = 4x and x = 3/2.

Solved Exercises

Q: Q1(i). Given that O is the centre of each of the following circles, find the value of x and y in the following case: a circle with centre O has a horizontal chord of length 12 near the top and a slanted chord on the lower-left side; the perpendicular distances of the two chords from O are marked equal; the slanted chord is labelled x and the angle at the foot of the perpendicular on the slanted chord is marked y.

Ans: Diagram: A circle with centre O. A horizontal chord of length 12 is drawn near the top of the circle, and a perpendicular segment is drawn from O up to this chord, with a right-angle mark at its foot on the chord. A second, slanted chord is drawn on the lower-left side of the circle, labelled x, and a segment is drawn from O perpendicular to this chord, with the angle at its foot marked y. The two perpendicular segments from O carry the same tick mark, so they are equal in length.
Chords of a circle which are equidistant from the centre are equal in length.
The perpendicular distance of the chord of length 12 from O is marked equal to the perpendicular distance of the chord labelled x from O.
So the two chords are equidistant from the centre, and therefore they are equal in length.
x = 12
The segment drawn from O to the chord labelled x is its perpendicular distance from the centre, so it meets the chord at a right angle.
y = 90°
Answer: x = 12, y = 90°

Q: Q1(ii). Given that O is the centre of each of the following circles, find the value of x and y in the following case: a circle with centre O has a chord of length 22 on the left side and a second chord on the right side; the perpendicular distances of the two chords from O are marked equal; x is the part of the right-hand chord from the foot of the perpendicular to one end of the chord, and y is the angle at the foot of the perpendicular on the right-hand chord.

Ans: Diagram: A circle with centre O. A chord of length 22 is drawn on the left side of the circle, with a perpendicular segment drawn from O to the chord and a right-angle mark at its foot. A second chord is drawn on the right side of the circle, with a perpendicular segment drawn from O to it; the angle at the foot of this perpendicular is marked y, and the part of the chord from the foot of the perpendicular to its lower end is labelled x. The two perpendicular segments from O carry the same tick mark, so they are equal in length.
Chords of a circle which are equidistant from the centre are equal in length.
The two chords are equidistant from O, so the right-hand chord is also 22 in length.
The perpendicular from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects the chord.
So the foot of the perpendicular divides the right-hand chord into two equal parts, each of length (22)/(2) = 11.
x = 11
The segment from O meets the right-hand chord at a right angle, because it is the perpendicular distance from the centre.
y = 90°
Answer: x = 11, y = 90°

Q: Q1(iii). Given that O is the centre of each of the following circles, find the value of x and y in the following case: a circle with centre O has a horizontal chord; the perpendicular from O to the chord has length 5 and bisects the chord; a radius drawn to the left-hand end of the chord has length 13; x is the right-hand half of the chord, and y is the angle at O between the perpendicular and the radius drawn to the right-hand end of the chord.

Ans: Diagram: A circle with centre O. A horizontal chord is drawn below O. A vertical segment of length 5 is drawn from O perpendicular to the chord, meeting it at its midpoint; the two halves of the chord carry the same tick mark. A radius of length 13 is drawn from O to the left-hand end of the chord, and another radius is drawn from O to the right-hand end of the chord. The right-hand half of the chord is labelled x, and the angle at O between the perpendicular segment and the right-hand radius is marked y.
The perpendicular from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects the chord, so each half of the chord is one side of a right-angled triangle whose hypotenuse is a radius.
In the right-hand triangle, the hypotenuse is the radius 13, one side is the perpendicular distance 5, and the other side is x.
By the Pythagoras theorem: x² + 5² = 13²
x² = 13² - 5²
x² = 169 - 25
x² = 144
x = √144 = 12
In the same right-angled triangle, y is the angle at O, whose adjacent side is 5 and whose hypotenuse is 13.
cos y = (5)/(13)
y = cos⁻¹((5)/(13))
y = 67.4° (to one decimal place)
Answer: x = 12, y = 67.4°

Q: Q1(iv). Given that O is the centre of each of the following circles, find the value of x and y in the following case: a circle with centre O has an upper chord of length 26 and a lower chord of length 16; the radius of the circle is 17; x is the perpendicular distance from O to the upper chord, and y is the angle at the lower-left end of the lower chord between the chord and the radius drawn to that end.

Ans: Diagram: A circle with centre O and radius 17. A chord of length 26 is drawn across the upper part of the circle, and a vertical perpendicular segment labelled x is drawn from O up to this chord, with a right-angle mark at its foot. A chord of length 16 is drawn across the lower part of the circle, and a radius of length 17 is drawn from O to the lower-left end of this chord. The angle at the lower-left end of the lower chord, between the chord and the radius, is marked y.
The perpendicular from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects the chord.
So the perpendicular from O divides the upper chord into two equal parts, each of length (26)/(2) = 13.
A radius to an end of the upper chord has length 17, so the radius, the half-chord 13 and the perpendicular distance x form a right-angled triangle with hypotenuse 17.
By the Pythagoras theorem: x² + 13² = 17²
x² = 17² - 13²
x² = 289 - 169
x² = 120
x = √120 = 10.954...
x = 11.0 (to one decimal place)
The perpendicular from O also bisects the lower chord, so each half of the lower chord has length (16)/(2) = 8.
In the right-angled triangle at the lower chord, y is the angle at the chord's end, whose adjacent side is the half-chord 8 and whose hypotenuse is the radius 17.
cos y = (8)/(17)
y = cos⁻¹((8)/(17))
y = 61.9° (to one decimal place)
Answer: x = 11.0, y = 61.9°

Q: Q1(v). Given that O is the centre of each of the following circles, find the value of x and y in the following case: a circle with centre O has a chord of length 20 across the top; the two ends of the chord are joined to O and the angle at O is a right angle; the segment from O to the left-hand end of the chord is labelled 12 and the segment from O to the right-hand end of the chord is labelled x; y is the angle at the left-hand end of the chord.

Ans: Diagram: A circle with centre O. A chord of length 20 is drawn across the top of the circle. The left-hand end of the chord is joined to O by a segment labelled 12, and the right-hand end of the chord is joined to O by a segment labelled x. The angle at O between the two segments is marked as a right angle, and the angle at the left-hand end of the chord, between the chord and the segment of length 12, is marked y.
The chord of length 20 and the two segments from O form a triangle which is right-angled at O.
So the chord of length 20 is the hypotenuse of this right-angled triangle, and the other two sides are 12 and x.
By the Pythagoras theorem: x² + 12² = 20²
x² = 20² - 12²
x² = 400 - 144
x² = 256
x = √256 = 16
In the same triangle, y is the angle at the left-hand end of the chord, whose adjacent side is 12 and whose hypotenuse is 20.
cos y = (12)/(20)
cos y = 0.6
y = cos⁻¹(0.6)
y = 53.1° (to one decimal place)
Answer: x = 16, y = 53.1°

Q: Q1(vi). Given that O is the centre of each of the following circles, find the value of x and y in the following case: a circle with centre O has an upper chord of length 10 and a lower chord of length 12; the perpendicular distance from O to the lower chord is 5; x is the perpendicular distance from O to the upper chord, and y is the angle at the left-hand end of the upper chord between the chord and the radius drawn to that end.

Ans: Diagram: A circle with centre O. A chord of length 10 is drawn across the top of the circle, with a vertical perpendicular segment labelled x drawn from O up to the chord and a right-angle mark at its foot; a radius is drawn from O to the left-hand end of this chord, and the angle at that end, between the chord and the radius, is marked y. A chord of length 12 is drawn on the lower-left side of the circle, with a perpendicular segment of length 5 drawn from O to it and a right-angle mark at its foot.
The perpendicular from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects the chord.
So the perpendicular from O divides the lower chord into two equal parts, each of length (12)/(2) = 6.
The radius, the half-chord 6 and the perpendicular distance 5 form a right-angled triangle.
By the Pythagoras theorem: radius² = 5² + 6²
radius² = 25 + 36
radius² = 61
The perpendicular from O also divides the upper chord into two equal parts, each of length (10)/(2) = 5.
The radius, the half-chord 5 and the perpendicular distance x form another right-angled triangle with the same hypotenuse, the radius.
By the Pythagoras theorem: x² + 5² = radius² = 61
x² = 61 - 25
x² = 36
x = √36 = 6
In the upper right-angled triangle, y is the angle at the end of the chord, whose opposite side is x = 6 and whose adjacent side is the half-chord 5.
tan y = (6)/(5)
y = tan⁻¹((6)/(5))
y = 50.2° (to one decimal place)
Answer: x = 6, y = 50.2°

Q: Q2. In ⊙Q, arc KL = arc LM. If CK = 2x + 3 and CM = 4x, find x.

Ans: Diagram: A circle with centre Q. A vertical line is drawn from Q down through a point C to the point L at the bottom of the circle. A horizontal chord MCK crosses this line at C, with M on the left of the circle, K on the right of the circle, and C between M and K on the line QL. The arc from K to L and the arc from L to M are equal (arc KL = arc LM). The segment CK is labelled 2x + 3 and the segment CM is labelled 4x.
Equal arcs of a circle subtend equal angles at the centre, so the line QL bisects the angle at Q between the radii to K and M.
The line from the centre of a circle which bisects the angle between the radii to the ends of a chord also bisects the chord.
Since arc KL = arc LM, the line QL passes through the midpoint of the chord KM.
Therefore C is the midpoint of chord KM, so CK = CM.
2x + 3 = 4x
3 = 4x - 2x
3 = 2x
x = (3)/(2)
Answer: x = (3)/(2)

mcqs.q: Two chords of a circle are equidistant from the centre. One chord has length 12. What is the length of the other chord?
mcqs.why: Chords equidistant from the centre are equal in length. The distances are marked equal, so the second chord equals the first chord, which is 12.

mcqs.q: A chord of length 22 is bisected by the perpendicular from the centre. What is the length of each half of an equal chord in the same figure?
mcqs.why: The perpendicular from the centre bisects a chord. Half of the chord = 22 divided by 2 = 11, so each half has length 11.

mcqs.q: The perpendicular distance from the centre to a chord is 5 and the radius is 13. What is the half-chord length x?
mcqs.why: By Pythagoras: x squared + 5 squared = 13 squared, so x squared = 169 - 25 = 144, and x = square root of 144 = 12.

mcqs.q: In the same triangle, y is the angle at the centre with adjacent side 5 and hypotenuse 13. What is y to one decimal place?
mcqs.why: cos y = adjacent / hypotenuse = 5 / 13. So y = cos inverse of (5/13), which evaluates to 67.4 degrees to one decimal place.

mcqs.q: A circle has radius 17 and a chord of length 26. What is the perpendicular distance x from the centre to the chord, to one decimal place?
mcqs.why: Half-chord = 26/2 = 13. By Pythagoras: x squared = 17 squared - 13 squared = 289 - 169 = 120, so x = square root of 120, about 11.0.

mcqs.q: A chord of length 20 is the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle at the centre, with one radius 12. What is the other radius x?
mcqs.why: By Pythagoras: x squared + 12 squared = 20 squared, so x squared = 400 - 144 = 256, and x = square root of 256 = 16.

mcqs.q: A chord of length 12 has perpendicular distance 5 from the centre. What is the square of the radius?
mcqs.why: Half-chord = 12/2 = 6. By Pythagoras: radius squared = 5 squared + 6 squared = 25 + 36 = 61.

mcqs.q: A second chord of length 10 is in the same circle, whose radius squared is 61. What is its perpendicular distance x from the centre?
mcqs.why: Half-chord = 10/2 = 5. By Pythagoras: x squared + 5 squared = 61, so x squared = 61 - 25 = 36, and x = square root of 36 = 6.

mcqs.q: In circle Q, arc KL = arc LM and QL meets chord KM at C. Why is CK equal to CM?
options: Because equal arcs make QL bisect chord KM
mcqs.why: Equal arcs subtend equal central angles, so QL bisects the angle at Q and therefore bisects chord KM. Hence C is the midpoint, so CK = CM.

mcqs.q: In circle Q, CK = 2x + 3 and CM = 4x, with CK = CM. What is x?
mcqs.why: Set the equal lengths equal: 2x + 3 = 4x. Then 3 = 4x - 2x = 2x, so x = 3 divided by 2 = 3/2.

lessons.title: Review Exercise 11
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • For radius 3 and a 90 degree chord AB, the chord length is 3 root 2, from the right-angled isosceles triangle of two radii and the chord.
  • Equal arcs have equal chords: if arc AB is congruent to arc CD then chord AB is congruent to chord CD.
  • If two diameters are perpendicular, joining their ends in order forms a square: all sides are equal by congruent triangles and each angle is an angle in a semicircle, 90 degrees.
  • With diameter AOC and angle AOB = 130 degrees, angle BOC = 50 degrees on a straight line, so measure of arc BC is 50 degrees.
  • The central angle is double the circumference angle on the same arc: angle ADB = 65 degrees and angle BDC = 25 degrees.
  • Angles in the same segment are equal, which proves angle A = angle C on arc DB and angle 1 = angle 2 on arc AC for chords meeting outside the circle.
  • Triangles ADE and CBE formed by two chords produced to meet outside the circle are equiangular.

Solved Exercises

Q: Q1(i). ⊙P has a radius of 3 and AB has a measure of 90°. What is the length of AB? (In the figure, P is the centre of the circle, A and B are points on the circle, and the radii PA and PB are drawn together with the chord AB.)

Options: (a) 3√2 (b) 3√3 (c) 6 (d) 9

Correct answer: 3√2

Q: Q1(ii). In the accompanying diagram of circle O, arc AB ≅ arc CD. Which statement is true? (In the figure, A is at the upper left of the circle, B at the upper right, C at the lower left and D at the lower right; the chords AB and CD are drawn, and the diagonal CB passes near the centre O.)

Options: (a) AB ≅ CD (b) arc AB ∥ arc CD (c) AC ≅ BD (d) ∠ABC = ∠BCD

Correct answer: AB ≅ CD

Q: Q2. In a circle if any pair of diameters are ⊥ each other then the lines joining its ends in order, form a square.

Ans: Diagram: A circle with centre O. Two diameters AC and BD are drawn perpendicular to each other, crossing at O. The ends of the diameters are joined in order by the segments AB, BC, CD and DA, forming a quadrilateral inside the circle.
Given: AC and BD are two diameters of a circle with centre O, and AC ⊥ BD. The ends of the diameters are joined in order by AB, BC, CD and DA.
To Prove: ABCD is a square.
Proof:
1. OA = OB = OC = OD (radii of the same circle)
2. In △AOB and △COD: OA = OC and OB = OD (radii of the same circle)
3. ∠AOB = ∠COD = 90° (vertically opposite angles, and AC ⊥ BD)
4. △AOB ≅ △COD (SAS congruence)
5. AB = CD (corresponding sides of congruent triangles)
6. In the same way, △BOC ≅ △DOA (SAS congruence), so BC = DA (corresponding sides of congruent triangles)
7. Also △AOB ≅ △BOC (SAS congruence), so AB = BC (corresponding sides of congruent triangles)
8. From steps 5, 6 and 7: AB = BC = CD = DA, so all four sides of ABCD are equal
9. The angle in a semicircle is a right angle, so the angle subtended by diameter AC at B is ∠ABC = 90° (angle in a semicircle)
10. Similarly ∠BCD = 90°, ∠CDA = 90° and ∠DAB = 90° (angles in semicircles on the diameters BD and AC)
11. ABCD has all four sides equal and all four angles equal to 90°, so ABCD is a square
Hence proved.

Q: Q3. In a circle with centre O, AOC is diameter. ∠AOB = 130°, find ∠ADB, ∠BDC and m arc BC.

Ans: Diagram: A circle with centre O. The diameter AOC runs diagonally from A at the lower right of the circle to C at the upper left. B is a point at the upper right of the circle and D is a point at the lower left. The radius OB is drawn, and the angle AOB at the centre is marked 130°. The chords AD (along the bottom), DC (up the left side) and DB (diagonally across the circle) are drawn.
AOC is a diameter, so A, O and C lie on a straight line.
∠AOB + ∠BOC = 180° (angles on a straight line)
130° + ∠BOC = 180°
∠BOC = 180° - 130°
∠BOC = 50°
The measure of an arc is the measure of its central angle, so m arc BC = ∠BOC.
m arc BC = 50°
The angle subtended by an arc at the centre is double the angle subtended by it at the circumference.
∠ADB stands on arc AB at the circumference, and ∠AOB is the angle on the same arc AB at the centre.
∠ADB = (1)/(2) × ∠AOB
∠ADB = (1)/(2) × 130°
∠ADB = 65°
∠BDC stands on arc BC at the circumference, and ∠BOC is the angle on the same arc BC at the centre.
∠BDC = (1)/(2) × ∠BOC
∠BDC = (1)/(2) × 50°
∠BDC = 25°
Answer: ∠ADB = 65°, ∠BDC = 25°, m arc BC = 50°

Q: Q4(a). Chords AB and CD of a circle meet at the point E outside the circle. Prove that ∠A = ∠C.

Ans: Diagram: A circle with centre O. A is a point at the left of the circle, B is at the upper right, D is at the lower right and C is at the bottom. The chord AB is extended beyond B to the point E outside the circle on the right, and the chord CD is extended beyond D to the same point E. The chords AD and CB are drawn across the circle, and the short chord BD is drawn on the right side. ∠A is the angle at A in △ADE, and ∠C is the angle at C in △CBE.
Given: Chords AB and CD of a circle are produced to meet at the point E outside the circle.
To Prove: ∠A = ∠C
Proof:
1. ∠A is the angle DAB, an angle of the circle standing on arc DB (angle at the circumference)
2. ∠C is the angle BCD, an angle of the circle also standing on arc DB (angle at the circumference)
3. Angles in the same segment of a circle are equal, so ∠DAB = ∠BCD
4. Therefore ∠A = ∠C
Hence proved.

Q: Q4(b). Chords AB and CD of a circle meet at the point E outside the circle. Prove that ∠1 = ∠2, where ∠1 is the angle at B between the chords BA and BC, and ∠2 is the angle at D between the chords AD and DC.

Ans: Diagram: The same circle as in Q4(a): A at the left of the circle, B at the upper right, D at the lower right and C at the bottom, with the chords AB and CD produced to meet at E outside the circle on the right, and the chords AD, CB and BD drawn. The angle at B between BA and BC is marked 1, and the angle at D between AD and DC is marked 2.
Given: Chords AB and CD of a circle are produced to meet at the point E outside the circle; ∠1 is the angle ABC at B and ∠2 is the angle ADC at D.
To Prove: ∠1 = ∠2
Proof:
1. ∠1 is the angle ABC, an angle of the circle standing on arc AC (angle at the circumference)
2. ∠2 is the angle ADC, an angle of the circle also standing on arc AC (angle at the circumference)
3. Angles in the same segment of a circle are equal, so ∠ABC = ∠ADC
4. Therefore ∠1 = ∠2
Hence proved.

Q: Q4(c). Chords AB and CD of a circle meet at the point E outside the circle. Prove that △ADE and △CBE are equiangular.

Ans: Diagram: The same circle as in Q4(a): A at the left of the circle, B at the upper right, D at the lower right and C at the bottom; the chords AB and CD are produced to meet at E outside the circle on the right. △ADE is formed by the points A, D and E, and △CBE is formed by the points C, B and E, and the two triangles share the angle at E.
Given: Chords AB and CD of a circle are produced to meet at the point E outside the circle.
To Prove: △ADE and △CBE are equiangular.
Proof:
1. ∠A = ∠C (proved in part (a): angles in the same segment on arc DB)
2. ∠AED = ∠CEB (the angle at E is common to both triangles)
3. ∠ADE + ∠2 = 180° (angles on the straight line CE at the point D)
4. ∠CBE + ∠1 = 180° (angles on the straight line AE at the point B)
5. ∠1 = ∠2 (proved in part (b): angles in the same segment on arc AC)
6. From steps 3, 4 and 5: ∠ADE = 180° - ∠2 = 180° - ∠1 = ∠CBE
7. So the three angles of △ADE are equal to the three angles of △CBE in order: ∠A = ∠C, ∠ADE = ∠CBE and ∠AED = ∠CEB
8. Therefore △ADE and △CBE are equiangular
Hence proved.

mcqs.q: ⊙P has a radius of 3 and AB has a measure of 90°. What is the length of AB? (In the figure, P is the centre of the circle, A and B are points on the circle, and the radii PA and PB are drawn together with the chord AB.)
mcqs.why: By Pythagoras on triangle PAB: AB squared = 3 squared + 3 squared = 18, so AB = square root of 18 = 3 root 2. The book key is correct.

mcqs.q: In the accompanying diagram of circle O, arc AB ≅ arc CD. Which statement is true? (In the figure, A is at the upper left of the circle, B at the upper right, C at the lower left and D at the lower right; the chords AB and CD are drawn, and the diagonal CB passes near the centre O.)
mcqs.why: Equal arcs of the same circle have equal chords. Since arc AB is congruent to arc CD, chord AB is congruent to chord CD. The book key is correct.

mcqs.q: Two diameters of a circle are perpendicular to each other. Joining their ends in order forms which figure?
mcqs.why: Radii are all equal and the four triangles at the centre are congruent by SAS, so all four sides are equal. Each vertex angle is an angle in a semicircle, 90 degrees, giving a square.

mcqs.q: AOC is a diameter and angle AOB = 130°. What is angle BOC?
mcqs.why: A, O and C lie on a straight line, so angles on a straight line sum to 180 degrees: angle BOC = 180 - 130 = 50 degrees.

mcqs.q: In the same figure, what is the measure of arc BC?
mcqs.why: The measure of an arc is the measure of its central angle. Arc BC has central angle BOC = 50 degrees, so measure of arc BC = 50 degrees.

mcqs.q: Angle ADB stands on arc AB, whose central angle AOB is 130°. What is angle ADB?
mcqs.why: The angle at the centre is double the angle at the circumference on the same arc: angle ADB = (1/2) x 130 degrees = 65 degrees.

mcqs.q: Angle BDC stands on arc BC, whose central angle BOC is 50°. What is angle BDC?
mcqs.why: The angle at the centre is double the angle at the circumference on the same arc: angle BDC = (1/2) x 50 degrees = 25 degrees.

mcqs.q: Chords AB and CD meet outside the circle at E. Why is angle A equal to angle C?
options: Both stand on arc DB in the same segment
mcqs.why: Angle A is angle DAB and angle C is angle BCD. Both are circumference angles standing on the same arc DB, and angles in the same segment are equal.

mcqs.q: In the same outside-meeting figure, angle 1 at B and angle 2 at D are equal because both stand on which arc?
mcqs.why: Angle 1 is angle ABC and angle 2 is angle ADC. Both stand on arc AC in the same segment, and angles in the same segment of a circle are equal.

mcqs.q: Why are triangles ADE and CBE equiangular when chords AB and CD meet outside at E?
options: They share angle E, angle A = angle C, and angle ADE = angle CBE
mcqs.why: Angle at E is common. Angle A = angle C on arc DB, and using angle 1 = angle 2 on arc AC with straight lines gives angle ADE = angle CBE, so all three angles match.

chapters.title: Unit 12: Angle in a Segment of a Circle

lessons.title: Exercise 12
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • The angle subtended by an arc at the centre is double the angle subtended by it at the circumference: central angle 70 degrees gives x = 35 degrees.
  • Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary: x + y = 180 degrees gives y = 145 degrees.
  • A regular hexagon has central angle 360 divided by 6 = 60 degrees for each side.
  • For a hexagon side at distance 5 root 3 from the centre, cos 30 degrees = 5 root 3 over R gives radius R = 10 units.
  • In cyclic quadrilateral STUV, c + (2c - 6) = 180 gives c = 62 and 10x + 8x = 180 gives x = 10.
  • In cyclic quadrilateral JKLM, 2a + 2a = 180 gives a = 45 and 2b + 4b = 180 gives b = 30.
  • A parallelogram inscribed in a circle is a rectangle, because its opposite angles are both equal and supplementary, so each is 90 degrees.

Solved Exercises

Q: Q1. O is the centre of the circle. Find the unknowns in the figure. (In the figure, the central angle at O is marked 70°; x is an angle at a vertex on the right-hand side of the circle and y is the obtuse angle at a vertex on the left-hand side of the circle, in the cyclic quadrilateral formed with the radii.)

Ans: Diagram: A circle with centre O. Two radii are drawn from O to points on the circle, making a central angle of 70° between them. The ends of the radii are joined to two further points on the circle to form a cyclic quadrilateral; the angle at the right-hand vertex of the quadrilateral is marked x, and the obtuse angle at the left-hand vertex is marked y.
The angle subtended by an arc at the centre is double the angle subtended by it at the circumference.
The angle x stands on the same arc as the central angle of 70°.
x = (1)/(2) × 70°
x = 35°
The opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary.
The angle y is opposite the angle x in the cyclic quadrilateral, so x + y = 180°.
y = 180° - x
y = 180° - 35°
y = 145°
Answer: x = 35°, y = 145°

Q: Q2. A regular hexagon is inscribed in a circle. Each side of the hexagon is 5√3 units from the centre of the circle. Find the radius of the circle.

Ans: Diagram: A circle with centre O and a regular hexagon inscribed in it, so that all six vertices of the hexagon lie on the circle. Radii are drawn from O to the two ends of one side of the hexagon, and a perpendicular segment is drawn from O to that side; the length of this perpendicular segment, the distance of the side from the centre, is 5√3 units.
A regular hexagon has six equal sides, so the radii drawn to the ends of one side make a central angle of (360°)/(6) = 60° at O.
The perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects the chord and also bisects the central angle, so it makes an angle of (60°)/(2) = 30° with each radius.
In the right-angled triangle so formed, the hypotenuse is the radius R of the circle, and the side adjacent to the 30° angle is the distance 5√3.
cos 30° = (adjacent)/(hypotenuse) = (5√3)/(R)
(√3)/(2) = (5√3)/(R)
R × √3 = 2 × 5√3
R × √3 = 10√3
R = (10√3)/(√3)
R = 10
Answer: The radius of the circle is 10 units.

Q: Q3(a). Find the value of each variable. The figure shows a cyclic quadrilateral STUV with S at the upper left, T at the upper right, U at the lower right and V at the bottom; ∠S = c°, ∠T = 10x°, ∠U = (2c - 6)° and ∠V = 8x°.

Ans: Diagram: A circle with a cyclic quadrilateral STUV inscribed in it, in order S at the upper left, T at the upper right, U at the lower right and V at the bottom. The angle at S is labelled c°, the angle at T is labelled 10x°, the angle at U is labelled (2c - 6)° and the angle at V is labelled 8x°.
The opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary.
S is opposite U, so ∠S + ∠U = 180°.
c + (2c - 6) = 180
3c - 6 = 180
3c = 180 + 6
3c = 186
c = (186)/(3)
c = 62
T is opposite V, so ∠T + ∠V = 180°.
10x + 8x = 180
18x = 180
x = (180)/(18)
x = 10
Answer: c = 62, x = 10

Q: Q3(b). Find the value of each variable. The figure shows a cyclic quadrilateral JKLM with L at the upper left, M at the right, J at the bottom and K at the left; ∠L = 2a°, ∠M = 2b°, ∠J = 2a° and ∠K = 4b°.

Ans: Diagram: A circle with a cyclic quadrilateral JKLM inscribed in it, in order L at the upper left, M at the right, J at the bottom and K at the left. The angle at L is labelled 2a°, the angle at M is labelled 2b°, the angle at J is labelled 2a° and the angle at K is labelled 4b°.
The opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary.
L is opposite J, so ∠L + ∠J = 180°.
2a + 2a = 180
4a = 180
a = (180)/(4)
a = 45
M is opposite K, so ∠M + ∠K = 180°.
2b + 4b = 180
6b = 180
b = (180)/(6)
b = 30
Answer: a = 45, b = 30

Q: Q4. Show that a parallelogram inscribed in a circle will be a rectangle.

Ans: Diagram: A circle with a parallelogram ABCD inscribed in it, so that A, B, C and D all lie on the circle, with AB parallel to CD and BC parallel to DA.
Given: ABCD is a parallelogram inscribed in a circle, so ABCD is also a cyclic quadrilateral.
To Prove: ABCD is a rectangle.
Proof:
1. ∠A + ∠C = 180° (opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary)
2. ∠A = ∠C (opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal)
3. From steps 1 and 2: ∠A + ∠A = 180°, so 2∠A = 180°
4. ∠A = (180°)/(2) = 90°
5. ∠C = ∠A = 90° (opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal)
6. ∠B = 180° - ∠A = 90° (consecutive angles of a parallelogram are supplementary)
7. ∠D = 180° - ∠A = 90° (consecutive angles of a parallelogram are supplementary)
8. ABCD is a parallelogram with all four angles equal to 90°, so ABCD is a rectangle
Hence proved.

mcqs.q: The central angle on an arc is 70°. What is the angle x subtended by the same arc at the circumference?
mcqs.why: The centre angle is double the circumference angle on the same arc: x = (1/2) x 70 degrees = 35 degrees.

mcqs.q: In a cyclic quadrilateral, x = 35° is opposite y. What is y?
mcqs.why: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary: y = 180 - x = 180 - 35 = 145 degrees.

mcqs.q: What is the central angle at the centre of a regular hexagon for one side?
mcqs.why: A regular hexagon has six equal sides around a full turn: central angle = 360 degrees / 6 = 60 degrees for each side.

mcqs.q: A regular hexagon side is 5√3 units from the centre. What is the radius R of the circle?
mcqs.why: The perpendicular bisects the 60 degree central angle to 30 degrees. cos 30 = (5 root 3)/R, so (root 3)/2 = (5 root 3)/R, giving R = 10 units.

mcqs.q: In cyclic quadrilateral STUV, angle S = c° and opposite angle U = (2c - 6)°. What is c?
mcqs.why: Opposite angles are supplementary: c + (2c - 6) = 180, so 3c - 6 = 180, 3c = 186, and c = 186/3 = 62.

mcqs.q: In the same quadrilateral STUV, angle T = 10x° and opposite angle V = 8x°. What is x?
mcqs.why: Opposite angles are supplementary: 10x + 8x = 180, so 18x = 180, and x = 180/18 = 10.

mcqs.q: In cyclic quadrilateral JKLM, angle L = 2a° and opposite angle J = 2a°. What is a?
mcqs.why: Opposite angles are supplementary: 2a + 2a = 180, so 4a = 180, and a = 180/4 = 45.

mcqs.q: In the same quadrilateral JKLM, angle M = 2b° and opposite angle K = 4b°. What is b?
mcqs.why: Opposite angles are supplementary: 2b + 4b = 180, so 6b = 180, and b = 180/6 = 30.

mcqs.q: Why must a parallelogram inscribed in a circle be a rectangle?
options: Its opposite angles are equal and supplementary, so each is 90°
mcqs.why: As a cyclic quadrilateral, angle A + angle C = 180 degrees. As a parallelogram, angle A = angle C. So 2 x angle A = 180, angle A = 90 degrees, and likewise all angles are 90 degrees.

mcqs.q: In the hexagon problem, the perpendicular from the centre to a side does which two things?
options: Bisects the chord and bisects the central angle
mcqs.why: The perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects the chord. In the isosceles triangle of two radii it also bisects the central angle, halving 60 degrees to 30 degrees.

lessons.title: Review Exercise 12
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • The centre angle is double the circumference angle on the same arc, including the reflex case: circumference angle 70 degrees gives reflex centre angle 220 degrees.
  • The exterior angle of a cyclic quadrilateral equals the interior opposite angle: exterior angle 82 degrees gives the opposite interior angle x = 82 degrees.
  • Angles in the same segment are equal: angles of 76 degrees and 3y degrees on arc LM give 3y = 76 and y = 25 1/3 degrees.
  • For a quadrilateral circumscribed about a circle, tangent segments from each external vertex are equal, proving AB + CD = BC + DA.
  • The angle in a semicircle is a right angle: a triangle in a semicircle with one base angle 40 degrees has the other base angle 50 degrees.
  • An isosceles triangle in a semicircle with vertex angle 90 degrees has each base angle 45 degrees.
  • Combining supplementary opposite angles with angles in the same segment solves the diagonal problems, giving y = 12 degrees and x = 70 degrees in Q4(v) and Q4(vi).

Solved Exercises

Q: Q1(i). In the figure, O is the centre of the circle, ∠TPR = 80° and ∠QPS = x°. Find x. (In the figure, T is a point outside the circle on the left; a straight line from T passes through P on the circle and continues to Q on the right of the circle; R is at the upper left of the circle; the chord PR and the radii OR and OQ are drawn, and x° is marked at the centre O.)

Options: (a) 80° (b) 160° (c) 100° (d) 120°

Correct answer: 160°

Q: Q1(ii). In the diagram, ∠ADC is a central angle and m∠ADC = 60°. What is m∠ABC? (In the figure, D is the centre of the circle, A is at the top, C is at the right and B is at the upper left; the radii DA and DC are drawn, together with the chords BA and BC.)

Options: (a) 15° (b) 60° (c) 120° (d) 30°

Correct answer: 30°

Q: Q1(iii). In the figure, O is centre of the circle and ∠PQR = 70°. Calculate the value of x. (In the figure, Q is at the top of the circle, P is at the lower left and R is at the right; the radii OP and OR are drawn, and x° is marked at O on the reflex angle POR.)

Options: (a) 140° (b) 220° (c) 290° (d) 110°

Correct answer: 220°

Q: Q1(iv). In the figure, ∠SPT = 100°, ∠PQS = 40° and ∠PRQ = x°. Calculate the value of x. (In the figure, the line TPQ is straight, with P on the left of the circle and Q at the upper right; R is at the right and S at the bottom; the chords PQ, PR, QR, QS, PS and SR are drawn.)

Options: (a) 30° (b) 40° (c) 50° (d) 60°

Correct answer: 40°

Q: Q1(v). In the adjacent figure if m∠3 = 75°, then find m∠1 and m∠2. (In the figure, A is at the lower left of the circle, B at the lower right, C at the upper left and D at the upper right; the diameters AOD and BOC cross at the centre O; ∠3 is the angle AOB at the centre, ∠1 is the angle ACB at C and ∠2 is the angle ADB at D.)

Options: (a) 37 (1/2)°, 37 (1/2)° (b) 37 (1/2)°, 75° (c) 75°, 37 (1/2)° (d) 75°, 75°

Correct answer: 37 (1/2)°, 37 (1/2)°

Q: Q1(vi). Given that O is the centre of the circle. The angle marked x will be: (In the figure, two diameters cross at the centre O; an angle of 25° is marked at the vertex at the upper right of the circle, and x is marked at O in the lower-right triangle formed by the diameters.)

Options: (a) 12 (1/2)° (b) 25° (c) 50° (d) 75°

Correct answer: 50°

Q: Q1(vii). Given that O is the centre of the circle, the angle marked y will be: (In the same figure as part (vi), two diameters cross at the centre O and an angle of 25° is marked at the vertex at the upper right of the circle; y is marked at the left-hand vertex of the circle, in the same segment as the 25° angle.)

Options: (a) 12 (1/2)° (b) 25° (c) 50° (d) 75°

Correct answer: 25°

Q: Q1(viii). In the figure, O is the centre of the circle then the angle x is: (In the figure, A is at the lower left of the circle, B at the lower right and C at the top; the radii OA and OB and the chords AC and BC are drawn; the angle at A between OA and AC is marked 20°, the angle at B between OB and BC is marked 30°, and x is the angle AOB at the centre.)

Options: (a) 50° (b) 75° (c) 100° (d) 125°

Correct answer: 100°

Q: Q2(i). O is the centre of the circle. Find the unknowns in the figure. (The figure shows a cyclic quadrilateral with the angle 120° at the upper-left vertex, x at the top vertex, the base side produced at the lower-left vertex so that the exterior angle there is 82°, and y at the lower-right vertex.)

Ans: Diagram: A circle with centre O and a cyclic quadrilateral inscribed in it. The angle at the upper-left vertex is marked 120°. The angle at the top vertex is marked x. The base side of the quadrilateral is produced beyond the lower-left vertex, making an exterior angle of 82° at that vertex. The angle at the lower-right vertex is marked y.
The exterior angle of a cyclic quadrilateral is equal to the interior opposite angle.
The exterior angle at the lower-left vertex is 82°, and the interior angle opposite it is the angle x at the top vertex.
x = 82°
As a check: the interior angle at the lower-left vertex is 180° - 82° = 98° (angles on a straight line), and x + 98° = 180°, giving x = 82° (opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary).
The opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary.
The angle y at the lower-right vertex is opposite the angle of 120° at the upper-left vertex.
y + 120° = 180°
y = 180° - 120°
y = 60°
Answer: x = 82°, y = 60°
Note: the printed Answers key gives x = 98°, but 98° is the interior angle at the lower-left vertex; the angle marked x is opposite it, so x = 82°.

Q: Q2(ii). O is the centre of the circle. Find the unknowns in the figure. (In the figure, L is at the left of the circle, N at the top, P at the right and M at the lower right; the chords LN, NM, MP and PL are drawn and the radii OL and OM are drawn; the angle at N between LN and NM is 76°, the angle at P between LP and PM is marked 3y°, and the angle LOM at the centre is marked 4x°.)

Ans: Diagram: A circle with centre O. The points L (left), N (top), P (right) and M (lower right) lie on the circle. The chords LN, NM, MP and PL are drawn, and the radii OL and OM are drawn from the centre. The angle at N, between the chords NL and NM, is marked 76°. The angle at P, between the chords PL and PM, is marked 3y°. The angle LOM at the centre, between the radii OL and OM, is marked 4x°.
Angles in the same segment of a circle are equal.
The angle at N (76°) and the angle at P (3y°) both stand on the same arc LM, in the same segment.
3y = 76
y = (76)/(3)
y = 25 (1/3)
The angle subtended by an arc at the centre is double the angle subtended by it at the circumference.
The central angle LOM (4x°) and the angle at N (76°) stand on the same arc LM.
4x = 2 × 76
4x = 152
x = (152)/(4)
x = 38
Answer: x = 38°, y = 25 (1/3)°

Q: Q3. ABCD is a quadrilateral circumscribed about a circle. Show that mAB + mCD = mBC + mDA.

Ans: Diagram: A circle with a quadrilateral ABCD drawn around it, so that each side of the quadrilateral is a tangent to the circle: side AB touches the circle at one point, side BC at another point, side CD at another point and side DA at another point. All four vertices A, B, C and D lie outside the circle.
Given: ABCD is a quadrilateral circumscribed about a circle, so all four sides AB, BC, CD and DA are tangents to the circle.
To Prove: mAB + mCD = mBC + mDA
Proof:
1. The two tangents drawn from an external point to a circle are equal in length (tangent segments from a common external point)
2. From the vertex A, the two tangent segments along the sides DA and AB are equal; call their common length w
3. From the vertex B, the two tangent segments along the sides AB and BC are equal; call their common length x
4. From the vertex C, the two tangent segments along the sides BC and CD are equal; call their common length y
5. From the vertex D, the two tangent segments along the sides CD and DA are equal; call their common length z
6. mAB = w + x (side AB is made up of the tangent segment w from A and the tangent segment x from B)
7. mBC = x + y (side BC is made up of the tangent segments from B and C)
8. mCD = y + z (side CD is made up of the tangent segments from C and D)
9. mDA = z + w (side DA is made up of the tangent segments from D and A)
10. mAB + mCD = (w + x) + (y + z) = w + x + y + z
11. mBC + mDA = (x + y) + (z + w) = w + x + y + z
12. From steps 10 and 11, the two sums are equal, so mAB + mCD = mBC + mDA
Hence proved.

Q: Q4(i). Find the value of x in the following figure where O is the centre of the circle. (Two radii from O are drawn to the ends of a chord, and the angle between them at O is marked x; chords from the ends of the same chord meet at a point on the upper part of the circle, where the angle is marked 40°.)

Ans: Diagram: A circle with centre O. Two radii are drawn from O to the ends of a chord, and the angle between them at O, on the lower side, is marked x. From the ends of the same chord, two chords are drawn meeting at a point on the upper part of the circle, and the angle at that point is marked 40°.
The angle subtended by an arc at the centre is double the angle subtended by it at the circumference.
The central angle x and the angle of 40° stand on the same arc.
x = 2 × 40°
x = 80°
Answer: x = 80°

Q: Q4(ii). Find the value of x in the following figure where O is the centre of the circle. (Two radii from O make an angle of 110° at the centre; the ends of the radii are joined by chords to a point at the bottom of the circle, on the major arc, and the angle at that point is marked x.)

Ans: Diagram: A circle with centre O. Two radii are drawn from O to points on the circle, making an angle of 110° at O on the upper side. The ends of the radii are joined by chords to a point at the bottom of the circle, which lies on the major arc, and the angle at that point is marked x.
The angle subtended by an arc at the centre is double the angle subtended by it at the circumference.
The angle x stands on the major arc, so the central angle belonging to it is the reflex angle at O.
Reflex angle at O = 360° - 110°
Reflex angle at O = 250°
x = (1)/(2) × 250°
x = 125°
Answer: x = 125°

Q: Q4(iii). Find the value of x in the following figure where O is the centre of the circle. (A diameter passes through O horizontally; a triangle is inscribed in the semicircle above it, with the angle at the left-hand end of the diameter marked 40° and x at the right-hand end of the diameter.)

Ans: Diagram: A circle with centre O and a diameter drawn horizontally through O. A point at the top of the circle is joined to both ends of the diameter, forming a triangle in the semicircle. The angle at the left-hand end of the diameter is marked 40°, and the angle at the right-hand end of the diameter is marked x.
The angle in a semicircle is a right angle.
So the angle at the top point of the triangle is 90°.
The angles of a triangle add up to 180°.
40° + 90° + x = 180°
x = 180° - 90° - 40°
x = 50°
Answer: x = 50°

Q: Q4(iv). Find the value of x in the following figure where O is the centre of the circle. (A diameter passes through O; a triangle is inscribed in the semicircle, and the two chords from the point on the circle to the ends of the diameter are marked equal with tick marks; x is the angle at the left-hand end of the diameter.)

Ans: Diagram: A circle with centre O and a diameter drawn through O. A point at the top of the circle is joined to both ends of the diameter, forming a triangle in the semicircle. The two chords forming the sides of the triangle carry the same tick mark, so they are equal. The angle at the left-hand end of the diameter, between the diameter and the chord, is marked x.
The angle in a semicircle is a right angle, so the angle at the top point of the triangle is 90°.
The two sides of the triangle are marked equal, so the triangle is isosceles and its base angles, at the two ends of the diameter, are equal.
So the angle at the right-hand end of the diameter is also x.
The angles of a triangle add up to 180°.
x + x + 90° = 180°
2x = 180° - 90°
2x = 90°
x = (90°)/(2)
x = 45°
Answer: x = 45°

Q: Q4(v). Find the value of the unknown angle in the following figure where O is the centre of the circle. (A cyclic quadrilateral has both diagonals drawn; the angle at the right-hand vertex is marked 100°, an angle of 68° is marked at the bottom vertex between one side and a diagonal, and the unknown angle, marked y, is at the top vertex between one side and a diagonal.)

Ans: Diagram: A circle with centre O marked by a dot. A cyclic quadrilateral is inscribed in the circle, with both diagonals drawn. The interior angle at the right-hand vertex of the quadrilateral is marked 100°. At the bottom vertex, the angle between one side of the quadrilateral and a diagonal is marked 68°. The unknown angle, marked y, is at the top vertex of the quadrilateral, between one side and a diagonal.
The opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary.
The angle at the bottom vertex is opposite the 100° angle, so it is 180° - 100° = 80°.
This angle at the bottom vertex is split by a diagonal into two parts, one of which is 68°.
So the other part = 80° - 68° = 12°.
Angles in the same segment of a circle are equal.
The angle y at the top vertex and this 12° part at the bottom vertex stand on the same chord, in the same segment.
y = 12°
Answer: y = 12°

Q: Q4(vi). Find the value of x in the following figure where O is the centre of the circle. (A cyclic quadrilateral has both diagonals drawn; an angle of 30° is marked at the lower-left vertex between a diagonal and the base side, the whole angle at the lower-right vertex is marked 80°, and x is marked at the upper-left vertex between a side and a diagonal.)

Ans: Diagram: A circle with centre O marked by a dot. A cyclic quadrilateral is inscribed in the circle, with both diagonals drawn, crossing inside the circle. At the lower-left vertex, the angle between one diagonal and the base side is marked 30°. The whole angle at the lower-right vertex, between the base side and the right-hand side, is marked 80°.
