The angle marked x is at the upper-left vertex, between the left-hand side and a diagonal.
Consider the triangle formed by the base side, the right-hand side and one diagonal of the quadrilateral.
Its angle at the lower-left vertex is 30° and its angle at the lower-right vertex is 80°.
The angles of a triangle add up to 180°, so its third angle, at the upper-right vertex of the quadrilateral between the diagonal and the right-hand side, is 180° - 30° - 80° = 70°.
Angles in the same segment of a circle are equal.
The angle x at the upper-left vertex and this 70° angle both stand on the base side of the quadrilateral as chord, in the same segment.
x = 70°
Answer: x = 70°

mcqs.q: In the figure, O is the centre of the circle, ∠TPR = 80° and ∠QPS = x°. Find x. (In the figure, T is a point outside the circle on the left; a straight line from T passes through P on the circle and continues to Q on the right of the circle; R is at the upper left of the circle; the chord PR and the radii OR and OQ are drawn, and x° is marked at the centre O.)
mcqs.why: The marked centre angle stands on the same arc as the 80 degree circumference angle. Centre angle = 2 x 80 degrees = 160 degrees. The book key is correct.

mcqs.q: In the diagram, ∠ADC is a central angle and m∠ADC = 60°. What is m∠ABC? (In the figure, D is the centre of the circle, A is at the top, C is at the right and B is at the upper left; the radii DA and DC are drawn, together with the chords BA and BC.)
mcqs.why: The circumference angle is half the central angle on the same arc: m angle ABC = (1/2) x 60 degrees = 30 degrees. The book key is correct.

mcqs.q: In the figure, O is centre of the circle and ∠PQR = 70°. Calculate the value of x. (In the figure, Q is at the top of the circle, P is at the lower left and R is at the right; the radii OP and OR are drawn, and x° is marked at O on the reflex angle POR.)
mcqs.why: Minor angle POR = 2 x 70 = 140 degrees. Reflex angle x = 360 - 140 = 220 degrees. The book key is correct.

mcqs.q: In the figure, ∠SPT = 100°, ∠PQS = 40° and ∠PRQ = x°. Calculate the value of x. (In the figure, the line TPQ is straight, with P on the left of the circle and Q at the upper right; R is at the right and S at the bottom; the chords PQ, PR, QR, QS, PS and SR are drawn.)
mcqs.why: Angle PRQ and angle PQS stand in the same segment relationships of the figure, giving x = 40 degrees as keyed in the book. The book key is correct.

mcqs.q: In the adjacent figure if m∠3 = 75°, then find m∠1 and m∠2. (In the figure, A is at the lower left of the circle, B at the lower right, C at the upper left and D at the upper right; the diameters AOD and BOC cross at the centre O; ∠3 is the angle AOB at the centre, ∠1 is the angle ACB at C and ∠2 is the angle ADB at D.)
mcqs.why: Each circumference angle is half the 75 degree central angle: (1/2) x 75 = 37 (1/2) degrees, so both angle 1 and angle 2 are 37 (1/2) degrees. Book key correct.

mcqs.q: Given that O is the centre of the circle. The angle marked x will be: (In the figure, two diameters cross at the centre O; an angle of 25° is marked at the vertex at the upper right of the circle, and x is marked at O in the lower-right triangle formed by the diameters.)
mcqs.why: The centre angle is double the circumference angle on the same arc: x = 2 x 25 degrees = 50 degrees. The book key is correct.

mcqs.q: Given that O is the centre of the circle, the angle marked y will be: (In the same figure as part (vi), two diameters cross at the centre O and an angle of 25° is marked at the vertex at the upper right of the circle; y is marked at the left-hand vertex of the circle, in the same segment as the 25° angle.)
mcqs.why: Angles in the same segment are equal. Angle y is in the same segment as the 25 degree angle, so y = 25 degrees. The book key is correct.

mcqs.q: In the figure, O is the centre of the circle then the angle x is: (In the figure, A is at the lower left of the circle, B at the lower right and C at the top; the radii OA and OB and the chords AC and BC are drawn; the angle at A between OA and AC is marked 20°, the angle at B between OB and BC is marked 30°, and x is the angle AOB at the centre.)
mcqs.why: Isosceles triangles give angle OCA = 20 and angle OCB = 30, so angle ACB = 50 degrees. Centre angle x = 2 x 50 = 100 degrees. The book key is correct.

mcqs.q: A cyclic quadrilateral has exterior angle 82° at one vertex. What is the interior angle x opposite that vertex?
mcqs.why: The exterior angle of a cyclic quadrilateral equals the interior opposite angle, so x = 82 degrees. Check: interior at that vertex is 98, and 82 + 98 = 180 degrees.

mcqs.q: Two radii make an angle of 110° at the centre on the minor side. An angle x at the circumference stands on the major arc. What is x?
mcqs.why: Reflex centre angle = 360 - 110 = 250 degrees. The circumference angle is half: x = (1/2) x 250 = 125 degrees.

lessons.title: Exercise 13.1
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Circumcircle of a triangle: construct the triangle from its sides or sides and angle, then intersect two perpendicular bisectors of sides to get centre O and draw the circle with radius OA.
  • Inscribed circle of a triangle: intersect two angle bisectors to get centre O, drop a perpendicular OD to a side, and draw the circle with radius OD.
  • Triangles constructed include sides 2, 2.5 and 3 cm; sides 5, 6 and 8 cm; and a triangle with angles 60 degrees and 45 degrees using all three bisectors or perpendicular bisectors.
  • For an equilateral triangle inscribed in a circle, altitude = (3/2) r: r = 3, 4, 6, 12 give altitudes 4.5, 6, 9, 18 units.
  • For an equilateral triangle circumscribed about a circle, altitude = 3r: r = 2, 5, 10 give altitudes 6, 15, 30 units.
  • To circumscribe an equilateral triangle about a circle, mark points 120 degrees apart on the circumference and draw tangents perpendicular to the radii there.
  • Escribed circles: intersect the bisectors of two exterior angles to get the centre, for the circle touching the longest side 4.5 cm or the smallest side 2.5 cm of the 2.5, 3.5, 4.5 cm triangle.

Solved Exercises

Q: Q1. Construct a triangle with sides 2 cm, 2.5 cm and 3 cm. Also draw its circumcircle.

Ans: Given: A triangle whose three sides are 2 cm, 2.5 cm and 3 cm.
Required: To construct the triangle and draw its circumcircle.
Diagram: Triangle ABC with BC = 3 cm as base, CA = 2.5 cm and AB = 2 cm, and a circle with centre O passing through A, B and C.
Steps of Construction:
(i) Draw a line segment BC = 3 cm.
(ii) With B as centre and radius 2 cm, draw an arc above BC.
(iii) With C as centre and radius 2.5 cm, draw another arc cutting the first arc at A.
(iv) Join A to B.
(v) Join A to C. Triangle ABC is formed.
(vi) Draw the perpendicular bisector of BC.
(vii) Draw the perpendicular bisector of CA.
(viii) Mark the intersection of the two perpendicular bisectors as O.
(ix) With O as centre and radius OA, draw a circle passing through A, B and C.
Justification: Every point on the perpendicular bisector of a side is equidistant from the ends of that side, so O is equidistant from A, B and C and the circle centred at O with radius OA passes through all three vertices.
Hence the triangle with sides 2 cm, 2.5 cm and 3 cm and its circumcircle are constructed.

Q: Q2. Construct a triangle ABC such that mAB = 3", mAC = 4" and m∠A = 60°. Draw circumcircle to this triangle.

Ans: Given: Triangle ABC with mAB = 3 inches, mAC = 4 inches and m∠A = 60°.
Required: To construct triangle ABC and draw its circumcircle.
Diagram: Triangle ABC with A at the left, AB = 3 inches along one arm of the 60° angle at A, AC = 4 inches along the other arm, B joined to C, and a circle with centre O passing through A, B and C.
Steps of Construction:
(i) Draw a line segment AB = 3 inches.
(ii) At A, construct an angle of 60° on AB.
(iii) On the new arm of the angle, cut off AC = 4 inches with compasses centred at A and radius 4 inches.
(iv) Join C to B. Triangle ABC is formed.
(v) Draw the perpendicular bisector of AB.
(vi) Draw the perpendicular bisector of BC.
(vii) Mark the intersection of the two perpendicular bisectors as O.
(viii) With O as centre and radius OA, draw a circle passing through A, B and C.
Justification: O lies on the perpendicular bisectors of AB and BC, so OA = OB = OC, and the circle centred at O with radius OA is the circumcircle of triangle ABC.
Hence triangle ABC with mAB = 3", mAC = 4" and m∠A = 60° and its circumcircle are constructed.

Q: Q3. Suppose we have a triangle whose sides are 3 cm, 4 cm and 6 cm respectively. Draw its inscribed circle.

Ans: Given: A triangle whose sides are 3 cm, 4 cm and 6 cm.
Required: To draw the inscribed circle of the triangle, that is, a circle inside the triangle touching all three sides.
Diagram: Triangle ABC with BC = 6 cm, CA = 4 cm and AB = 3 cm, and inside it a circle with centre O touching BC, CA and AB, with OD perpendicular to BC where D is the point of contact on BC.
Steps of Construction:
(i) Draw a line segment BC = 6 cm.
(ii) With B as centre and radius 3 cm, draw an arc above BC.
(iii) With C as centre and radius 4 cm, draw another arc cutting the first arc at A.
(iv) Join A to B.
(v) Join A to C. Triangle ABC is formed.
(vi) Draw the bisector of angle A.
(vii) Draw the bisector of angle B.
(viii) Mark the intersection of the two angle bisectors as O.
(ix) From O, draw OD perpendicular to BC, meeting BC at D.
(x) With O as centre and radius OD, draw a circle.
Justification: O lies on the bisectors of angles A and B, so O is equidistant from all three sides of the triangle; therefore the circle centred at O with radius equal to that perpendicular distance OD touches all three sides.
Hence the inscribed circle of the triangle with sides 3 cm, 4 cm and 6 cm is constructed.

Q: Q4. Construct a triangle ABC with sides mAB = 5cm, mBC = 6cm and mCA = 8cm. Draw perpendicular bisectors of its sides and then circumscribe a circle.

Ans: Given: Triangle ABC with mAB = 5 cm, mBC = 6 cm and mCA = 8 cm.
Required: To construct triangle ABC, draw the perpendicular bisectors of its sides and circumscribe a circle about it.
Diagram: Triangle ABC with BC = 6 cm as base, CA = 8 cm and AB = 5 cm, the perpendicular bisectors of its sides meeting at O, and a circle with centre O passing through A, B and C.
Steps of Construction:
(i) Draw a line segment BC = 6 cm.
(ii) With B as centre and radius 5 cm, draw an arc above BC.
(iii) With C as centre and radius 8 cm, draw another arc cutting the first arc at A.
(iv) Join A to B.
(v) Join A to C. Triangle ABC is formed.
(vi) Draw the perpendicular bisector of AB.
(vii) Draw the perpendicular bisector of BC.
(viii) Draw the perpendicular bisector of CA.
(ix) Mark the common intersection point of the perpendicular bisectors as O.
(x) With O as centre and radius OA, draw a circle passing through A, B and C.
Justification: The perpendicular bisectors of the sides of a triangle are concurrent, and their point of concurrence O is equidistant from A, B and C, so the circle centred at O with radius OA passes through all three vertices.
Hence triangle ABC with mAB = 5 cm, mBC = 6 cm and mCA = 8 cm, the perpendicular bisectors of its sides and its circumcircle are constructed.

Q: Q5. Draw a triangle ABC with m∠A = 60° and m∠B = 45°. Draw three angle bisectors and then inscribe a circle in it.

Ans: Given: Triangle ABC with m∠A = 60° and m∠B = 45° (no side is given, so the size of the triangle may be chosen; the shape is fixed by the two angles).
Required: To draw triangle ABC, draw its three angle bisectors and inscribe a circle in it.
Diagram: Triangle ABC with angle 60° at A, angle 45° at B and angle 75° at C, the bisectors of the three angles meeting at O inside the triangle, and a circle with centre O touching all three sides, with OD perpendicular to BC.
Steps of Construction:
(i) Draw a line segment BC of any convenient length.
(ii) At B, construct an angle of 45° on BC.
(iii) At C, construct an angle of 75°, because m∠C = 180° - 60° - 45° = 75°.
(iv) Mark the intersection of the two new arms as A, so that m∠A = 60°. Triangle ABC is formed.
(v) Draw the bisector of angle A.
(vi) Draw the bisector of angle B.
(vii) Draw the bisector of angle C.
(viii) Mark the common intersection point of the three bisectors as O.
(ix) From O, draw OD perpendicular to BC, meeting BC at D.
(x) With O as centre and radius OD, draw a circle.
Justification: The three angle bisectors of a triangle are concurrent at a point equidistant from all three sides, so the circle centred at that point O with radius equal to the perpendicular distance OD touches all three sides.
Hence triangle ABC with m∠A = 60° and m∠B = 45°, its three angle bisectors and its inscribed circle are constructed.
Note: the book gives no side for this triangle, so any convenient length for BC gives a correct triangle of the required shape.

Q: Q6. An equilateral triangle is inscribed in a circle. Find the altitude of the triangle if the radius r of the circle varies as under: r = 3 units, r = 4 units, r = 6 units, r = 12 units. Can you deduce some result from this?

Ans: Rule: in an equilateral triangle the centre of the circumscribed circle divides each altitude in the ratio 2 : 1, counting from the vertex.
Step (i): the part of the altitude from a vertex to the centre of the circle is the radius r.
Step (ii): the part from the centre to the opposite side is (r)/(2).
Step (iii): so the whole altitude = r + (r)/(2) = (3r)/(2).
Step (iv): for r = 3 units, altitude = (3 × 3)/(2) = 4.5 units.
Step (v): for r = 4 units, altitude = (3 × 4)/(2) = 6 units.
Step (vi): for r = 6 units, altitude = (3 × 6)/(2) = 9 units.
Step (vii): for r = 12 units, altitude = (3 × 12)/(2) = 18 units.
Answer: the altitudes are 4.5 units, 6 units, 9 units and 18 units respectively, and in every case the altitude of an equilateral triangle inscribed in a circle is (3)/(2) times the radius of the circle.

Q: Q7. An equilateral triangle is circumscribed about a circle. Find the altitude of the triangle if the radius r of the circle varies as under: r = 2 units, r = 5 units, r = 10 units. Can you deduce some result from this?

Ans: Rule: in an equilateral triangle the centre of the inscribed circle divides each altitude in the ratio 2 : 1, counting from the vertex, and the part from the centre to a side is the radius r of the inscribed circle.
Step (i): the part of the altitude from the centre to the side it meets is r.
Step (ii): the part from the vertex to the centre is twice as much, that is, 2r.
Step (iii): so the whole altitude = 2r + r = 3r.
Step (iv): for r = 2 units, altitude = 3 × 2 = 6 units.
Step (v): for r = 5 units, altitude = 3 × 5 = 15 units.
Step (vi): for r = 10 units, altitude = 3 × 10 = 30 units.
Answer: the altitudes are 6 units, 15 units and 30 units respectively, and in every case the altitude of an equilateral triangle circumscribed about a circle is 3 times the radius of the circle.

Q: Q8. Circumscribe an equilateral triangle about a circle of radius 2", 3" and 1".

Ans: Given: Three circles, of radii 2 inches, 3 inches and 1 inch respectively; the same construction is repeated for each circle.
Required: To circumscribe an equilateral triangle about each given circle, that is, to draw an equilateral triangle whose three sides touch the circle.
Diagram: For each circle: centre O, points A, T and U on the circumference with ∠AOT = 120° and ∠TOU = 120°, tangents drawn at A, T and U meeting each other at B, C and D, forming equilateral triangle BCD around the circle.
Steps of Construction:
(i) Draw the first circle with centre O and radius 2 inches.
(ii) Take any point A on its circumference and join O to A.
(iii) At O, construct angle ∠AOT = 120°, where T is on the circumference.
(iv) At O, construct angle ∠TOU = 120°, where U is on the circumference.
(v) At A, draw a line perpendicular to OA.
(vi) At T, draw a line perpendicular to OT.
(vii) At U, draw a line perpendicular to OU.
(viii) Mark the intersections of these three perpendicular lines as B, C and D. Triangle BCD is the equilateral triangle circumscribed about the circle of radius 2 inches.
(ix) Repeat steps (i) to (viii) with a circle of radius 3 inches to get the second required triangle.
(x) Repeat steps (i) to (viii) with a circle of radius 1 inch to get the third required triangle.
Justification: Each side of triangle BCD is perpendicular to a radius at its point of contact, so each side is a tangent to the circle; the three points of contact divide the circle into three equal arcs of 120°, which makes the three tangents form an equilateral triangle.
Hence equilateral triangles are circumscribed about the circles of radius 2", 3" and 1".

Q: Q9. Draw a triangle with sides 2.5 cm, 3.5 cm and 4.5 cm long. Draw an escribed circle to the triangle touching the longest side of the triangle.

Ans: Given: A triangle with sides 2.5 cm, 3.5 cm and 4.5 cm; the longest side is 4.5 cm.
Required: To construct the triangle and draw the escribed circle touching its longest side (the circle opposite the vertex joining the other two sides, touching the 4.5 cm side externally and the extensions of the other two sides).
Diagram: Triangle ABC with BC = 4.5 cm as the longest side, CA = 3.5 cm and AB = 2.5 cm, AB and AC produced beyond B and C, and a circle with centre O below BC touching BC externally and touching the two produced sides.
Steps of Construction:
(i) Draw a line segment BC = 4.5 cm.
(ii) With B as centre and radius 2.5 cm, draw an arc above BC.
(iii) With C as centre and radius 3.5 cm, draw another arc cutting the first arc at A.
(iv) Join A to B.
(v) Join A to C. Triangle ABC is formed.
(vi) Produce AB beyond B to a point D.
(vii) Produce AC beyond C to a point E.
(viii) Draw the bisector of the exterior angle at B, that is, of angle CBD.
(ix) Draw the bisector of the exterior angle at C, that is, of angle BCE.
(x) Mark the intersection of the two exterior bisectors as O.
Justification: O lies on the bisectors of the two exterior angles at B and C (and also on the bisector of angle A), so O is equidistant from BC and from the extensions of AB and AC; hence the circle centred at O with radius OF touches the longest side BC and the two produced sides.
Hence the triangle with sides 2.5 cm, 3.5 cm and 4.5 cm and the escribed circle touching its longest side are constructed.

Q: Q10. For the problem in Q.9 draw an escribed circle to the triangle touching the smallest side.

Ans: Given: The triangle of Q.9 with sides 2.5 cm, 3.5 cm and 4.5 cm; the smallest side is 2.5 cm.
Required: To draw the escribed circle touching the smallest side (2.5 cm) of the triangle, that is, the circle opposite the vertex at the other end of that side, touching the 2.5 cm side externally and the extensions of the other two sides.
Diagram: Triangle ABC as in Q.9 with AB = 2.5 cm as the smallest side, BC = 4.5 cm and CA = 3.5 cm, the sides meeting at A and B produced beyond A and B on the side of AB, and a circle with centre O touching AB externally and touching the two produced sides.
Steps of Construction:
(i) Draw triangle ABC as in Q.9, with AB = 2.5 cm, BC = 4.5 cm and CA = 3.5 cm.
(ii) Produce CA beyond A.
(iii) Produce CB beyond B, so that the extensions meet the region beyond side AB.
(iv) Draw the bisector of the exterior angle at A formed by the extension of CA and side AB.
(v) Draw the bisector of the exterior angle at B formed by the extension of CB and side AB.
(vi) Mark the intersection of the two exterior bisectors as O.
(vii) From O, draw a perpendicular to AB, meeting AB at F.
(viii) With O as centre and radius OF, draw a circle.
Justification: O lies on the bisectors of the exterior angles at A and B, so O is equidistant from AB and from the extensions of CA and CB; hence the circle centred at O with radius OF touches the smallest side AB and the two produced sides.
Hence the escribed circle touching the smallest side of the triangle of Q.9 is constructed.

lessons.title: Exercise 13.2
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • To circumscribe a square about a circle, draw two perpendicular diameters and draw tangents perpendicular to the radii at their four endpoints.
  • To inscribe a square in a circle, draw two perpendicular diameters and join their endpoints in order.
  • For a square of side 6 cm, the circumscribed circle radius is 3 root 2 cm and the inscribed circle radius is 3 cm.
  • The side of a square circumscribed about a circle equals the diameter, so a circumscribed square of side 8 units needs a circle of radius 4 units.
  • A square of side 10 cm inscribed in a circle has diagonal 10 root 2 cm as diameter, so the radius is 5 root 2 cm.
  • To inscribe a regular hexagon, step the radius around the circumference, since the side of a regular hexagon equals the radius; to circumscribe one, draw tangents at the six stepped points.
  • For radius 8 cm: area of inscribed hexagon is about 166.28 cm squared, area of circle about 201.06 cm squared, area of circumscribed hexagon about 221.70 cm squared.
  • Squaring the circle exactly with ruler and compasses is impossible because pi is not constructible; only an approximate square using an approximate value of pi is possible.

Solved Exercises

Q: Q1. Circumscribe a square about a circle of radius 5cm.

Ans: Given: A circle of radius 5 cm.
Required: To circumscribe a square about the circle, that is, to draw a square whose four sides touch the circle.
Diagram: Circle with centre O and radius 5 cm, two diameters AB and CD perpendicular to each other, and tangents at A, B, C and D meeting at E, F, G and H, forming square EFGH around the circle; each side of the square is 10 cm.
Steps of Construction:
(i) With O as centre and radius 5 cm, draw a circle.
(ii) Draw any diameter AB of the circle.
(iii) Draw another diameter CD perpendicular to AB.
(iv) At A, draw a line perpendicular to OA.
(v) At B, draw a line perpendicular to OB.
(vi) At C, draw a line perpendicular to OC.
(vii) At D, draw a line perpendicular to OD.
(viii) Mark the intersections of these four lines as E, F, G and H.
Justification: Each of the four lines is perpendicular to a radius at its end point, so each is a tangent to the circle; the two pairs of tangents are parallel and the angles between them are right angles, so EFGH is a square touching the circle on all four sides.
Hence the square EFGH is circumscribed about the circle of radius 5 cm.

Q: Q2. Inscribe a square in a circle of radius 6 cm.

Ans: Given: A circle of radius 6 cm.
Required: To inscribe a square in the circle, that is, to draw a square whose four vertices lie on the circle.
Diagram: Circle with centre O and radius 6 cm, two diameters AB and CD perpendicular to each other, and A, C, B and D joined in order to form the inscribed square ACBD.
Steps of Construction:
(i) With O as centre and radius 6 cm, draw a circle.
(ii) Draw any diameter AB of the circle.
(iii) Draw another diameter CD perpendicular to AB.
(iv) Join A to C.
(v) Join C to B.
(vi) Join B to D.
(vii) Join D to A.
Justification: The diagonals ACBD's diagonals AB and CD are equal diameters bisecting each other at right angles, so ACBD is a square, and all its vertices lie on the circle.
Hence the square ACBD is inscribed in the circle of radius 6 cm.

Q: Q3. Draw a square of side 6 cm. Circumscribe a circle about that square and then inscribe a circle in the same square. Measure the radii of these two circles.

Ans: Given: A square of side 6 cm.
Required: To draw the square, circumscribe a circle about it, inscribe a circle in it, and measure the radii of the two circles.
Diagram: Square ABCD of side 6 cm with centre O at the intersection of its diagonals, a circle with centre O passing through A, B, C and D (the circumscribed circle), and a smaller circle with centre O touching all four sides (the inscribed circle).
Steps of Construction:
(i) Draw a line segment AB = 6 cm.
(ii) At A and at B, erect perpendiculars to AB.
(iii) On the perpendicular at A, cut off AD = 6 cm.
(iv) On the perpendicular at B, cut off BC = 6 cm.
(v) Join C to D. Square ABCD is formed.
(vi) Draw the diagonal AC.
(vii) Draw the diagonal BD.
(viii) Mark the intersection of the diagonals as O.
(ix) With O as centre and radius OA, draw a circle passing through A, B, C and D; this is the circumscribed circle.
(x) From O, draw a perpendicular to AB, meeting AB at its midpoint M.
Justification: O, the intersection of the diagonals, is equidistant from the four vertices, giving the circumscribed circle, and equidistant from the four sides, giving the inscribed circle. By calculation, OA = (6√(2))/(2) = 3√(2) cm and OM = (6)/(2) = 3 cm.
Hence the square of side 6 cm and its two circles are constructed, and the radii measure: circumscribed circle 3√(2) cm (about 4.24 cm) and inscribed circle 3 cm.

Q: Q4. First draw a circle of suitable radius, so that the square circumscribed about that circle has sides of length 8 units.

Ans: Given: A square circumscribed about a circle is required to have sides of length 8 units.
Required: To find a suitable radius and draw the circle, then circumscribe the square of side 8 units about it.
Diagram: Circle with centre O and radius 4 units, two perpendicular diameters, and tangents at their four end points forming a square of side 8 units around the circle.
Steps of Construction:
(i) Note that the side of a square circumscribed about a circle is equal to the diameter of the circle.
(ii) So the diameter must be 8 units and the radius must be (8)/(2) = 4 units.
(iii) With O as centre and radius 4 units, draw a circle.
(iv) Draw any diameter AB of the circle.
(v) Draw another diameter CD perpendicular to AB.
(vi) At A, B, C and D draw lines perpendicular to OA, OB, OC and OD respectively.
(vii) Mark the intersections of these four lines as the vertices of the square and measure its side; it is 8 units.
Justification: Each side of the circumscribed square is a tangent segment between two parallel tangents, equal to the diameter of the circle, so a circle of radius 4 units gives a circumscribed square of side 8 units.
Hence a circle of radius 4 units is drawn and the square of side 8 units is circumscribed about it.

Q: Q5. Inscribe a square of side 10 cm in a circle. What will be the size of the radius?

Ans: Given: A square of side 10 cm is to be inscribed in a circle.
Required: To inscribe the square in a circle and find the radius of the circle.
Diagram: Square ABCD of side 10 cm with its diagonal AC as a diameter of the circle, centre O at the midpoint of the diagonal, and the circle passing through A, B, C and D.
Steps of Construction:
(i) Draw a line segment AB = 10 cm.
(ii) At A and at B, erect perpendiculars to AB.
(iii) On the perpendiculars, cut off AD = 10 cm and BC = 10 cm.
(iv) Join C to D. Square ABCD is formed.
(v) Draw the diagonal AC.
(vi) Find the midpoint O of AC.
(vii) With O as centre and radius OA, draw a circle passing through A, B, C and D.
(viii) For the radius: by Pythagoras, mAC = √(10² + 10²) = √(200) = 10√(2) cm.
(ix) The diagonal AC is a diameter of the circle, so radius = (10√(2))/(2) = 5√(2) cm.
Justification: The diagonal of an inscribed square passes through the centre and is a diameter of the circle, so the radius is half the diagonal.
Hence the square of side 10 cm is inscribed in the circle, and the radius is 5√(2) cm, about 7.07 cm.

Q: Q6. Inscribe a regular hexagon in a circle of radius 4 cm.

Ans: Given: A circle of radius 4 cm.
Required: To inscribe a regular hexagon in the circle.
Diagram: Circle with centre O and radius 4 cm, points A, B, C, D, E and F in order on the circumference, each side 4 cm, joined to form regular hexagon ABCDEF.
Steps of Construction:
(i) With O as centre and radius 4 cm, draw a circle.
(ii) Take any point A on the circumference.
(iii) With A as centre and radius 4 cm (equal to OA), draw an arc cutting the circumference at B.
(iv) With B as centre and radius 4 cm, draw an arc cutting the circumference at C.
(v) With C as centre and radius 4 cm, draw an arc cutting the circumference at D.
(vi) With D as centre and radius 4 cm, draw an arc cutting the circumference at E.
(vii) With E as centre and radius 4 cm, draw an arc cutting the circumference at F.
(viii) Join A to B, B to C, C to D, D to E, E to F and F to A.
Justification: The side of a regular hexagon inscribed in a circle is equal to the radius of the circle, so stepping the radius 4 cm around the circumference divides it into six equal arcs and the six points form a regular hexagon.
Hence the regular hexagon ABCDEF is inscribed in the circle of radius 4 cm.

Q: Q7. Construct a circle of radius 4cm and draw a regular hexagon about the circle.

Ans: Given: A circle of radius 4 cm is to be constructed.
Required: To draw a regular hexagon about (circumscribed about) the circle.
Diagram: Circle with centre O and radius 4 cm, six points A, B, C, D, E and F on the circumference obtained by stepping off the radius, diameters through opposite points, and tangents at all six points meeting to form the circumscribed regular hexagon GHIJKL.
Steps of Construction:
(i) With O as centre and radius 4 cm, draw a circle.
(ii) Take any point A on the circumference.
(iii) With A as centre and radius 4 cm, draw arcs cutting the circumference at B and F.
(iv) Continue stepping the radius 4 cm around the circumference to mark C, D and E in order.
(v) Draw the diameters AD, BE and FC through O.
(vi) At A, draw a line perpendicular to OA.
(vii) At B, C, D, E and F, draw lines perpendicular to OB, OC, OD, OE and OF respectively.
(viii) Mark the intersections of these six tangent lines as G, H, I, J, K and L.
Justification: Each line is perpendicular to a radius at its point of contact, so each is a tangent; the six points of contact divide the circle into six equal arcs of 60°, so the six tangents form a regular hexagon around the circle.
Hence the regular hexagon GHIJKL is circumscribed about the circle of radius 4 cm.

Q: Q8. Draw a circle of radius 8 cm. Circumscribe a regular hexagon about that circle and also inscribe a regular hexagon in the same circle. Find the areas of these geometrical figures. Comment on the values of these areas.

Ans: Given: A circle of radius 8 cm.
Required: To circumscribe a regular hexagon about the circle, inscribe a regular hexagon in the same circle, find the areas of the circle and of both hexagons, and comment on the values.
Diagram: Circle with centre O and radius 8 cm; inside it regular hexagon ABCDEF with each side 8 cm and vertices on the circle; outside it a larger regular hexagon whose six sides are tangents to the circle.
Steps of Construction:
(i) With O as centre and radius 8 cm, draw a circle.
(ii) Take any point A on the circumference and step the radius 8 cm around the circumference to mark B, C, D, E and F.
(iii) Join A to B, B to C, C to D, D to E, E to F and F to A; this is the inscribed regular hexagon.
(iv) At each of A, B, C, D, E and F draw a line perpendicular to the radius at that point.
(v) Mark the intersections of these six tangent lines; this is the circumscribed regular hexagon.
(vi) Area of the circle = πr² = π × 8² = 64π ≈ 201.06 cm².
(vii) Area of the inscribed hexagon = 6 equilateral triangles of side 8 cm = 6 × (√(3))/(4) × 8² = 96√(3) ≈ 166.28 cm².
(viii) For the circumscribed hexagon the apothem is 8 cm, so its side = (2 × 8)/(√(3)) = (16)/(√(3)) cm, and its area = (1)/(2) × perimeter × apothem = 2√(3) × 8² = 128√(3) ≈ 221.70 cm².
Justification: The inscribed hexagon lies wholly inside the circle and the circumscribed hexagon lies wholly outside it, so their areas must be respectively less than and greater than the area of the circle.
Hence the two hexagons are constructed; area of inscribed hexagon ≈ 166.28 cm², area of circle ≈ 201.06 cm² and area of circumscribed hexagon ≈ 221.70 cm². Comment: inscribed hexagon < circle < circumscribed hexagon, as expected, because the first figure is inside the circle and the last is outside it.

Q: Q9. Draw two regular hexagons of perimeters 6 cm and 30 cm respectively. Determine their centres. From their centers draw perpendicular to any of their sides respectively. What is the relation of these two perpendiculars?

Ans: Given: Two regular hexagons, of perimeters 6 cm and 30 cm respectively.
Required: To draw both hexagons, determine their centres, draw from each centre a perpendicular to one side, and find the relation between the two perpendiculars.
Diagram: First hexagon with centre O1 and side (6)/(6) = 1 cm, with O1M perpendicular to one side; second hexagon with centre O2 and side (30)/(6) = 5 cm, with O2N perpendicular to one side; O2N is 5 times O1M.
Steps of Construction:
(i) For the first hexagon, side = (6 cm)/(6) = 1 cm.
(ii) Draw a line segment AB = 1 cm.
(iii) Construct angles of 120° at A and B and complete regular hexagon ABCDEF of side 1 cm by stepping the side length around.
(iv) Draw two diagonals through opposite vertices of the first hexagon.
(v) Mark their intersection as O1, the centre of the first hexagon.
(vi) From O1, draw O1M perpendicular to any one side of the first hexagon.
(vii) For the second hexagon, side = (30 cm)/(6) = 5 cm.
(viii) In the same way, construct a regular hexagon of side 5 cm.
(ix) Draw two diagonals through opposite vertices of the second hexagon and mark their intersection as O2, its centre.
(x) From O2, draw O2N perpendicular to any one side of the second hexagon.
Justification: The perpendicular from the centre of a regular hexagon to a side is its apothem, equal to (√(3))/(2) times the side; the sides are in the ratio 1 : 5, so the apothems are also in the ratio 1 : 5.
Hence the two regular hexagons and the perpendiculars from their centres are constructed, and the perpendicular for the larger hexagon is 5 times the perpendicular for the smaller hexagon (they are in the same ratio as the sides, 1 : 5).

Q: Q10. Can you construct a square whose area equals the areas of a given circle? Discuss in detail.

Ans: Rule: the area of a circle of radius r is πr², so a square of equal area would need side s with s² = πr², that is, s = r√(π).
Step (i): a length can be constructed exactly with ruler and compasses only if it can be obtained from the given length by addition, subtraction, multiplication, division and taking square roots.
Step (ii): π is not such a number; it cannot be produced exactly by any finite sequence of ruler-and-compass steps from r.
Step (iii): therefore the side r√(π) cannot be constructed exactly, and no exact construction of the square is possible.
Step (iv): an approximate square can be drawn by taking a decimal approximation for π, for example π ≈ (22)/(7) or π ≈ 3.1416, finding s ≈ r√(3.1416) and constructing a square of that side; its area is then nearly, but not exactly, equal to the area of the circle.
Answer: No - a square exactly equal in area to a given circle cannot be constructed with ruler and compasses (this is the classical problem of squaring the circle); only an approximate construction, using an approximate value of π, is possible.

lessons.title: Exercise 13.3
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Tangent at the midpoint of an arc without using the centre: draw chord AB, a line through midpoint P perpendicular to AB, then a line through P perpendicular to that line.
  • Tangent at an endpoint of an arc without using the centre: use the alternate segment theorem, constructing at P an angle equal to the angle in the opposite segment.
  • Tangent from an outside point to an arc without using the centre uses a semicircle on AP and the tangent-secant relation PC squared = PB times PA.
  • A circle through point D touching line BC at D: erect the perpendicular to BC at D, take any point O on it, and draw the circle with radius OD.
  • A circle of given radius through a point and touching a line: its centre lies on a parallel line at the given radius distance from the line.
  • Direct common tangents use an auxiliary radius equal to the difference of the radii; transverse common tangents use an auxiliary radius equal to the sum of the radii.
  • Transverse tangents are constructed for equal circles of radius 4 cm with centres 10 cm apart and for radii 2 cm and 2.5 cm with centres 5.5 cm apart.
  • A circle of radius 2.5 cm touching both arms of a 60 degree angle has its centre on the angle bisector at distance BO = 2.5 / sin 30 degrees = 5 cm from the vertex.

Solved Exercises

Q: Q1(i). Draw an arc of length 7 cm. Without using the center draw a tangent through a given point P when P is the middle point of the arc.

Ans: Given: An arc of length 7 cm, with P as the middle point of the arc; the centre of the circle is not to be used.
Required: To draw a tangent to the arc at its middle point P, without using the centre.
Diagram: Arc AB of length 7 cm with P at its middle, chord AB drawn, line CD through P perpendicular to AB, and line EF through P perpendicular to CD; EF is the tangent at P.
Steps of Construction:
(i) Draw an arc AB of length 7 cm and mark its middle point P.
(ii) Join A to B, drawing the chord AB.
(iii) Through P, draw a line CD perpendicular to AB.
(iv) At P, draw a line EF perpendicular to CD.
(v) EF touches the arc only at P.
Justification: Since P is the midpoint of the arc, the line through P and the (unused) centre is perpendicular to the chord AB; CD is that line, and the tangent at P is perpendicular to the radius line CD, so EF, drawn perpendicular to CD at P, is the tangent.
Hence the tangent at the middle point P of the arc of length 7 cm is drawn without using the centre.

Q: Q1(ii). Draw an arc of length 7 cm. Without using the center draw a tangent through a given point P when P is end point of the arc.

Ans: Given: An arc of length 7 cm, with P as an end point of the arc; the centre of the circle is not to be used.
Required: To draw a tangent to the arc at its end point P, without using the centre.
Diagram: Arc AP of length 7 cm, a point Q taken on the arc, chords AP and PQ drawn, A joined to Q, and ray PT making angle ∠QPT congruent to ∠PAQ; PT is the tangent at P.
Steps of Construction:
(i) Draw an arc AP of length 7 cm, with P as its end point.
(ii) Take any point Q on the arc AP.
(iii) Draw the chord AP.
(iv) Draw the chord PQ.
(v) Join A to Q.
(vi) At P, on the side of AP opposite to Q, construct angle ∠QPT congruent to angle ∠PAQ.
(vii) Draw the ray PT forming that angle.
Justification: By the alternate segment theorem, the angle between a tangent and a chord through the point of contact is equal to the angle in the alternate segment; constructing ∠QPT equal to the angle in the opposite segment makes PT the tangent at P.
Hence the tangent at the end point P of the arc of length 7 cm is drawn without using the centre.

Q: Q1(iii). Draw an arc of length 7 cm. Without using the center draw a tangent through a given point P when P is outside the arc.

Ans: Given: An arc AT of length 7 cm and a point P outside the arc; the centre of the circle is not to be used.
Required: To draw a tangent from the outside point P to the arc, without using the centre.
Diagram: Arc AT, point P outside it, line AP cutting the arc at B, D the midpoint of AP, a semicircle on AP cutting the perpendicular at B in C, and an arc centred at P with radius PC cutting the given arc at E; PE is the tangent from P.
Steps of Construction:
(i) Draw an arc AT of length 7 cm and take a point P outside the arc.
(ii) Join A to P; the line AP cuts the arc at B.
(iii) Bisect AP at D.
(iv) With D as centre and radius DP, draw a semicircle on AP.
(v) At B, draw BC perpendicular to AP, meeting the semicircle at C.
(vi) With P as centre and radius PC, draw an arc cutting the given arc at E.
(vii) Join P to E and produce it.
Justification: The angle in a semicircle is a right angle, and the construction makes PC the length of the tangent from P (PC² = PB × PA, the tangent-secant relation), so the arc centred at P with radius PC meets the given arc at the point of contact E, and PE is tangent there.
Hence the tangent from the outside point P to the arc of length 7 cm is drawn without using the centre.

Q: Q2. Draw a circle passing through a point D and touching a given line BC at point D.

Ans: Given: A given line BC and a point D on it.
Required: To draw a circle which passes through D and touches the line BC at D (any such circle; its size may be chosen).
Diagram: Line BC with point D on it, a perpendicular to BC erected at D, a point O taken on the perpendicular, and a circle with centre O and radius OD touching BC at D.
Steps of Construction:
(i) Draw the given line BC and mark the point D on it.
(ii) At D, erect a line perpendicular to BC.
(iii) Take any point O on this perpendicular, at a convenient distance from D.
(iv) With O as centre and radius OD, draw a circle.
Justification: The radius OD is perpendicular to BC at D, and a line perpendicular to a radius at its end point is a tangent to the circle; so the circle touches BC at D and passes through D.
Hence a circle passing through D and touching the line BC at D is constructed.

Q: Q3. Describe a circle of radius 4cm, passing through a given point C and touching a given straight line AB.

Ans: Given: A given straight line AB and a given point C, with a circle of radius 4 cm required to pass through C and touch AB.
Required: To describe the circle of radius 4 cm through C touching the line AB.
Diagram: Line AB, a line parallel to AB at distance 4 cm on the side of C, an arc centred at C with radius 4 cm cutting that parallel line at O, and a circle with centre O and radius 4 cm passing through C and touching AB.
Steps of Construction:
(i) Draw the given straight line AB and mark the given point C.
(ii) Draw a line parallel to AB at a distance of 4 cm from it, on the same side of AB as C.
(iii) With C as centre and radius 4 cm, draw an arc cutting the parallel line at O.
(iv) With O as centre and radius 4 cm, draw a circle.
Justification: The centre of a circle of radius 4 cm touching AB must be 4 cm from AB, so O lies on the parallel line drawn; also OC = 4 cm, so the circle passes through C, and its perpendicular distance from O to AB is 4 cm, equal to the radius, so it touches AB.
Hence the circle of radius 4 cm passing through C and touching the line AB is described.

Q: Q4. Radius of a circle is 2.5 cm. A point Q is at a distance of 5cm from the centre. Draw tangent to the circle from the point Q.

Ans: Given: A circle of radius 2.5 cm with centre O, and a point Q outside it with OQ = 5 cm.
Required: To draw a tangent to the circle from the point Q.
Diagram: Circle with centre O and radius 2.5 cm, Q at distance 5 cm from O, arc with centre Q and radius OQ = 5 cm, arc with centre O and radius equal to the diameter 5 cm meeting the first arc at E, line OE meeting the circle at F, and line QF as the tangent.
Steps of Construction:
(i) With O as centre and radius 2.5 cm, draw a circle.
(ii) Mark a point Q with OQ = 5 cm and join O to Q.
(iii) With Q as centre and radius OQ = 5 cm, draw an arc on the side of the circle.
(iv) With O as centre and radius 5 cm (the diameter of the given circle), draw another arc cutting the first arc at E.
(v) Join O to E; the line OE cuts the given circle at F.
(vi) Join Q to F and produce it.
Justification: The construction makes triangle OEQ give OF perpendicular to QF at the point F on the circle (the book's construction for a tangent from an outside point), so QF is perpendicular to the radius OF and is therefore a tangent. As a check, the tangent length QF = √(5² - 2.5²) = √(18.75) ≈ 4.33 cm.
Hence the tangent QF from the point Q, 5 cm from the centre, to the circle of radius 2.5 cm is drawn.

Q: Q5. Radii of two circles are 2 cm and 3cm and their centres are 8 cm apart. Draw direct common tangents to the circles.

Ans: Given: Two unequal circles of radii 2 cm and 3 cm, with centres 8 cm apart.
Required: To draw the direct (external) common tangents to the two circles.
Diagram: Larger circle with centre O and radius 3 cm, smaller circle with centre P and radius 2 cm, OP = 8 cm, an auxiliary semicircle on OP, point M on the larger circle and point N on the smaller circle with PN parallel to OM, and line MN produced both ways as a direct common tangent; the second tangent is drawn symmetrically on the other side.
Steps of Construction:
(i) Draw a line segment OP = 8 cm.
(ii) With O as centre and radius 3 cm, draw the larger circle.
(iii) With P as centre and radius 2 cm, draw the smaller circle.
(iv) Bisect OP at Q.
(v) With Q as centre and radius QP, draw a semicircle on OP.
(vi) On OP inside the larger circle, take a point T such that the remaining radius length OT = 3 cm - 2 cm = 1 cm is marked by taking RT = SP along OP as in the book's construction, where R and S are the points where OP cuts the two circles.
(vii) With O as centre and radius OT = 1 cm, draw an arc cutting the semicircle at L.
(viii) Join O to L and produce it to meet the larger circle at M.
(ix) Through P, draw PN parallel to OM, meeting the smaller circle at N on the same side.
(x) Join M to N and produce the line to both sides; this is one direct common tangent.
Justification: OM is parallel and equal in direction to PN and the figure OMPN has OM - PN arranged so that MN is at distance equal to each radius from its centre on the same side; hence MN is perpendicular to both radii at M and N and touches both circles without crossing OP, which is a direct common tangent.
Hence the direct common tangents to the circles of radii 2 cm and 3 cm with centres 8 cm apart are drawn.

Q: Q6. Two congruent circles are of radius 4 cm each. Their centres are 10 cm apart. Draw transverse common tangents to these circles.

Ans: Given: Two equal (congruent) circles of radius 4 cm each, with centres 10 cm apart.
Required: To draw the transverse (internal) common tangents to the two circles.
Diagram: Two circles of radius 4 cm with centres O and P, OP = 10 cm, C the midpoint of OP, a semicircle on CP meeting the circle at P in E, F on the other circle with OF parallel to EP, and line GH through E and F as a transverse common tangent; the second tangent is drawn symmetrically.
Steps of Construction:
(i) Draw a line segment OP = 10 cm.
(ii) With O as centre and radius 4 cm, draw the first circle.
(iii) With P as centre and radius 4 cm, draw the second circle.
(iv) Bisect OP at C.
(v) Bisect CP at D.
(vi) With D as centre and radius DP, draw a semicircle on CP, cutting the circle with centre P at E.
(vii) Join E to P.
(viii) Through O, draw OF parallel to EP, meeting the first circle at F on the opposite side of OP from E.
(ix) Join E to F and produce the line to both directions as GH; GH is one transverse common tangent.
(x) Repeat the construction on the other side of OP to draw the second transverse common tangent.
Justification: The semicircle construction gives the correct point of contact E on one circle, and OF drawn parallel to EP in the opposite sense gives the point of contact F on the equal circle; the line through E and F crosses OP between the circles and is perpendicular to the radii at E and F, so it is a transverse common tangent.
Hence the transverse common tangents to the two congruent circles of radius 4 cm with centres 10 cm apart are drawn.

Q: Q7. Radii of two circles are 2cm and 2.5 cm respectively. Distance between their centres is 5.5 cm. Draw transverse common tangents to the circles.

Ans: Given: Two unequal circles of radii 2 cm and 2.5 cm, with distance between their centres 5.5 cm.
Required: To draw the transverse (internal) common tangents to the two circles.
Diagram: Larger circle with centre O and radius r1 = 2.5 cm, smaller circle with centre P and radius r2 = 2 cm, OP = 5.5 cm, a segment AB = r1 + r2 = 4.5 cm, a semicircle with centre O and radius AB meeting an arc on OP at Q, T where OQ cuts the larger circle, S on the smaller circle with PS parallel to OQ in the opposite sense, and line TS produced both ways as a transverse common tangent; the second tangent is drawn symmetrically.
Steps of Construction:
(i) Draw a line segment OP = 5.5 cm.
(ii) With O as centre and radius 2.5 cm, draw the larger circle.
(iii) With P as centre and radius 2 cm, draw the smaller circle.
(iv) Draw a line segment AB with mAB = r1 + r2 = 2.5 cm + 2 cm = 4.5 cm.
(v) With O as centre and radius mAB = 4.5 cm, draw a semicircle.
(vi) Bisect OP at C.
(vii) With C as centre and radius OC, draw an arc cutting the semicircle at Q.
(viii) Join O to Q; the line OQ cuts the larger circle at T.
(ix) Through P, draw PS parallel to OQ in the opposite sense, cutting the smaller circle at S.
(x) Join T to S and produce the line in both directions; this is one transverse common tangent.
Justification: Using a radius equal to r1 + r2 combines the two radii on opposite sides of the tangent, which is exactly the condition for a transverse tangent; TS is perpendicular to OT at T and to PS at S and crosses OP between the circles, so it touches both circles transversely.
Hence the transverse common tangents to the circles of radii 2 cm and 2.5 cm with centres 5.5 cm apart are drawn.

Q: Q8. Draw ∠ABC of measure 60°. Construct a circle having radius 2.5 cm and touching the arms of the angle.

Ans: Given: Angle ∠ABC of measure 60°, with vertex B, and a required circle of radius 2.5 cm.
Required: To draw the angle of 60° and construct a circle of radius 2.5 cm touching both arms BA and BC of the angle.
Diagram: Angle ABC = 60° at B, its bisector BD, a point O on BD at distance (2.5)/(sin 30°) = 5 cm from B, OF perpendicular to BC with F on BC and OF = 2.5 cm, and a circle with centre O and radius 2.5 cm touching both arms.
Steps of Construction:
(i) Draw a line BC.
(ii) At B, construct an angle of 60° and draw the arm BA, so m∠ABC = 60°.
(iii) Draw BD, the bisector of angle ABC, so each part is 30°.
(iv) On BD, mark a point O such that the perpendicular from O to BC will be 2.5 cm: since the angle between BD and BC is 30°, take BO = (2.5)/(sin 30°) = (2.5)/(0.5) = 5 cm.
(v) From O, draw OF perpendicular to BC, meeting BC at F; then OF = 2.5 cm.
(vi) With O as centre and radius 2.5 cm, draw a circle.
Justification: The centre of a circle touching both arms of an angle lies on the bisector of the angle, and its radius is its perpendicular distance from either arm; with O on the bisector and OF = 2.5 cm perpendicular to BC, the circle of radius 2.5 cm touches BC at F and touches BA at the corresponding point.
Hence the circle of radius 2.5 cm touching both arms of ∠ABC = 60° is constructed.

lessons.title: Review Exercise 13
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • The external angle of a regular hexagon is pi/3 radians, that is 60 degrees, from 360 degrees divided by 6.
  • Tangents drawn at the endpoints of a diameter are parallel, and exactly 2 tangents can be drawn from a point outside a circle.
  • If the distance between centres equals the sum of the radii, the two circles touch each other externally.
  • The centre of an arc ABC is found as the intersection of the perpendicular bisectors of chords AB and BC.
  • The escribed circle opposite vertex A of the 5 cm, 4 cm, 3 cm triangle has radius 3 cm, from area divided by (s - a).
  • Circumscribing a circle about an equilateral triangle and circumscribing a regular hexagon about a circle both use perpendicular bisectors or tangents perpendicular to radii at stepped radius points.
  • Two intersecting circles have exactly two common tangents, both direct; two touching circles have three common tangents in total.

Solved Exercises

Q: Q1(i). The measure of the external angle of a regular hexagon is

Options: (a) π/(3) (b) π/(4) (c) π/(6) (d) none of these

Correct answer: π/(3)

Q: Q1(ii). Tangents drawn at the end points of the diameter of circle are

Options: (a) parallel (b) perpendicular (c) intersecting (d) none of these

Correct answer: parallel

Q: Q1(iii). How many tangents can be drawn from a point outside the circle?

Options: (a) 1 (b) 2 (c) 3 (d) 4

Correct answer: 2

Q: Q1(iv). If the distance between the centers of two circles is equal to the sum of their radii, then the circles will

Options: (a) intersect (b) do not intersect (c) touch each other externally (d) touch each other internally

Correct answer: touch each other externally

Q: Q2. Practically find the centre of an arc ABC.

Ans: Given: An arc ABC (part of the circumference of a circle), with A, B and C points on the arc.
Required: To find, by construction, the centre of the circle to which the arc ABC belongs.
Diagram: Arc ABC, chords AB and BC drawn, the perpendicular bisectors of AB and BC meeting at O inside the region of the arc; O is the centre.
Steps of Construction:
(i) On the given arc, mark the three points A, B and C as given.
(ii) Join A to B, drawing chord AB.
(iii) Join B to C, drawing chord BC.
(iv) Draw the perpendicular bisector of AB.
(v) Draw the perpendicular bisector of BC.
(vi) Mark the intersection of the two perpendicular bisectors as O.
Justification: The perpendicular bisector of any chord of a circle passes through the centre of the circle; two such bisectors therefore meet at the centre.
Hence the centre O of the arc ABC is found.

Q: Q3. Escribe a circle opposite to vertex A of a triangle ABC with sides |AB| = 5cm, |BC| = 4cm, |CA| = 3cm. Find its radius also.

Ans: Given: Triangle ABC with |AB| = 5 cm, |BC| = 4 cm and |CA| = 3 cm; the escribed circle opposite vertex A touches side BC externally.
Required: To construct the triangle, escribe the circle opposite to vertex A, and find the radius of that escribed circle.
Diagram: Triangle ABC with BC = 4 cm, CA = 3 cm and AB = 5 cm, AB and AC produced beyond B and C, the escribed circle with centre O touching BC and the two produced sides, with OF perpendicular to BC and OF = 3 cm.
Steps of Construction:
(i) Draw a line segment BC = 4 cm.
(ii) With B as centre and radius 5 cm, draw an arc above BC.
(iii) With C as centre and radius 3 cm, draw another arc cutting the first arc at A.
(iv) Join A to B.
(v) Join A to C. Triangle ABC is formed.
(vi) Produce AB beyond B.
(vii) Produce AC beyond C.
(viii) Draw the bisector of the exterior angle at B.
(ix) Draw the bisector of the exterior angle at C.
(x) Mark the intersection of the two exterior bisectors as O.
Justification: O lies on the bisectors of the exterior angles at B and C, so it is equidistant from BC and the extensions of AB and AC, and the circle centred at O with that distance as radius touches all three lines; the exradius formula (area)/(s - a) gives its radius.
Hence the escribed circle opposite to vertex A is constructed, and its radius is 3 cm.

Q: Q4. Circumscribe a circle about an equilateral triangle ABC with each side of length 5cm.

Ans: Given: An equilateral triangle ABC with each side of length 5 cm.
Required: To construct the equilateral triangle and circumscribe a circle about it.
Diagram: Equilateral triangle ABC with all sides 5 cm, the perpendicular bisectors of its sides meeting at O, and a circle with centre O passing through A, B and C.
Steps of Construction:
(i) Draw a line segment BC = 5 cm.
(ii) With B as centre and radius 5 cm, draw an arc above BC.
(iii) With C as centre and radius 5 cm, draw another arc cutting the first arc at A.
(iv) Join A to B.
(v) Join A to C. Equilateral triangle ABC is formed.
(vi) Draw the perpendicular bisector of BC.
(vii) Draw the perpendicular bisector of CA.
(viii) Mark the intersection of the two perpendicular bisectors as O.
(ix) With O as centre and radius OA, draw a circle passing through A, B and C.
Justification: O is equidistant from A, B and C because it lies on the perpendicular bisectors of the sides, so the circle centred at O with radius OA passes through all three vertices.
Hence the circle is circumscribed about the equilateral triangle ABC of side 5 cm.

Q: Q5. Circumscribe a regular hexagon about a circle of radius 4cm.

Ans: Given: A circle of radius 4 cm.
Required: To circumscribe a regular hexagon about the circle.
Diagram: Circle with centre O and radius 4 cm, six points on the circumference obtained by stepping off the 4 cm radius, and tangents at those six points meeting to form the circumscribed regular hexagon.
Steps of Construction:
(i) With O as centre and radius 4 cm, draw a circle.
(ii) Take any point A on the circumference.
(iii) With A as centre and radius 4 cm, draw arcs cutting the circumference at the neighbouring points.
(iv) Continue stepping the radius 4 cm around the circumference until six points A, B, C, D, E and F are marked in order.
(v) At A, draw a line perpendicular to OA.
(vi) At B, C, D, E and F, draw lines perpendicular to OB, OC, OD, OE and OF respectively.
(vii) Mark the intersections of these six tangent lines in order; they form the required hexagon.
Justification: Each line is perpendicular to a radius at its point of contact, hence a tangent, and the six points of contact divide the circle into six equal arcs of 60°, so the six tangents form a regular hexagon.
Hence the regular hexagon is circumscribed about the circle of radius 4 cm.

Q: Q6. Construct a circle of radius 3 cm. Draw two tangents making an angle of 60° with each other.

Ans: Given: A circle of radius 3 cm is to be constructed, and the two tangents are to be inclined to each other at 60°.
Required: To construct the circle and draw two tangents to it meeting each other at an angle of 60°.
Diagram: Circle with centre O and radius 3 cm, diameter AB, point D on the circle with ∠BOD congruent to the given angle 60°, tangents at D and at A meeting at H, with the angle at H equal to 60° as constructed in the book's method (section 13.3.3).
Steps of Construction:
(i) With O as centre and radius 3 cm, draw a circle.
(ii) Draw any diameter AB of the circle.
(iii) At O, construct angle ∠BOD congruent to 60°, where D is on the circumference.
(iv) At D, draw a line perpendicular to OD.
(v) At A, draw a line perpendicular to OA.
(vi) Mark the intersection of the two perpendicular lines as H.
(vii) The two lines through H touching the circle at D and A are the required tangents.
Justification: A line perpendicular to a radius at its end point is a tangent to the circle; the construction of section 13.3.3 places the two points of contact so that the two tangents meet at the given angle.
Hence the circle of radius 3 cm is constructed and the two tangents making an angle of 60° with each other are drawn.

Q: Q7. Draw two equal circles each of radius 3.5cm. If the distance between their centres is 7cm, then draw their transverse tangents.

Ans: Given: Two equal circles each of radius 3.5 cm, with distance between their centres 7 cm. Note that 7 cm = 3.5 cm + 3.5 cm, so the two circles touch each other externally at the midpoint of the line of centres.
Required: To draw the transverse tangents to the two equal circles.
Diagram: Two circles of radius 3.5 cm with centres O and P, OP = 7 cm, touching at C, the midpoint of OP; the transverse tangents are the lines through the touching region constructed by the equal-circles method, crossing OP at C.
Steps of Construction:
(i) Draw a line segment OP = 7 cm.
(ii) With O as centre and radius 3.5 cm, draw the first circle.
(iii) With P as centre and radius 3.5 cm, draw the second circle; it touches the first circle at the midpoint C of OP.
(iv) Bisect OP at C.
(v) Bisect CP at D.
(vi) With D as centre and radius DP, draw a semicircle on CP, cutting the circle with centre P at E.
(vii) Join E to P.
(viii) Through O, draw OF parallel to EP, meeting the first circle at F on the opposite side of OP from E.
(ix) Join E to F and produce the line in both directions; this is one transverse tangent.
(x) Repeat steps (v) to (viii) on the other side of OP to draw the second transverse tangent.
Justification: This is the book's construction for a transverse common tangent to two equal circles; the resulting line is perpendicular to the radii at its points of contact on the two circles and crosses the line of centres between them, so it is a transverse tangent. Because the circles touch at C, both transverse tangents pass through the point of contact C.
Hence the transverse tangents to the two equal circles of radius 3.5 cm with centres 7 cm apart are drawn.

Q: Q8. Draw two common tangents to two intersecting circles of radii 2.5cm and 3.5cm.

Ans: Given: Two intersecting circles of radii 2.5 cm and 3.5 cm (their centres are taken less than 2.5 + 3.5 = 6 cm apart and more than 3.5 - 2.5 = 1 cm apart, so the circles intersect at two points; two intersecting circles have exactly two common tangents, both direct).
Required: To draw the two common tangents to the two intersecting circles.
Diagram: Larger circle with centre O and radius 3.5 cm and smaller circle with centre P and radius 2.5 cm intersecting at two points, with a direct common tangent touching the larger circle at M and the smaller at N, and the second such tangent on the other side of OP.
Steps of Construction:
(i) Draw a line segment OP of a length for which the circles intersect, for example 5 cm.
(ii) With O as centre and radius 3.5 cm, draw the larger circle.
(iii) With P as centre and radius 2.5 cm, draw the smaller circle; the two circles intersect at two points.
(iv) Bisect OP at Q.
(v) With Q as centre and radius QP, draw a semicircle on OP.
(vi) On OP, mark the point T given by the book's direct-tangent construction, so that the auxiliary radius is 3.5 cm - 2.5 cm = 1 cm.
(vii) With O as centre and radius 1 cm, draw an arc cutting the semicircle at L.
(viii) Join O to L and produce it to meet the larger circle at M.
(ix) Through P, draw PN parallel to OM, meeting the smaller circle at N on the same side.
(x) Join M to N and produce the line to both sides; this is the first common tangent.
Justification: Two intersecting circles have no transverse common tangent, because such a line would have to cross the overlapping region; their only common tangents are the two direct ones, and the construction gives lines perpendicular to the radii at M and N on the same side, hence tangent to both circles.
Hence the two common tangents to the two intersecting circles of radii 2.5 cm and 3.5 cm are drawn.
Note: the book does not give the distance between the centres for this question; a distance of 5 cm, for which the circles of radii 2.5 cm and 3.5 cm do intersect, has been used.

Q: Q9. Draw two common tangents to two touching circle of radii 3 cm and 4cm.

Ans: Given: Two touching circles of radii 3 cm and 4 cm; touching externally, their centres are 3 cm + 4 cm = 7 cm apart.
Required: To draw two common tangents to the two touching circles (the two direct common tangents are drawn; a third common tangent exists at the point of contact).
Diagram: Larger circle with centre O and radius 4 cm, smaller circle with centre P and radius 3 cm, OP = 7 cm, the circles touching at one point on OP, and two direct common tangents, one on each side of OP, touching the circles at M and N.
Steps of Construction:
(i) Draw a line segment OP = 7 cm.
(ii) With O as centre and radius 4 cm, draw the larger circle.
(iii) With P as centre and radius 3 cm, draw the smaller circle; it touches the larger circle at the point on OP between O and P.
(iv) Bisect OP at Q.
(v) With Q as centre and radius QP, draw a semicircle on OP.
(vi) On OP, mark the point T given by the book's direct-tangent construction, so that the auxiliary radius is 4 cm - 3 cm = 1 cm.
(vii) With O as centre and radius 1 cm, draw an arc cutting the semicircle at L.
(viii) Join O to L and produce it to meet the larger circle at M.
(ix) Through P, draw PN parallel to OM, meeting the smaller circle at N on the same side.
(x) Join M to N and produce the line to both sides; this is the first common tangent.
Justification: The construction is the direct common tangent construction for two unequal circles, giving lines perpendicular to the radii at their points of contact on the same side of OP, hence tangent to both circles; for touching circles these are two of the three common tangents, the third being the tangent at the point of contact.
Hence the two common tangents to the two touching circles of radii 3 cm and 4 cm are drawn.

mcqs.q: The measure of the external angle of a regular hexagon is
mcqs.why: External angle = 360 degrees / 6 = 60 degrees. In radians, 60 degrees = pi/3. The book key is correct; the original 'none of these' option was replaced.

mcqs.q: Tangents drawn at the end points of the diameter of circle are
mcqs.why: Each tangent is perpendicular to the same diameter line at its endpoint, so the two tangents are both perpendicular to one line and are therefore parallel. Book key correct; 'none of these' replaced.

mcqs.q: How many tangents can be drawn from a point outside the circle?
mcqs.why: From an external point exactly two tangents can be drawn to a circle, one touching on each side. The book key is correct.

mcqs.q: If the distance between the centers of two circles is equal to the sum of their radii, then the circles will
mcqs.why: Distance between centres = r1 + r2 means the circles meet at exactly one point on the line of centres, on the outside of each other: they touch externally. Book key correct.

mcqs.q: How is the centre of a given arc ABC found by construction?
options: By intersecting the perpendicular bisectors of chords AB and BC
By drawing a tangent at B
mcqs.why: The perpendicular bisector of any chord passes through the centre. The bisectors of chords AB and BC therefore intersect at the centre O of the arc.

mcqs.q: Triangle ABC has sides AB = 5 cm, BC = 4 cm and CA = 3 cm. What is the radius of the escribed circle opposite vertex A?
mcqs.why: The triangle is right-angled with area 6 cm squared and s = 6 cm. Exradius opposite A = area / (s - a) = 6 / (6 - 4) = 6/2 = 3 cm.

mcqs.q: To circumscribe a regular hexagon about a circle of radius 4 cm, the six points of contact are obtained by doing what?
options: Stepping the 4 cm radius around the circumference
mcqs.why: Stepping the radius 4 cm around the circumference marks six points dividing it into six equal 60 degree arcs. Tangents perpendicular to the radii at those points form the hexagon.

mcqs.q: Two equal circles of radius 3.5 cm have centres 7 cm apart. How do the circles relate, and where do their transverse tangents cross the line of centres?
options: They are separate; tangents cross outside
They touch externally at the midpoint; transverse tangents pass through the touching point
mcqs.why: 7 cm = 3.5 + 3.5, so the circles touch externally at the midpoint C of the line of centres. For touching equal circles both transverse tangents pass through that point of contact C.

mcqs.q: Two intersecting circles of radii 2.5 cm and 3.5 cm have how many common tangents, and of what type?
options: Four: two direct and two transverse
mcqs.why: Intersecting circles have no transverse common tangent, because it would cross the overlapping region. Their only common tangents are the two direct ones.

mcqs.q: To draw two tangents to a circle of radius 3 cm making an angle of 60° with each other, each tangent line is drawn how?
options: Perpendicular to a radius at its endpoint on the circle
mcqs.why: A line perpendicular to a radius at its endpoint on the circumference is a tangent to the circle. The construction places two such perpendiculars so the tangents meet at 60 degrees.
